ED:061.title: Read physics from the Maxwell capacitance matrix
ED:061.objective: Derive symmetry, gauge nullspace, sign structure, and energy positivity for a complete conductor capacitance matrix.
ED:061.statement:
Let $N$ conductor boundary components enclose a connected dielectric region, and include the enclosing reference conductor in the list rather than silently fixing it as ground. No conductor potential is fixed a priori. Define $Q_i=\sum_jC_{ij}V_j$. Use reciprocity to prove $C_{ij}=C_{ji}$. Use invariance under the simultaneous shift $V_j\mapsto V_j+V_0$ to derive the row sums. Explain why $C_{ii}>0$ and $C_{ij}\le0$ for $i\ne j$, and show
$$U=\frac12\mathbf V^TC\mathbf V\ge0.$$
Why is this complete all-boundary matrix singular, and how does choosing one conductor as the voltage reference produce a nonsingular reduced matrix?
permittedResults: The electrostatic field energy is nonnegative and reciprocity is available.

acceptableStrategies.description: Excite one conductor at a time for reciprocity and signs, use the included reference conductor to make a common potential shift a genuine gauge transformation, and identify the quadratic energy with field energy.

milestones.criterion: Uses reciprocity to establish matrix symmetry.
Derives the zero row sums and common-voltage nullspace using the explicitly included reference conductor, and obtains the physical entry signs from controlled excitations.
Connects the quadratic form to field energy and explains reference reduction.

commonErrors.description: Claims every row sums to a positive self-capacitance.
commonErrors.consequence: Gauge invariance under common voltage shifts is violated.

commonErrors.description: Calls the complete matrix positive definite.
commonErrors.consequence: Its unavoidable common-voltage null vector is ignored.

hintTree.content: A unit excitation of conductor $j$ defines column $j$.
A common voltage produces no electric field and no charge.
Off-diagonal charge induced on grounded conductors opposes the excited conductor.

ED:061.canonicalSolution:
Applying reciprocity to unit-voltage excitations of conductors $i$ and $j$ gives $C_{ij}=C_{ji}$. Because the enclosing reference conductor is included and no external potential has been fixed, a common shift of every listed conductor potential produces no electric field and no charge. Hence
$$\boxed{\sum_jC_{ij}=0},$$
and $C\mathbf1=0$. With only conductor $i$ positive relative to all the others, it carries positive charge, so $C_{ii}>0$, while the other grounded conductors acquire nonpositive induced charges, so $C_{ij}\le0$ for $i\ne j$. Finally,
$$\frac12\mathbf V^TC\mathbf V=\frac12\sum_iQ_iV_i=\frac{\epsilon_0}{2}\int|\mathbf E|^2d\tau\ge0.$$
The common-voltage vector is a null vector, making the complete all-boundary matrix singular. Fixing one conductor voltage and deleting its row and column removes that gauge degree and yields the usual positive-definite reduced matrix for a connected finite geometry. By contrast, a matrix listing only finite conductors while holding spatial infinity at zero is already reference-fixed; it is generally nonsingular and its row sums need not vanish.

Each diagonal entry $C_{ii}$ is a positive self-capacitance, so I conclude that the sum of row $i$ is $C_{ii}>0$. A simultaneous shift of all conductor voltages therefore changes the listed conductor charges.

ED:062.title: Assemble a three-shell capacitance matrix from two gaps
ED:062.objective: Compute conductor charges and energy for three concentric spherical shells by treating adjacent dielectric gaps as coupled capacitors.
ED:062.statement:
Three thin concentric conducting shells have radii $a<b<c$ and potentials $V_a,V_b,V_c$. Assume zero exterior field outside $c$. Define
$$C_1=4\pi\epsilon_0\frac{ab}{b-a},\qquad C_2=4\pi\epsilon_0\frac{bc}{c-b}.$$
Derive $Q_a,Q_b,Q_c$, write the full $3\times3$ capacitance matrix, and verify symmetry, row sums, total charge, and energy. Evaluate the charges when $(V_a,V_b,V_c)=(V_0,0,0)$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Write each gap charge as capacitance times its voltage difference, assign equal opposite charges to its two faces, then sum the two contributions on the middle shell.

milestones.criterion: Assigns equal-opposite gap charges and sums the middle-shell contributions.
Builds the exact symmetric matrix and verifies its row sums and total charge.
Obtains the voltage-difference energy and requested excitation charges.

commonErrors.description: Sets $Q_b=C_2(V_b-V_c)$ and omits the inner-gap face.
commonErrors.consequence: Charge conservation and the matrix middle diagonal fail.

commonErrors.description: Writes energy using absolute potentials rather than gap differences.
commonErrors.consequence: A common voltage shift incorrectly changes the energy.

hintTree.content: The middle shell receives one contribution from each gap.
Zero exterior field makes the three total charges sum to zero.

The charges are
$$\boxed{Q_a=C_1(V_a-V_b)},$$
$$\boxed{Q_b=C_1(V_b-V_a)+C_2(V_b-V_c)},$$
$$\boxed{Q_c=C_2(V_c-V_b)}.$$
Thus
$$C=\begin{pmatrix}C_1&-C_1&0\\-C_1&C_1+C_2&-C_2\\0&-C_2&C_2\end{pmatrix}.$$
It is symmetric, each row sums to zero, and $Q_a+Q_b+Q_c=0$. The energy is
$$U=\frac12C_1(V_a-V_b)^2+\frac12C_2(V_b-V_c)^2.$$
For $(V_0,0,0)$, $(Q_a,Q_b,Q_c)=(C_1V_0,-C_1V_0,0)$.

$$\boxed{Q_b=C_1(V_b-V_a)+C_2(V_b-V_c)},$$
$$\boxed{Q_c=C_2(V_c-V_b)}.$$
Thus
$$C=\begin{pmatrix}C_1&-C_1&0\\-C_1&C_1+C_2&-C_2\\0&-C_2&C_2\end{pmatrix}.$$

ED:063.title: A linear coaxial trial potential bounds the capacitance from above
ED:063.objective: Apply the Dirichlet principle to a nonharmonic trial function and interpret the resulting fixed-voltage energy bound correctly.
ED:063.statement:
A coaxial capacitor has radii $a<b$, length $L$, and fixed boundary values $V(a)=V_0$, $V(b)=0$. The exact capacitance per length is $C/L=2\pi\epsilon_0/\ln(b/a)$. Use the admissible trial potential
$$V_t(s)=V_0\frac{b-s}{b-a}$$
to compute $U_t/L=(\epsilon_0/2)\int_a^b|V_t'|^2\,2\pi s\,ds$. By the Dirichlet principle, the harmonic solution minimizes this fixed-boundary energy. Derive the resulting capacitance bound and verify it for $b=2a$.

The exact capacitance is supplied for comparison.

acceptableStrategies.description: Compute the trial gradient and cylindrical measure exactly, translate the energy inequality at fixed voltage into a capacitance inequality, and check its direction numerically.

milestones.criterion: Evaluates the trial field energy with the cylindrical measure.
Converts the minimizing-energy statement into the correct fixed-voltage capacitance bound.
Checks the inequality numerically at $b=2a$.

commonErrors.description: Interprets minimum fixed-voltage energy as an upper bound on the exact energy.
commonErrors.consequence: The capacitance inequality is reversed.

commonErrors.description: Uses planar measure $ds$ instead of $2\pi s\,ds$.
commonErrors.consequence: The estimate has wrong geometry and dimensions.

hintTree.content: Integrate $s$ from $a$ to $b$.
A larger trial energy at the same $V_0$ means a larger trial capacitance estimate.

ED:063.canonicalSolution:
The trial energy is
$$\frac{U_t}{L}=\frac{\epsilon_0}{2}\frac{V_0^2}{(b-a)^2}2\pi\int_a^b s\,ds =\frac{\pi\epsilon_0V_0^2(b+a)}{2(b-a)}.$$
Therefore
$$\boxed{\frac{C}{L}\le\frac{C_t}{L}=\frac{2U_t/L}{V_0^2} =\pi\epsilon_0\frac{b+a}{b-a}}.$$
For $b=2a$, the trial bound is $3\pi\epsilon_0$, while the exact value is $2\pi\epsilon_0/\ln2\approx2.885\pi\epsilon_0$, so the direction is correct. The bound is on capacitance because voltage, not charge, is fixed.

$$\boxed{\frac{C}{L}\le\frac{C_t}{L}=\frac{2U_t/L}{V_0^2} =\pi\epsilon_0\frac{b+a}{b-a}}.$$

ED:065.title: Mixed boundary data are unique when a Dirichlet piece is present
ED:065.objective: Extend the energy uniqueness proof to disjoint Dirichlet and Neumann boundary portions and identify the pure-Neumann exception.
ED:065.statement: Let $\partial\Omega=\Gamma_D\cup\Gamma_N$ with disjoint pieces. Two Poisson solutions have the same $V$ on $\Gamma_D$ and the same $\partial_nV$ on $\Gamma_N$. Prove uniqueness if $\Gamma_D$ contains a nonempty open boundary piece. Explain why the proof leaves an additive constant when $\Gamma_D$ is empty. Apply the result to the rectangle in ED047.
permittedResults: Green's first identity may be used for the harmonic difference.

acceptableStrategies.description: Apply the energy identity to the difference and split the boundary integral according to which factor vanishes on each piece.

milestones.criterion: Forms the harmonic difference and partitions the boundary term correctly.

commonErrors.consequence: The mixed proof is incorrectly declared impossible.

commonErrors.description: Claims a nonempty Neumann piece fixes the additive constant.
commonErrors.consequence: Normal derivatives are unchanged by constants.

hintTree.content: On $\Gamma_D$, the difference $u$ is zero.
On $\Gamma_N$, its normal derivative is zero.

ED:065.canonicalSolution:
The difference $u$ is harmonic. Green's identity gives
$$\int_\Omega|\nabla u|^2d\tau=\oint_{\Gamma_D}u\partial_nu\,da+ \oint_{\Gamma_N}u\partial_nu\,da.$$
The first integral vanishes because $u=0$ on $\Gamma_D$ and the second because $\partial_nu=0$ on $\Gamma_N$. Thus $\nabla u=0$, so $u$ is constant. A nonempty Dirichlet piece forces that constant to zero. If $\Gamma_D$ is empty, the constant survives, subject also to Neumann compatibility. In ED047, the three Dirichlet sides form a nonempty set and the bottom is Neumann, so the separated solution is unique.

ED:067.title: Perturb the field of a nearly spherical conductor without moving its voltage

A conductor held at fixed voltage $V_0$ has surface
$$r_s(\theta)=a[1+\eta P_2(\cos\theta)],\qquad |\eta|\ll1,$$
and $V\to0$ at infinity. Starting from the spherical solution $V^{(0)}=V_0a/r$, write $V=V^{(0)}+\eta V^{(1)}+O(\eta^2)$. Taylor-expand the boundary condition at $r=a$ to determine $V^{(1)}$, then find the exterior potential and surface charge density through first order. Finally integrate the charge over the deformed surface and decide whether the capacitance changes at order $\eta$.

Use the normal from the conductor into vacuum and retain all first-order effects from evaluating the field and area at $r=r_s$.

$\int P_2(\cos\theta)d\Omega=0$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Expand the fixed-potential condition on the reference sphere, continue the resulting quadrupole boundary value outward, and separately expand the radial field and surface measure.

milestones.criterion: Linearizes the displaced equipotential and obtains the correct exterior quadrupole amplitude.
Expands the normal field at the displaced surface with the correct sign and coefficient.
Includes the area change, integrates the charge, and correctly identifies the absent first-order capacitance shift.

commonErrors.description: Imposes $V^{(1)}(a)=0$ because the conductor voltage is fixed.
commonErrors.consequence: The displacement of the zeroth-order potential is omitted and the deformed surface is not equipotential.

commonErrors.description: Integrates the perturbed density using the undeformed area and treats the $P_2$ term as a nonzero mean.
commonErrors.consequence: A spurious first-order capacitance change is reported.

Expanding $V(r_s,\theta)=V_0$ gives
$$V^{(1)}(a,\theta)+aP_2\partial_r\left(\frac{V_0a}{r}\right)_{r=a}=0,$$
so $V^{(1)}(a,\theta)=V_0P_2(\cos\theta)$. The unique decaying continuation is therefore
$$\boxed{V=V_0\left[\frac ar+\eta\left(\frac ar\right)^3P_2(\cos\theta)\right]+O(\eta^2)}.$$

$$E_n=\frac{V_0}{a}[1-2\eta P_2+3\eta P_2]+O(\eta^2) =\frac{V_0}{a}[1+\eta P_2]+O(\eta^2).$$

$$\boxed{\sigma(\theta)=\frac{\epsilon_0V_0}{a}[1+\eta P_2(\cos\theta)]+O(\eta^2)}.$$
Using $da=a^2(1+2\eta P_2)d\Omega$ and the zero angular mean of $P_2$,
$$Q=\int\sigma da=4\pi\epsilon_0aV_0+O(\eta^2).$$
Thus $C=Q/V_0=4\pi\epsilon_0a+O(\eta^2)$: the quadrupolar deformation redistributes charge locally but does not change capacitance at first order.

ED:068.title: Trap a finite two-conductor capacitance between dual trial fields
ED:068.objective: Combine the Dirichlet and Thomson principles into certified upper and lower bounds with consistent units.
ED:068.statement:
An inner finite conductor is surrounded by a finite grounded outer conductor in a homogeneous dielectric of permittivity $\epsilon$. Let $C$ be their capacitance. A dimensionless trial potential $u_t$ equals $1$ on the inner conductor and $0$ on the outer conductor. A normalized flux field $\mathbf d_t$, with units $\mathrm{m^{-2}}$, is divergence-free in the dielectric, has zero normal component on any insulating symmetry boundary, and carries dimensionless outward flux $1$ from the inner conductor to the outer. ED:069.objective: Construct the canonical grounded-sphere image solution, derive induced charge and force, and test planar and far-field limits.
ED:069.statement:
A grounded conducting sphere of radius $a$ is centered at the origin. A point charge $q$ lies on the positive $z$ axis at $z=d>a$. Construct the Kelvin image charge and its location, prove the resulting exterior potential vanishes on $r=a$, and compute: (i) the total induced charge, (ii) the surface charge density as a function of polar angle, (iii) the physical interaction energy, and (iv) the force on $q$.

For points on $r=a$, the distances to axial points at $d$ and $a^2/d$ differ by the factor $d/a$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Choose the inverted source so the two Coulomb terms cancel pointwise on the sphere, then derive charge, energy, and force from distinct physical rules rather than differentiating a moving image naively.

milestones.criterion: Constructs the inverted image and verifies the boundary value pointwise.
Derives the induced total and surface charge with correct sign and dimensions.
Uses the one-half factor only in energy, obtains the exact force, and verifies both near-plane and far-field limits.

commonErrors.consequence: The potential does not cancel at every point of the spherical boundary and the induced total charge is wrong.

commonErrors.description: Applies the energy one-half factor to the force from the image.
commonErrors.consequence: The physical force is incorrectly smaller by a factor of two.

ED:069.canonicalSolution:
The image is
$$\boxed{q'=-\frac{a}{d}q,\qquad d'=\frac{a^2}{d}}.$$
Thus, in the exterior region,
$$V=k_e\left[\frac q{|\mathbf r-d\hat z|}+\frac{q'}{|\mathbf r-d'\hat z|}\right].$$
On $r=a$, the distance ratio is $|\mathbf r-d\hat z|=(d/a)|\mathbf r-d'\hat z|$, so the two terms cancel. At large $r$, the conductor contributes the image monopole; hence
$$\boxed{Q_{\rm ind}=q'=-\frac{qa}{d}}.$$
Normal differentiation on the sphere gives
$$\boxed{\sigma(\theta)=-\frac{q}{4\pi a}\frac{d^2-a^2}{(d^2+a^2-2ad\cos\theta)^{3/2}}}.$$
The physical energy and force are
$$\boxed{U=\frac12k_e\frac{qq'}{d-d'}=-\frac{k_eq^2a}{2(d^2-a^2)}},$$
$$\boxed{\mathbf F=-\frac{k_eq^2ad}{(d^2-a^2)^2}\hat z}.$$

ED:070.title: Close a rational-angle wedge image group and sum its energy
ED:070.objective: Build the finite image orbit for a grounded wedge of angle $\pi/N$ and evaluate a nontrivial $N=3$ energy.
ED:070.statement:
A point charge $q$ lies at cylindrical coordinates $(\rho,\phi_0,z=0)$ inside the grounded wedge $0<\phi<\alpha$, where $\alpha=\pi/N$ and $N$ is an integer at least $2$. Construct the full finite image system using rotations and reflections, prove that it grounds both faces, and count the images.

Then set $N=3$. Derive an exact expression for the physical interaction energy for general $0<\phi_0<\pi/3$, and simplify it on the bisector $\phi_0=\pi/6$. State why the energy, rather than $qV_{\rm image}$, contains a factor of one-half.
permittedResults: Two points at the same radius $\rho$ and angular separation $\Delta\phi$ are separated by $2\rho|\sin(\Delta\phi/2)|$.
Grounded image energy is $qV_{\rm image}/2$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Generate an even rotational orbit of positive charges and its reflected negative orbit, pair contributions on each face, then use chord lengths to sum the $N=3$ image potential.

milestones.criterion: Constructs the two finite charge orbits, counts $2N-1$ images, and proves both boundary cancellations.
Uses chord distances and the physical one-half factor to obtain the general $N=3$ energy.

commonErrors.description: Stops after a single reflection in each wedge face.
commonErrors.consequence: Repeated reflections fail to close and one boundary is regrounded only at the expense of the other.

commonErrors.description: Includes the real $+q$ member in $V_{\rm image}$ or omits the physical one-half factor.
commonErrors.consequence: The energy is divergent or double-counted.

hintTree.content: Use $+q$ at $\phi_0+2k\alpha$ and $-q$ at $-\phi_0+2k\alpha$ for $k=0,\ldots,N-1$.

For $N=3$, the two positive images are each a distance $\sqrt3\rho$ away.

ED:070.canonicalSolution:
Take the $2N$-charge orbit
$$+q:\ \phi=\phi_0+2k\alpha,\qquad -q:\ \phi=-\phi_0+2k\alpha, \qquad k=0,\ldots,N-1.$$
The $k=0$ positive member is the real charge, leaving $2N-1$ images. Reflection pairs have equal distance and opposite sign on $\phi=0$; after a rotation-index shift the same is true on $\phi=\alpha$. Thus both wedge faces are grounded.

For $N=3$, the two positive images contribute $2/(\sqrt3\rho)$ to $V_{\rm image}/(k_eq)$. The three negative images have distances $2\rho|\sin(k\pi/3-\phi_0)|$. Therefore
$$\boxed{U(\phi_0)=\frac{k_eq^2}{4\rho}\left[\frac4{\sqrt3}- \sum_{k=0}^2\frac1{|\sin(k\pi/3-\phi_0)|}\right]}.$$
On the bisector the three cosecant magnitudes are $2,2,1$, so
$$\boxed{U(\pi/6)=\frac{k_eq^2}{4\rho}\left(\frac4{\sqrt3}-5\right)}.$$
The factor $1/2$ accounts for the gradual work required to build the induced conductor charge; the image potential itself already gives the full physical force field at the real charge.

ED:071.title: Separate eccentric cylinders in a bipolar coordinate strip
ED:071.objective: Use bipolar coordinates to derive the capacitance of nested nonconcentric cylinders and recover both concentric and near-contact limits.
ED:071.statement:
An infinite conducting cylinder of radius $a$ is held at $V_0$ inside a grounded cylinder of radius $b>a$. Their axes are parallel and their center separation is $c$, where $0\le c<b-a$. In bipolar coordinates $(\tau,\sigma)$ the two circular boundaries are $\tau=\tau_1$ and $\tau=\tau_2$, with $\Delta\tau=\tau_1-\tau_2>0$, and the common scale factor is
$$h_\tau=h_\sigma=\frac{s}{\cosh\tau-\cos\sigma}.$$
You may use the geometric relation
$$\cosh\Delta\tau=\frac{b^2+a^2-c^2}{2ab}.$$
Find the potential, integrate the inner-cylinder charge per unit length, and derive $C/L$. Check the limits $c\to0$ and $c\to(b-a)^-$, including the physical direction of the capacitance change.
permittedResults: The bipolar-coordinate scale factor and circle-separation relation are supplied.
$\operatorname{arcosh}[(x+x^{-1})/2]=|\ln x|$ for $x>0$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Solve the strip problem linearly in $\tau$, use cancellation of the metric factor in $E_n dl$, and translate the strip width into physical radii and offset only at the end.

milestones.criterion: Constructs the affine bipolar-coordinate potential and invokes uniqueness.
Integrates the surface charge with the two metric factors correctly canceled.
Obtains the eccentric capacitance formula and verifies both concentric and near-contact limits.

commonErrors.description: Leaves an uncanceled scale factor in the charge integral.
commonErrors.consequence: The result depends spuriously on $\sigma$ and does not reduce to a simple strip width.

commonErrors.description: Uses $b^2+a^2+c^2$ in the arcosh argument.
commonErrors.consequence: The predicted capacitance decreases and remains finite at internal tangency.

hintTree.content: The boundary values make $V$ affine in $\tau$.
On the inner boundary, $|E_n|=V_0/(h_\tau\Delta\tau)$ and $dl=h_\sigma d\sigma$.

ED:071.canonicalSolution:
The unique harmonic strip solution is
$$\boxed{V(\tau)=V_0\frac{\tau-\tau_2}{\Delta\tau}}.$$
The field points from the inner conductor into the dielectric. Because the two scale factors agree,
$$\frac QL=\int_0^{2\pi}\epsilon\frac{V_0}{h_\tau\Delta\tau}h_\sigma d\sigma =\frac{2\pi\epsilon V_0}{\Delta\tau}.$$
Therefore
$$\boxed{\frac CL=\frac{2\pi\epsilon}{\operatorname{arcosh}\!\left[(b^2+a^2-c^2)/(2ab)\right]}}.$$
When $c=0$, the arcosh is $\ln(b/a)$ and the familiar coaxial result $C/L=2\pi\epsilon/\ln(b/a)$ is recovered. As $c\to(b-a)^-$, the arcosh argument approaches $1^+$, so $\Delta\tau\to0$ and $C/L\to\infty$. The narrowing local gap strengthens charge storage at fixed voltage, so the increasing capacitance has the correct physical direction.

ED:073.title: Reconstruct a three-conductor Maxwell matrix and expose its gauge mode
ED:073.objective: Recover a capacitance matrix from voltage experiments, prove its positive-semidefinite energy form, and compute a gauge-invariant test case.
ED:073.statement:
Three isolated conductors form a closed electrostatic system. Charges and voltages obey $\mathbf Q=C\mathbf V$, where the Maxwell capacitance matrix is symmetric and every row sum is zero. Two one-volt experiments produce
$$\mathbf V^{(1)}=(1,0,0),\quad \mathbf Q^{(1)}=(3,-2,-1)\ \mathrm{nC},$$
$$\mathbf V^{(2)}=(0,1,0),\quad \mathbf Q^{(2)}=(-2,5,-3)\ \mathrm{nC}.$$
Reconstruct the full matrix in nanofarads. Express $\tfrac12\mathbf V^TC\mathbf V$ as a sum of nonnegative pair-voltage terms and identify the complete nullspace. For $\mathbf V=(4,-1,2)\,\mathrm V$, find all charges and the energy. Finally add $6\,\mathrm V$ to every conductor and verify what changes.
permittedResults: Reciprocity makes $C$ symmetric, and a uniform voltage shift leaves all charges unchanged in a closed system.

milestones.criterion: Reconstructs every matrix entry from the two columns, symmetry, and row-sum constraint.

commonErrors.description: Treats the experimental charge vectors as rows while ignoring reciprocity.
commonErrors.consequence: The reconstructed matrix is asymmetric or conflicts with the measured second experiment.

commonErrors.description: Declares the full matrix positive definite.
commonErrors.consequence: The unavoidable uniform-voltage gauge null vector is missed.

hintTree.content: The experimental charge vectors are columns of $C$.

when voltages are in volts. This is nonnegative. It vanishes only when $V_1=V_2=V_3$, so the nullspace is exactly the uniform gauge vector $\operatorname{span}\{(1,1,1)\}$.

ED:074.title: Differentiate Dirichlet energy into Maxwell boundary pressure
ED:074.objective: Derive the first shape variation of electrostatic field energy and verify its sign on a movable parallel plate.
ED:074.statement:
A charge-free dielectric region $\Omega$ has permittivity $\epsilon$ and electrostatic potential $V$ with fixed constant values on its conducting boundary components. Let a smooth conducting boundary piece $\Gamma$ move by normal displacement $\xi(\mathbf x)$ along the unit normal $\mathbf n$ pointing outward from the dielectric region. Denote the Eulerian shape derivative of the potential at fixed reference coordinates by $\dot V$; this is distinct from the material derivative following a moving boundary point.

Show that fixed boundary voltage implies $\dot V=-\xi\partial_nV$ on $\Gamma$, and derive the Hadamard variation
$$\delta U_{\rm field}=-\frac\epsilon2\int_\Gamma(\partial_nV)^2\xi\,da.$$
Interpret the result as Maxwell pressure. Check the sign and magnitude for parallel plates of area $A$, separation $d$, and voltage difference $V_0$ when the upper plate moves by $\delta d>0$. State the smooth-boundary assumptions under which the derivation is valid.

The unperturbed and material-derivative potentials are harmonic in the charge-free region.

acceptableStrategies.description: Differentiate both the boundary condition and the volume energy, integrate the cross term by parts, and combine it with the moving-domain term before interpreting signs.

milestones.criterion: Differentiates the moving fixed-potential boundary to obtain the correct Eulerian shape-derivative boundary data.

commonErrors.description: Sets $\dot V=0$ on the reference boundary because the conductor voltage is fixed.
commonErrors.consequence: The geometric change of the boundary condition is omitted and the shape derivative has the wrong coefficient.

commonErrors.description: Reports pressure $\epsilon E_n^2$ without the one-half or directs it out of the dielectric.
commonErrors.consequence: The result disagrees with the parallel-plate energy derivative and force direction.

hintTree.content: Differentiate $V(\mathbf x+\xi\mathbf n)=V_{\rm conductor}$.

ED:074.canonicalSolution:
Differentiating the fixed boundary value along the moving surface yields
$$\boxed{\dot V+\xi\partial_nV=0\quad\text{on }\Gamma}.$$
For $U_{\rm field}=\frac\epsilon2\int_\Omega|\nabla V|^2d\tau$, the transport and field variations give
$$\delta U_{\rm field}=\epsilon\int_\Omega\nabla V\cdot\nabla\dot Vd\tau +\frac\epsilon2\int_\Gamma|\nabla V|^2\xi da.$$
Integration by parts removes the volume term because $\nabla^2V=0$, leaving $\epsilon\int_\Gamma\dot V\partial_nVda$. Substitution of the boundary derivative and use of zero tangential field give
$$\boxed{\delta U_{\rm field}=-\frac\epsilon2\int_\Gamma(\partial_nV)^2\xi da}.$$
Thus the Maxwell pressure magnitude is $p=\epsilon E_n^2/2$, and the traction on the conductor is $-p\mathbf n$: it points into the dielectric.

For parallel plates, $U_{\rm field}=\epsilon AV_0^2/(2d)$, so
$$\delta U_{\rm field}=-\frac{\epsilon AV_0^2}{2d^2}\delta d=-pA\delta d,$$
with $p=\epsilon V_0^2/(2d^2)$. The upper plate is pulled downward, opposite its positive displacement. The derivation assumes a smooth displacement, a smooth equipotential surface, no edge or corner singular contribution, and no topology change.

ED:075.title: Optimize a two-parameter Rayleigh-Ritz capacitance bound
ED:075.objective: Minimize a coupled trial-energy quadratic, prove the stationary point is global, and combine it with a dual flux bound.
ED:075.statement:
A long two-conductor capacitor has a square grounded outer shield and a centered diamond-shaped inner conductor at voltage $V_0$. A boundary-conforming finite-element interpolation on one symmetry cell has been assembled as
$$u_t=g+\alpha f_1+\beta f_2,$$
where $u_t=1$ on the inner conductor and $u_t=0$ on the shield for every $\alpha,\beta$. After exact cell integration and symmetry restoration, its Dirichlet functional is
$$\frac{C_t/L}{\epsilon}=J(\alpha,\beta) =5+4\alpha^2+6\beta^2+2\alpha\beta-4\alpha+2\beta.$$
Find the optimal parameters and the certified upper bound on $C/L$. Prove the stationary point is the unique global minimizer, compare it with the best one-parameter restriction $\beta=0$, and combine it with an independently admissible normalized-flux trial giving $C/L\ge3.40\epsilon$. commonErrors.description: Treats a trial potential as a lower bound on capacitance.
commonErrors.consequence: The final variational bracket is reversed.

The normal equations give

$$J_{\min}=\frac{1909}{529}=3.60869\ldots,$$

$$\boxed{\frac CL\le\frac{1909}{529}\epsilon\approx3.609\epsilon}.$$

$$\boxed{3.40\epsilon\le\frac CL\le3.609\epsilon}.$$

ED:077.title: Build a mixed-boundary Green function and reconcile its corners and energy
ED:077.objective: Construct a Dirichlet-Neumann Green series, derive the full representation formula, and connect corner compatibility to the energy identity.
ED:077.statement:
Let $\Omega=(0,L)\times(0,H)$. Impose Dirichlet data on $x=0$, $x=L$, and $y=H$, and outward-normal Neumann data on $y=0$. For the homogeneous mixed Green function use
$$\nabla^2G(\mathbf r,\mathbf r')=-\delta(\mathbf r-\mathbf r'),$$
with $G=0$ on the Dirichlet pieces and $\partial_nG=0$ on the bottom.

Then derive the representation of a Poisson solution $-\epsilon\nabla^2V=\rho$ with Dirichlet value $f$ and bottom flux $g=\partial_nV$. State the classical corner compatibility conditions at the two bottom corners. Finally derive the energy identity and specialize it to homogeneous boundary data to prove uniqueness and positivity.
permittedResults: Green's second identity and orthogonality of sine and cosine eigenfunctions may be used.
$\int_0^L\sin^2(n\pi x/L)dx=L/2$ and $\int_0^H\cos^2((m+1/2)\pi y/H)dy=H/2$.

Obtains the energy identity and uses homogeneous data to prove uniqueness and positivity.

commonErrors.consequence: The Green function solves a different boundary-value problem.

commonErrors.description: Drops the Neumann boundary term from the representation because $\partial_nG=0$ there.
commonErrors.consequence: The factor that vanishes is confused with $G$, so prescribed bottom flux has no effect.

hintTree.content: Use $\sin(n\pi x/L)\cos(\mu_my)$ with $\mu_m=(m+1/2)\pi/H$.

$$\boxed{G(\mathbf r,\mathbf r')=\frac4{LH}\sum_{n=1}^\infty\sum_{m=0}^\infty \frac{\sin(k_nx)\sin(k_nx')\cos(\mu_my)\cos(\mu_my')} {k_n^2+\mu_m^2}}.$$
It has the required zero values and zero bottom normal derivative; applying $-\nabla^2$ produces the mixed delta expansion. Every term is symmetric under $\mathbf r\leftrightarrow\mathbf r'$, so $G$ is symmetric.

Green's identity gives
$$\boxed{V(\mathbf r)=\frac1\epsilon\int_\Omega G\rho\,dA' -\int_{\Gamma_D}f\,\partial_{n'}G\,ds' +\int_{y'=0}Gg\,dx'}.$$
If the side data are $f_L(y)$ and $f_R(y)$, classical $C^1$ compatibility at the bottom corners requires
$$\boxed{g(0)=-f_L'(0),\qquad g(L)=-f_R'(0)}.$$
Failure need not destroy a weak solution, but it produces a corner singularity and prevents the claimed classical regularity.

The same identity gives nonnegative field energy $U=(1/2)\int\rho V$ for homogeneous data.

ED:078.title: Renormalize an infinite image group into a finite self-energy

$$\boxed{F_s=+\frac12\mathbf V^TC_1\mathbf V=17\ \mathrm{\mu N}},$$

$$\frac{dW_{\rm batt}}{ds}=\mathbf V^TC_1\mathbf V=\boxed{34\ \mathrm{nJ/mm}}.$$

ED:080.title: Solve a multiply connected capacitor by modulus, reciprocity, and uniqueness
ED:080.objective: Combine conformal invariance, harmonic measure, reciprocity, and an energy proof in a doubly connected electrostatic domain.
ED:080.statement:
A long two-dimensional capacitor has a doubly connected dielectric cross-section $\Omega$ with inner conductor $A$ and outer conductor $B$. A known conformal map $w=f(z)$ sends $\Omega$ onto the annulus
$$1<|w|<R,\qquad R>1,$$
with $A$ mapped to $|w|=1$ and $B$ to $|w|=R$. First hold $A$ at $V_0$ and ground $B$. Find the potential in physical coordinates and derive $C/L$ by either charge integration or conformal invariance of Dirichlet energy.

Next ground both conductors and place a line charge of density $\lambda$ at $z_0\in\Omega$. Use a separate unit-voltage weighting problem and Green reciprocity to find the total induced charges on $A$ and $B$ without constructing the sourced Green function. Prove uniqueness even though the domain is multiply connected. Analyze the limits $z_0$ approaching either boundary, $R\downarrow1$ at fixed conformal fraction $t=\ln|f(z_0)|/\ln R$, and $R\to\infty$ with $|f(z_0)|$ fixed.
permittedResults: Two-dimensional Laplace equations and Dirichlet energy are conformally invariant.
Green reciprocity may be applied between the sourced grounded state and a source-free unit-voltage weighting state.

acceptableStrategies.description: Solve the annulus once to obtain its harmonic measure, reuse that function as the reciprocity weight, and close every result with an energy uniqueness argument and degeneration limits.

milestones.criterion: Pulls back the annular potential and derives capacitance from the conformal modulus.
Uses the harmonic measure in a distinct reciprocity experiment to partition both induced charges.
Proves multiply connected Dirichlet uniqueness and correctly evaluates all boundary and modulus limits.

commonErrors.description: Assumes multiply connectedness introduces an arbitrary additive harmonic function even with both boundary potentials fixed.
commonErrors.consequence: A nonexistent nonuniqueness is added despite the energy identity.

commonErrors.description: Assigns $Q_A/L=-\lambda[1-\omega_A(z_0)]$.
commonErrors.consequence: A charge approaching the inner conductor is incorrectly predicted to induce its charge on the remote outer boundary.

hintTree.content: The inner-conductor harmonic measure is $\omega_A(z)=\ln[R/|f(z)|]/\ln R$.
Reciprocity gives $Q_A/L=-\lambda\omega_A(z_0)$.
The two induced charges must sum to $-\lambda$.

ED:080.canonicalSolution:
The annular Dirichlet solution pulls back to
$$\boxed{V(z)=V_0\frac{\ln[R/|f(z)|]}{\ln R}}.$$
On either circular image boundary, integrating $\epsilon E_n$ gives
$$\boxed{\frac CL=\frac{2\pi\epsilon}{\ln R}}.$$
This also follows because $\int|\nabla V|^2dA$ is unchanged by the conformal map.

Define the harmonic measure
$$\omega_A(z)=\frac{\ln[R/|f(z)|]}{\ln R},$$
equal to one on $A$ and zero on $B$. Apply reciprocity between the grounded state containing $\lambda$ and the source-free state with weighting voltage $\omega_A$. The volume-source term is $\lambda\omega_A(z_0)$ per length, while the conductor term is the grounded-state charge $Q_A/L$. Hence
$$\boxed{\frac{Q_A}{L}=-\lambda\omega_A(z_0)},\qquad \boxed{\frac{Q_B}{L}=-\lambda[1-\omega_A(z_0)]}.$$
The second result follows either from the complementary weight or total induced charge $-\lambda$.

If two scalar potentials have the same Dirichlet data, their difference $u$ is harmonic and zero on both boundary components. Green's first identity gives $\int_\Omega|\nabla u|^2dA=0$, so $u=0$. Multiply connectedness permits harmonic vector fields with circulation only if one abandons a single-valued electrostatic potential; it does not spoil this Dirichlet uniqueness.

As $z_0\to A$, $\omega_A\to1$ and $Q_A/L\to-\lambda$; as $z_0\to B$, the outer conductor receives all induced charge. If $R\downarrow1$ with $t=\ln|f(z_0)|/\ln R$ fixed, then $C/L\to\infty$ and $(Q_A,Q_B)/L\to[-\lambda(1-t),-\lambda t]$. If $R\to\infty$ with $|f(z_0)|$ fixed, $C/L\to0$ logarithmically while $\omega_A\to1$, so the receding outer boundary carries a vanishing share of the induced charge.

ED:084.title: A polarized sphere has a measurable dipole moment
ED:084.objective: Relate a uniform polarization to its total dipole moment and evaluate a far-axis field numerically.
ED:084.statement: A sphere of radius $2.00\,\mathrm{cm}$ is uniformly polarized with $P_0=3.00\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm{C/m^2}$ along $+z$. Find its electric dipole moment. acceptableStrategies.description: Form the dipole moment from polarization times volume before inserting any numbers. Convert all lengths to SI units, apply the axial far-field expression, and use the radius-to-distance ratio to audit the approximation.

Computes $E_z=14.5\,\mathrm{V/m}$ with the correct direction.

ED:087.title: A free sheet fixes the normal jump of D
ED:087.objective: Apply the oriented displacement boundary condition and distinguish it from tangential electric-field continuity.
ED:087.statement: Linear isotropic media 1 and 2, with permittivities $\epsilon_1$ and $\epsilon_2$, meet at a plane with unit normal $\hat{\mathbf n}$ pointing from 1 to 2. A free surface charge density $\sigma_f$ lies on the interface. Derive the electrostatic conditions for the normal component of $\mathbf D$ and the tangential component of $\mathbf E$. Then evaluate $D_{2n}$ when $D_{1n}=2.00\,\mu\mathrm{C/m^2}$ and $\sigma_f=-0.500\,\mu\mathrm{C/m^2}$. Finally, explain why the normal component of $\mathbf E$ may be discontinuous and derive the jump in tangential $\mathbf D$ from the common tangential field.
permittedResults: $\nabla\cdot\mathbf D=\rho_f$
$\nabla\times\mathbf E=\mathbf0$ in electrostatics

acceptableStrategies.description: Derive the normal displacement jump with an oriented pillbox and the tangential electric condition with a shrinking loop. Apply the signed numerical sheet charge only after those vector conventions are fixed.

milestones.criterion: Derives both oriented interface conditions.
Computes $D_{2n}=1.50\,\mu\mathrm{C/m^2}$.
Explains the possible normal-$\mathbf E$ discontinuity and derives the tangential-$\mathbf D$ jump in linear isotropic media.

commonErrors.description: Sets the normal D components equal despite nonzero free charge.
commonErrors.consequence: The pillbox flux fails to account for its enclosed free sheet.

commonErrors.description: Applies tangential continuity to D.
commonErrors.consequence: A constitutive field is substituted for the curl-free electric field.

hintTree.content: Keep the pillbox normal aligned with the declared direction from medium 1 to medium 2.
The loop law constrains tangential $\mathbf E$, not tangential $\mathbf D$.
Add the signed free density to the side-1 normal component.

ED:087.canonicalSolution: A thin pillbox gives $(\mathbf D_2-\mathbf D_1)\cdot\hat{\mathbf n}=\sigma_f$. A thin rectangular loop and $\nabla\times\mathbf E=0$ give $\hat{\mathbf n}\times(\mathbf E_2-\mathbf E_1)=\mathbf0$. Thus $D_{2n}=D_{1n}+\sigma_f=1.50\,\mu\mathrm{C/m^2}$. The normal component of $\mathbf E$ need not be continuous because the permittivities may differ. For linear isotropic media, the common tangential field $\mathbf E_t$ gives $\mathbf D_{2t}-\mathbf D_{1t}=(\epsilon_2-\epsilon_1)\mathbf E_t$, so tangential $\mathbf D$ is generally discontinuous unless the permittivities are equal or $\mathbf E_t=\mathbf0$.

The normal component of $\mathbf E$ need not be continuous because the permittivities may differ. For linear isotropic media, the common tangential field $\mathbf E_t$ gives $\mathbf D_{2t}-\mathbf D_{1t}=(\epsilon_2-\epsilon_1)\mathbf E_t$, so tangential $\mathbf D$ is generally discontinuous unless the permittivities are equal or $\mathbf E_t=\mathbf0$.

The normal component of $\mathbf D$ is continuous across every dielectric interface, even with a free sheet, so $D_{2n}=D_{1n}=2.00\,\mu\mathrm{C/m^2}$. The tangential electric field remains continuous by the electrostatic loop law.

ED:088.title: Two dielectrics in series share D, not E
ED:088.objective: Solve a layered parallel-plate capacitor from free-charge boundary data and compute voltage and capacitance.
ED:088.statement: A parallel-plate capacitor of area $A$ contains dielectric 1 of thickness $d_1$ and permittivity $\epsilon_1$ and dielectric 2 of thickness $d_2$ and permittivity $\epsilon_2$, stacked normal to the plates. The plates carry free charges $\pm Q$ and fringing is neglected. Find $\mathbf D$, the field in each layer, the voltage magnitude, and the capacitance. Check the equal-permittivity limit.
permittedResults: $\mathbf D=\epsilon\mathbf E$
$V=\int\mathbf E\cdot d\boldsymbol\ell$

acceptableStrategies.description: Use the electrode free charge to establish one common normal displacement through the stack. Translate it into two fields, add their voltage drops, and invert the result for the series capacitance.

milestones.criterion: Finds common $D=Q/A$ and both electric fields.
Adds the layer voltage drops with correct dimensions.
Obtains $C=A/(d_1/\epsilon_1+d_2/\epsilon_2)$ and checks an equal-material limit.

commonErrors.description: Assumes the electric field is the same in both layers.
commonErrors.consequence: The normal displacement condition is confused with electric-field continuity.

commonErrors.description: Adds layer capacitances directly.
commonErrors.consequence: Stacking along the field direction is a series, not parallel, geometry.

hintTree.content: Use the plate free charge to set $D_n=Q/A$.
Convert the same displacement into a different electric field in each medium.
Add the two potential drops before taking the ratio Q over V.

ED:088.canonicalSolution: There is no free charge at the internal interface, so the normal displacement is constant: $D=Q/A$. Each field is $E_i=D/\epsilon_i=Q/(A\epsilon_i)$. The voltage is $V=E_1d_1+E_2d_2=(Q/A)(d_1/\epsilon_1+d_2/\epsilon_2)$. Hence $C=Q/V=A/(d_1/\epsilon_1+d_2/\epsilon_2)$. The result is the series combination of the two layer capacitances and reduces to $\epsilon A/(d_1+d_2)$ when the permittivities are equal.

graderFixtures.proofText: There is no free charge at the internal interface, so the normal displacement is constant: $D=Q/A$. Each field is $E_i=D/\epsilon_i=Q/(A\epsilon_i)$. The voltage is $V=E_1d_1+E_2d_2=(Q/A)(d_1/\epsilon_1+d_2/\epsilon_2)$. Hence $C=Q/V=A/(d_1/\epsilon_1+d_2/\epsilon_2)$. The result is the series combination of the two layer capacitances and reduces to $\epsilon A/(d_1+d_2)$ when the permittivities are equal.

Electric-field continuity makes $E_1=E_2$ even when $\epsilon_1\ne\epsilon_2$, so the same field must be used for both layer voltage drops. This equality is the interface condition that determines the two layer fields.

ED:093.title: Match a dielectric sphere to a uniform applied field
ED:093.objective: Determine the scalar potentials and induced dipole of a dielectric sphere by enforcing electrostatic interface conditions.
ED:093.statement: A sphere of radius $R$ and permittivity $\epsilon$ sits in vacuum in an applied field $E_0\hat{\mathbf z}$. Assume $V_{\rm in}=-Ar\cos\theta$ and $V_{\rm out}=-E_0r\cos\theta+B\cos\theta/r^2$. Determine $A$ and $B$, then identify the induced dipole moment. Check the equal-permittivity and conducting-sphere limits.
permittedResults: Continuity of electrostatic potential
Continuity of normal D when free surface charge is absent

acceptableStrategies.description: Match the two scalar potentials at the sphere first, then differentiate with the radial sign intact and impose normal displacement continuity. Read the dipole moment from the exterior inverse-square coefficient and test material-matching limits.

milestones.criterion: Derives the two independent boundary equations.
Solves for A and B without a sign or permittivity swap.
Extracts the induced dipole and checks equal-material and large-permittivity limits.

commonErrors.description: Matches normal E instead of normal D.
commonErrors.consequence: The dielectric discontinuity is erased and the coefficients are wrong.

commonErrors.description: Differentiates the inverse-square potential term with the wrong sign.
commonErrors.consequence: The radial boundary equation and induced dipole fail the vacuum limit.

hintTree.content: Evaluate both potentials at $r=R$ before differentiating.
Use $E_r=-\partial V/\partial r$ with the sign intact.

Since a dipole potential is $p\cos\theta/(4\pi\epsilon_0r^2)$, the induced moment is $\mathbf p=4\pi\epsilon_0R^3(\epsilon-\epsilon_0)\mathbf E_0/(\epsilon+2\epsilon_0)$. Equal permittivities give no dipole, and large permittivity gives the conducting-sphere exterior coefficient.

ED:099.objective: Use the electrostatic stress tensor to compute traction on a conductor and recover the capacitor pressure.

ED:100.title: Charging work selects the one-half factor
ED:100.objective: Derive linear-dielectric field energy by quasistatic charging and distinguish it from an arbitrary nonlinear constitutive law.
ED:100.statement: A linear dielectric region is charged quasistatically from zero field to final fields $\mathbf E$ and $\mathbf D=\epsilon\mathbf E$. In a nonlinear dielectric, E is not proportional to D, so the area under the constitutive curve is generally not half the final rectangle. Hysteresis would add path dependence and dissipation, outside the assumed reversible model.

ED:103.title: The Clausius-Mossotti pole marks model failure
ED:103.objective: Analyze the apparent constitutive pole and identify which microscopic assumptions fail before treating it as a material prediction.
ED:103.statement: Let $x=N\alpha/(3\epsilon_0)$ in the Clausius-Mossotti formula $\kappa=(1+2x)/(1-x)$. Analyze the limits $x\to0$, $x\to1^-$, and $x>1$. Explain why the pole is not by itself a controlled prediction of infinite static permittivity for an ordinary molecular dielectric.

Near the pole the assumed noninteracting linear polarizabilities and Lorentz continuum local field are no longer perturbative. Correlations, lattice structure, saturation, phase transitions, dispersion, and loss can dominate. Thus the pole diagnoses an instability or breakdown of the model; it does not license extrapolating the dilute formula as a complete material law.

ED:107.title: A graded dielectric hides bound volume charge in its profile
ED:107.objective: Solve a one-dimensional graded capacitor and derive its capacitance and induced bound charge density.
ED:107.statement: Between plates at $z=0$ and $z=d$, a linear dielectric has $\epsilon(z)=\epsilon_0(1+\alpha z/d)$ with $\alpha>0$. There is no free volume charge. For voltage magnitude $V$, find $D$, $E(z)$, the capacitance per area, and the bound volume charge density. Show how the bound surface charge compensates the volume bound charge.

$\rho_b=-dP_z/dz$

acceptableStrategies.description: With no free volume charge, keep normal displacement constant while the graded permittivity makes electric field vary. Use the voltage integral to determine that constant, and differentiate polarization to expose the bound volume density.

ED:107.canonicalSolution: The free-charge form of Gauss's law gives constant normal $D$. Thus $E(z)=D/[\epsilon_0(1+\alpha z/d)]$ and $C/A=D/V=\epsilon_0\alpha/[d\ln(1+\alpha)]$. Since $P(z)=D-\epsilon_0E(z)=D[1-1/(1+\alpha z/d)]$, one obtains $\rho_b=-dP/dz=-D(\alpha/d)/(1+\alpha z/d)^2$. At $z=0$, $P(0)=0$ and the dielectric outward normal is $-\hat{\mathbf z}$, so $\sigma_b(0)=0$. At $z=d$, the outward normal is $+\hat{\mathbf z}$ and $\sigma_b(d)=P(d)=D\alpha/(1+\alpha)$. Meanwhile $\int_0^d\rho_b\,dz=-[P(d)-P(0)]=-D\alpha/(1+\alpha)$, so the volume and surface bound charges cancel exactly per unit area.

An unknown free sheet may lie at their interface, and the fields point along $+z$. Measurements give lower-electrode free charge density $\sigma_0=(6.00\times10^3\,\mathrm{V/m})\epsilon_0$, voltage drop $V=7.00\,\mathrm V$, and stored energy per area $W_A=(2.90\times10^4\,\mathrm{V^2/m})\epsilon_0$. (b) Find the buried free sheet charge, the bound charge on all four material faces, and the free charge on both electrodes. The measured value therefore gives $5.80\times10^4=1.80\times10^4+(4.00\,\mathrm V)(D_2/\epsilon_0)$ in $\mathrm{V^2/m}$ units, so $D_2=(1.00\times10^4\,\mathrm{V/m})\epsilon_0$. Layer 1 has polarization $P_1=(3.00\times10^3\,\mathrm{V/m})\epsilon_0$, giving bound charge densities $-P_1$ at the lower face and $+P_1$ at the interface. Layer 2 has $P_2=(8.00\times10^3\,\mathrm{V/m})\epsilon_0$, giving $-P_2$ at the interface and $+P_2$ at the upper face. Thus the net interface bound charge density is $-5.00\times10^3\epsilon_0\,\mathrm{V/m}$ and its total free-plus-bound charge density is $-1.00\times10^3\epsilon_0\,\mathrm{V/m}=\epsilon_0(E_2-E_1)$. The upper electrode carries $-D_2$, so the electrode and buried free charges sum to $D_1+(D_2-D_1)-D_2=0$; the four bound faces also sum to zero. The right-hand rule makes all four contributions point along $+\hat{\mathbf z}$, hence $\mathbf B(0)=\mu_0I\sqrt{a^2+b^2}\,\hat{\mathbf z}/(\pi ab)$. For a square, $a=b$, this becomes $\mathbf B(0)=\sqrt2\mu_0I\hat{\mathbf z}/(\pi a)$. If $a\gg b$, the horizontal sides give the leading term $\mu_0I/(\pi b)$, while the vertical-pair contribution is smaller by order $b^2/a^2$.

The reason is not a failure of midpoint-circle symmetry: an isolated open segment is not a divergence-free steady-current source because charge would accumulate at its endpoints. In a physical closed circuit, Ampere's law applies to the total field, $\oint_C\mathbf B_{\rm total}\cdot d\boldsymbol\ell=\mu_0I_{\rm enc}$. The return path supplies the rest of the source and generally destroys the rotational symmetry of the total field on $C$, so the circulation alone does not determine the field pointwise. ED:142.canonicalSolution: The demagnetizing field of a uniformly magnetized sphere is $\mathbf H_{\rm in}=-\mathbf M/3$. Therefore $\mathbf B_{\rm in}=\mu_0(\mathbf H+\mathbf M)=2\mu_0\mathbf M/3$. Outside the sphere, $\mathbf M=\mathbf0$, and the field is exactly the dipole field of this moment for the uniform-sphere solution. The nonzero $\mathbf H$ is produced by the finite body's pole-equivalent boundary data even though free current is absent.

ED:144.title: Hysteresis is not a single-valued constitutive relation
ED:144.objective: Explain why a global single-valued relation $\mathbf B(\mathbf H)$ fails for a hysteretic ferromagnet and identify the additional state information required.
ED:144.statement: A solver models a ferromagnetic core by a single-valued relation $\mathbf B=\mathbf B(\mathbf H)$ and predicts the same $\mathbf B$ whenever $\mathbf H$ returns to a previous value. Explain why this can fail under cyclic drive. Distinguish differential permeability, remanence, coercivity, and hysteretic loss, and state when a single-valued approximation is defensible.
permittedResults: Work per volume over a magnetic cycle is represented by the appropriate constitutive loop integral

acceptableStrategies.description: Treat magnetization as a history-dependent branch variable rather than a function of instantaneous field alone. Locate remanence and coercivity on the loop, then connect its oriented area with dissipated energy per cycle.

Correctly distinguishes slope, intercept, reversal scale, and loop loss.

commonErrors.description: Calls the differential permeability $B/H$ everywhere.
commonErrors.consequence: A local branch slope is confused with a secant ratio and history dependence disappears.

commonErrors.description: Treats remanence as free current remaining in the coil.
commonErrors.consequence: Material magnetization memory is assigned to the external circuit source.

hintTree.content: Ask whether the material state is determined by instantaneous $\mathbf H$ alone.

ED:144.canonicalSolution: A ferromagnet can retain domain-state memory, so $B$ depends on the drive history as well as the instantaneous $H$. Differential permeability is the local slope $dB/dH$ along a specified branch, not a global ratio. Remanence is nonzero $B$ after $H$ returns to zero, coercivity is the reverse $H$ needed to bring $B$ or $M$ through zero under a declared convention, and the loop area is energy dissipated per volume per cycle. A single-valued law is defensible for a specified reversible small-signal regime, an anhysteretic model, or a path restricted to one calibrated branch. It cannot predict branch switching or loss without internal state variables and evolution rules.

A single-valued law is defensible for a specified reversible small-signal regime, an anhysteretic model, or a path restricted to one calibrated branch. ED:145.objective: Compute the distributed bound current of a radially graded axial magnetization and determine its surface current.

commonErrors.consequence: The bound-current circulation direction is reversed.

commonErrors.description: Creates a surface current from the nonzero interior derivative.

ED:145.canonicalSolution: For an axial function of $r$, $(\nabla\times\mathbf M)_\phi=-dM_z/dr$. Here $dM_z/dr=-2M_0r/a^2$, so $\mathbf J_b=(2M_0r/a^2)\hat{\boldsymbol\phi}$. At the curved surface, $\mathbf K_b=\mathbf M(a)\times\hat{\mathbf r}=\mathbf0$ because $\mathbf M(a)=0$. A derivative discontinuity changes the volume-current profile but does not create a delta-function surface current unless $\mathbf M$ has a finite tangential jump. The positive azimuthal direction follows $\hat{\mathbf z}\times\hat{\mathbf r}=\hat{\boldsymbol\phi}$.

ED:153.title: Virtual work changes sign when the source constraint changes
ED:153.objective: Derive electromechanical force from inductance at fixed current and reconcile it with fixed-flux energy.
ED:153.statement: A single-coil actuator has inductance $L(x)$ that increases with insertion coordinate $x$. Derive the quasistatic force at fixed current $I$ using magnetic coenergy. Then hold the flux linkage $\lambda$ fixed and derive the force from stored energy. Show that the physical direction agrees when the correct independent variable is used.
permittedResults: $W=LI^2/2=\lambda^2/(2L)$ for a linear coil
Force from the appropriate energy or coenergy derivative

acceptableStrategies.description: Use magnetic coenergy when current is the controlled source variable and ordinary energy when flux linkage is controlled. Differentiate the appropriate potential at fixed control variable and reconcile the apparently opposite algebraic signs.

milestones.criterion: Derives the fixed-current coenergy force.
Derives the fixed-flux energy force with the correct minus sign.
Shows equality and explains the source-work sign trap.

commonErrors.description: Uses $-(\partial W/\partial x)_I$ without including source work.
commonErrors.consequence: The actuator is predicted to move toward lower inductance.

commonErrors.description: Replaces fixed $\lambda$ by $L$ times a fixed $I$ before differentiating.
commonErrors.consequence: The independent-variable constraint is changed mid-derivative.

hintTree.content: Choose current as the independent variable for coenergy.
Choose flux linkage as the independent variable for ordinary stored energy.
Substitute $\lambda=LI$ only after taking the specified derivative.

ED:153.canonicalSolution: For a linear coil, coenergy at fixed current is $W'(I,x)=L(x)I^2/2$, so $F_x=(\partial W'/\partial x)_I=I^2L'(x)/2$, toward larger inductance. At fixed flux linkage, the stored energy is $W(\lambda,x)=\lambda^2/[2L(x)]$. With no source work, $F_x=-(\partial W/\partial x)_\lambda=\lambda^2L'(x)/[2L(x)^2]$. Since $I=\lambda/L$, this is again $I^2L'(x)/2$. Using minus the fixed-current field-energy derivative without including source work would predict the wrong sign.

Since $I=\lambda/L$, this is again $I^2L'(x)/2$. Using minus the fixed-current field-energy derivative without including source work would predict the wrong sign.

ED:154.title: Inductance eigenmodes expose the lowest-energy current ratio
ED:154.objective: Diagonalize a coupled-coil energy form, optimize it under a current-norm constraint, and interpret signed mutual coupling without confusing a negative cross term with negative energy.

(a) Find the coupling coefficient and the two eigenvalues of the inductance matrix. (b) Subject to $I_1^2+I_2^2=5.00\,\mathrm{A^2}$, find the signed ratio $I_2/I_1$ for each extremizing mode, give one normalized current pair for each mode up to an overall sign, and compute the minimum and maximum stored energies. (c) Evaluate the energy at $(I_1,I_2)=(2.00,-1.00)\,\mathrm A$ and compare it with the true minimum. (d) Explain what changes, and what does not, if the reference direction of coil 2 is reversed.

$W=\mathbf I^{\mathsf T}\mathbf L\mathbf I/2$

milestones.criterion: Computes $k=0.500$ and both exact inductance eigenvalues.
Finds and normalizes the two extremizing current ratios under the stated constraint.
Compares the specified current pair with the true minimum and proves dot-reference invariance.

commonErrors.description: Extremizes the mutual term while ignoring both self-energy terms.
commonErrors.consequence: The proposed current ratio is not an eigenmode of the full quadratic form.

commonErrors.description: Reverses the coil-2 current coordinate without reversing signed M.
commonErrors.consequence: A change of dot convention is mistaken for a physical change in stored energy.

For either eigenvalue, use $I_2/I_1=(\lambda-L_1)/M$ before normalizing.
Reversing coil 2 changes both $I_2$ and signed M in the coordinate description.

ED:155.title: A solenoid plunger is pulled toward larger overlap
ED:155.objective: Derive a constant-force ideal magnetic actuator from overlap-dependent inductance and connect it to gap stress.
ED:155.statement: An ideal high-permeability plunger enters a long coil. Over a working range, its inductance is $L(x)=L_0+\alpha x$ with $\alpha>0$, and the current $I$ is held fixed. Find the force and the source-energy partition for a quasistatic displacement $dx$. Explain how this agrees with magnetic pressure pulling high-permeability material into a strong-field region, and state the limitations caused by saturation, leakage, and end fringing.
permittedResults: $F_x=(I^2/2)dL/dx$ at fixed current
$dW_{\rm source}=I\,d\lambda$

acceptableStrategies.description: Differentiate the overlap-dependent inductance at fixed current to obtain the mechanical force. Balance source work, changing field energy, and motion so the direction toward larger overlap is not inferred from Lenz's law alone.

milestones.criterion: Derives $F_x=\alpha I^2/2$ and its inward direction.
Computes the two-to-one source work and its equal field/mechanical split.
Connects the inductance gradient to magnetic stress and states the real-device limitations.

commonErrors.description: Uses $F_x=I^2dL/dx$.
commonErrors.consequence: The coenergy one-half factor is omitted and mechanical work is doubled.

commonErrors.description: Says all source work becomes mechanical work.
commonErrors.consequence: The simultaneous increase in stored field energy is ignored.

hintTree.content: Differentiate the linear inductance with current held fixed.
Compare the source work with $d(LI^2/2)$.
Relate the sign of $dL/dx$ to the reduction in magnetic reluctance.

ED:155.canonicalSolution: Fixed-current coenergy gives $F_x=(1/2)I^2dL/dx=\alpha I^2/2$, constant and directed toward increasing overlap. The field energy changes by $dW=(1/2)I^2dL=F_x\,dx$. The source changes the flux linkage by $d\lambda=I\,dL$, so it supplies $I\,d\lambda=I^2dL=2F_x\,dx$. Half becomes increased field energy and half becomes mechanical work. The direction agrees with Maxwell stress: replacing part of a high-reluctance gap by high-permeability material increases $L$ and pulls the plunger inward. Saturation, leakage, and end fringing make the real $L(x)$ nonlinear.

ED:156.title: A field jump fixes current but not magnetic loading
ED:156.objective: Invert two-sided magnetic data for a surface current, reconcile Lorentz and stress-tensor loads, and expose the common-mode null space of the local inverse problem.
ED:156.statement: In vacuum, a planar sheet at $z=0$ has measured fields $\mathbf B_+=B_+\hat{\mathbf x}+B_n\hat{\mathbf z}$ above and $\mathbf B_-=B_-\hat{\mathbf x}+B_n\hat{\mathbf z}$ below, with normal $+\hat{\mathbf z}$. (a) Reconstruct the surface current. (b) Compute its force per area both as $\mathbf K\times\mathbf B_{\rm avg}$ and as the upper-minus-lower jump in Maxwell traction. (c) Add the same uniform field $\mathbf C=C_t\hat{\mathbf x}+C_n\hat{\mathbf z}$ to both measured sides. Prove that this common mode leaves the reconstructed current unchanged, find the change in load, and explain why the load changes. (d) Identify the additional global boundary, circulation, or flux data needed to distinguish the two physical configurations, and explain why a jump-only inverse problem cannot predict stress.
permittedResults: Vacuum magnetic boundary condition
Vacuum Maxwell stress tensor
$\mathbf f/A=\mathbf K\times\mathbf B_{\rm avg}$ for an ideal sheet

acceptableStrategies.description: Separate measured data into jump and mean components before calculating force. Use the jump for surface current, the mean for Lorentz loading, reproduce both components from traction, and perturb only the mean to expose the inverse null space.

milestones.criterion: Reconstructs the signed surface current from jump data and separates jump from mean field.
Derives both load components by Lorentz force and independently by the Maxwell-traction jump.
Computes the common-mode load shift and identifies the global circulation or flux information missing from a jump-only inverse.

commonErrors.description: Uses one side's total field instead of the side average in the sheet Lorentz force.
commonErrors.consequence: The self-field is included asymmetrically, so the stress comparison and common-mode decomposition both fail.

commonErrors.description: Concludes that an unchanged field jump implies unchanged force.
commonErrors.consequence: The mean field that couples to the reconstructed current is discarded even though local boundary data do not fix it.

hintTree.content: The boundary law depends on $\mathbf B_+-\mathbf B_-$, whereas the sheet force depends on their arithmetic mean.
For each side, evaluate $\mathbf T\cdot\hat{\mathbf z}$ before taking the upper-minus-lower difference.
Under the common-mode addition, compute $\mathbf K\times\mathbf C$ rather than repeating the entire stress algebra.

ED:156.canonicalSolution: The boundary law gives $\mathbf K=\hat{\mathbf z}\times(\mathbf B_+-\mathbf B_-)/\mu_0=[(B_+-B_-)/\mu_0]\hat{\mathbf y}$. With $\bar B_t=(B_++B_-)/2$, the average-field force is $\mathbf f/A=[(B_+-B_-)/\mu_0](B_n\hat{\mathbf x}-\bar B_t\hat{\mathbf z})$, equivalently $(B_+-B_-)B_n\hat{\mathbf x}/\mu_0-(B_+^2-B_-^2)\hat{\mathbf z}/(2\mu_0)$. Vacuum stress gives $\mathbf T\cdot\hat{\mathbf z}=[B_nB_t\hat{\mathbf x}+(B_n^2-B_t^2)\hat{\mathbf z}/2]/\mu_0$ on either side, and the upper-minus-lower traction reproduces the same two components. Adding $\mathbf C$ to both sides leaves their difference and therefore $\mathbf K$ invariant, but shifts the mean. The load changes by $\Delta(\mathbf f/A)=\mathbf K\times\mathbf C=[(B_+-B_-)/\mu_0](C_n\hat{\mathbf x}-C_t\hat{\mathbf z})$. Thus the local jump identifies the sheet source but not its mechanical loading. Remote boundary values, the tangential circulation around a noncontractible or enclosing contour, and the normal flux through a spanning surface can fix the common tangential and normal modes. Without such global data, two fields with identical local inverse-current evidence exert different stresses.

ED:158.title: Design an azimuthal current that confines an axial field
ED:158.objective: Invert a prescribed compact axial magnetic profile into volume and surface current and verify field confinement.
ED:158.statement: Design a cylindrically symmetric current distribution that produces $\mathbf B=B_0(1-r^2/a^2)^2\hat{\mathbf z}$ for $r<a$ and $\mathbf B=\mathbf0$ for $r\ge a$. Find the required volume current, determine whether a surface current is needed at $r=a$, and verify current continuity.

Cylindrical divergence formula

acceptableStrategies.description: Convert the prescribed axial field profile into azimuthal current with the relevant cylindrical curl component. Differentiate the taper, check regularity and boundary smoothness, and verify that the designed source confines the field without a hidden sheet.

The field and its first derivative both vanish at $r=a$, so tangential $\mathbf B$ is continuous to zero and no delta-function surface current is required. The azimuthal current is divergence free because it is independent of $\phi$ and has no radial or axial component. It also vanishes at the axis and boundary, forming closed current rings that confine the prescribed axial field.

ED:159.title: Optimize a magnetic gap before core saturation
ED:159.objective: Optimize an actuator air gap at a fixed current limit while enforcing core saturation, then quantify the active-constraint and gap-dominated regimes.
ED:159.statement: An ideal magnetic circuit has core length $\ell_c$, permeability $\mu_c$, cross-sectional area $A$, one adjustable air gap constrained by $g\ge g_{\min}>0$, and $N$ turns. The drive is limited to $I_{\max}$, and the design must satisfy $B\le B_{\rm sat}$ at that current. Neglect leakage and fringing. (a) Derive $B(g)$ and the attractive force at $I_{\max}$. (b) Choose the feasible gap that maximizes the force without exceeding saturation, giving a piecewise answer according to whether the saturation constraint is active above the manufacturing minimum. (c) Find the maximum force in each case and compute $d\ln F/d\ln g$ in the gap-dominated unsaturated regime. (d) Explain why the linear-core model cannot be extrapolated beyond the saturation constraint to claim additional force.
permittedResults: Ampere law along a magnetic circuit
Flux continuity in equal cross section
Vacuum gap pressure

acceptableStrategies.description: Express the common induction through the sum of core and gap magnetomotive drops at the fixed current ceiling. Since force decreases monotonically with gap, combine the saturation-derived lower bound with the positive manufacturing minimum and distinguish the saturation-limited and manufacturing-limited branches.

milestones.criterion: Derives the exact field and force at the current ceiling and converts saturation into a gap inequality.
Obtains the piecewise optimal gap and corresponding maximum force.
Finds logarithmic sensitivity minus two in the gap-dominated regime and rejects post-saturation extrapolation.

commonErrors.description: Chooses the largest gap satisfying the saturation constraint.
commonErrors.consequence: A feasible but strictly weaker force is selected because force decreases with gap.

commonErrors.description: Uses the active-saturation formula when its required gap lies below the manufacturing minimum.
commonErrors.consequence: The feasible unsaturated branch at $g_{\min}$ is omitted.

hintTree.content: At fixed current, maximizing force is equivalent to maximizing B.
Combine $B(I_{\max},g)\le B_{\rm sat}$ with the manufacturing lower bound on g.
When $g/\mu_0$ dominates the core term, use $F\propto g^{-2}$ for logarithmic sensitivity.

Saturation requires $g\ge g_{\rm sat}=\mu_0[NI_{\max}/B_{\rm sat}-\ell_c/\mu_c]$. Because $F$ decreases with $g$, $g_{\rm opt}=\max\{g_{\min},g_{\rm sat}\}$. If $g_{\rm sat}>g_{\min}$, saturation is active, $B=B_{\rm sat}$, and $F_{\max}=AB_{\rm sat}^2/(2\mu_0)$. If $g_{\rm sat}<g_{\min}$, the minimum manufacturable gap is strictly unsaturated and $F_{\max}=A[NI_{\max}/(\ell_c/\mu_c+g_{\min}/\mu_0)]^2/(2\mu_0)$. At the threshold $g_{\rm sat}=g_{\min}$, the constraints meet with $B=B_{\rm sat}$ and the two force formulas coincide. In the gap-dominated unsaturated regime, $B\simeq\mu_0NI_{\max}/g$ and $F\simeq A\mu_0N^2I_{\max}^2/(2g^2)$, so $d\ln F/d\ln g=-2$. Driving beyond $B_{\rm sat}$ invalidates constant $\mu_c$; the extrapolated quadratic force is not an admissible improvement.

ED:161.statement: An infinite sheet at $z=0$ in vacuum carries uniform surface charge $\sigma=+4.00\ \mathrm{nC\,m^{-2}}$. Let $\hat{\mathbf n}=\hat{\mathbf z}$ point from $z<0$ to $z>0$, with one-sided fields $\mathbf E_-$ and $\mathbf E_+$. The field is finite away from the sheet, and no external field is applied. (a) A thin Gaussian pillbox has top outward normal $+\hat{\mathbf n}$ and bottom outward normal $-\hat{\mathbf n}$. The side flux vanishes as the pillbox height tends to zero. The two flat faces give

$$\hat{\mathbf n}\cdot(\mathbf E_+-\mathbf E_-)=\frac{\sigma}{\epsilon_0}.$$
For the isolated sheet, write $\mathbf E_+=E_0\hat{\mathbf n}$ and $\mathbf E_-=-E_0\hat{\mathbf n}$. The jump condition gives $2E_0=\sigma/\epsilon_0$, hence
$$\mathbf E_+=\frac{\sigma}{2\epsilon_0}\hat{\mathbf z},\qquad \mathbf E_-=-\frac{\sigma}{2\epsilon_0}\hat{\mathbf z}.$$
Numerically,
$$E_0=\frac{4.00\times10^{-9}}{2(8.8541878128\times10^{-12})}=2.26\times10^2\ \mathrm{V\,m^{-1}}.$$

ED:163.title: A field jump becomes a delta-function charge density
ED:163.objective: Use a supplied distributional derivative to recover the sheet charge from its discontinuous electric field and verify the result by a Gaussian slab.
ED:163.statement:
A stationary sheet at $z=0$ has field
$$\mathbf E(z)=\frac{\sigma}{2\epsilon_0}\operatorname{sgn}(z)\hat{\mathbf z}.$$
Use the distributional identity $d\,\operatorname{sgn}(z)/dz=2\delta(z)$. (a) Compute $\boldsymbol\nabla\cdot\mathbf E$ distributionally and determine $\rho(\mathbf r)$ from Gauss's law. (b) Independently integrate Gauss's law over a slab of face area $A$ spanning the sheet. (c) State the SI units of $\delta(z)$ and $\rho$, and explain why differentiating only at $z\ne0$ misses the charge.

$\boldsymbol\nabla\cdot\mathbf E=\rho/\epsilon_0$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Differentiate only the scalar coefficient of the fixed unit vector, then compare the resulting distribution with Gauss's law. Use the slab as a sign and normalization check.

milestones.criterion: Obtains $\boldsymbol\nabla\cdot\mathbf E=(\sigma/\epsilon_0)\delta(z)$ and $\rho=\sigma\delta(z)$.

commonErrors.description: Uses $d\,\operatorname{sgn}/dz=\delta$ instead of $2\delta$.
commonErrors.consequence: Produces only half of the sheet charge.

commonErrors.description: Subtracts the bottom-face flux even though both its field and outward normal reverse.
commonErrors.consequence: Incorrectly makes the slab flux vanish.

Distributionally,
$$\boldsymbol\nabla\cdot\mathbf E=\frac{\sigma}{2\epsilon_0}\frac{d}{dz}\operatorname{sgn}(z)=\frac{\sigma}{\epsilon_0}\delta(z).$$
Gauss's law therefore gives
$$\rho(\mathbf r)=\sigma\delta(z).$$
For a slab of face area $A$, the field is $+\sigma\hat{\mathbf z}/(2\epsilon_0)$ on the top face and $-\sigma\hat{\mathbf z}/(2\epsilon_0)$ on the bottom. Each dot product with its outward normal is positive, so the total flux is $\sigma A/\epsilon_0$. The enclosed charge is
$$\int_V\rho\,dV=\sigma A\int_{-a}^{a}\delta(z)\,dz=\sigma A,$$
which gives the same flux. Since $\int\delta(z)\,dz$ is dimensionless, $[\delta]=\mathrm{m^{-1}}$ and $[\rho]=\mathrm{C\,m^{-3}}$. Pointwise differentiation away from the jump gives zero and omits the singular source.

Distributionally, use
$$\frac{d}{dz}\operatorname{sgn}(z)=\delta(z).$$
Then
$$\boldsymbol\nabla\cdot\mathbf E=\frac{\sigma}{2\epsilon_0}\delta(z),$$

ED:164.title: Four macroscopic interface conditions share one normal convention
ED:164.objective: Apply the four supplied macroscopic boundary conditions to fields at a planar interface while keeping free sources, constitutive relations, and sign conventions distinct.
ED:164.statement:

$$\hat{\mathbf n}\cdot(\mathbf D_2-\mathbf D_1)=\sigma_f,\quad \hat{\mathbf n}\cdot(\mathbf B_2-\mathbf B_1)=0,$$
$$\hat{\mathbf n}\times(\mathbf E_2-\mathbf E_1)=\mathbf0,\quad \hat{\mathbf n}\times(\mathbf H_2-\mathbf H_1)=\mathbf K_f.$$

$$\mathbf E_1=(3\hat{\mathbf x}+2\hat{\mathbf z})\ \mathrm{kV\,m^{-1}},\quad \mathbf H_1=(2\hat{\mathbf y}-4\hat{\mathbf z})\ \mathrm{A\,m^{-1}},$$
$$\sigma_f=4\epsilon_0(10^3\ \mathrm{V\,m^{-1}}),\qquad \mathbf K_f=\hat{\mathbf x}\ \mathrm{A\,m^{-1}},$$

ED:175.title: Polarization work separates field storage from material heating
ED:175.objective: Derive the macroscopic local energy balance, separate vacuum field storage from power transferred to polarization and magnetization, and use a prescribed polarization lag to distinguish cyclic material absorption from a universal material state energy.
ED:175.statement:
Work in a fixed, stationary macroscopic region in SI units. All fields are differentiable, and there are no moving boundaries. The macroscopic Maxwell equations are
$$\nabla\times\mathbf H=\mathbf J_f+\partial_t\mathbf D,\qquad \nabla\times\mathbf E=-\partial_t\mathbf B.$$
Here $\mathbf J_f$ is free-current density. Use the decompositions
$$\mathbf D=\epsilon_0\mathbf E+\mathbf P,\qquad \mathbf B=\mu_0(\mathbf H+\mathbf M),$$
without assuming linearity, passivity, or an evolution law for $\mathbf P$ or $\mathbf M$.

(b) Split this balance into a vacuum storage density, an electromagnetic energy-flux density, and power densities transferred to free current, polarization, and magnetization. Explain why the latter terms are not automatically instantaneous heating rates or derivatives of positive material energies.

ED:175.canonicalSolution:
Dotting the Ampere-Maxwell equation with $\mathbf E$ gives
$$\mathbf E\cdot(\nabla\times\mathbf H)=\mathbf J_f\cdot\mathbf E+\mathbf E\cdot\partial_t\mathbf D.$$
Dotting Faraday's law with $\mathbf H$ gives
$$\mathbf H\cdot(\nabla\times\mathbf E)=-\mathbf H\cdot\partial_t\mathbf B.$$
The stated vector identity therefore yields
$$\nabla\cdot(\mathbf E\times\mathbf H)=-\mathbf J_f\cdot\mathbf E-\mathbf E\cdot\partial_t\mathbf D-\mathbf H\cdot\partial_t\mathbf B.$$
Thus the unsplit local balance is
$$\boxed{\mathbf E\cdot\partial_t\mathbf D+\mathbf H\cdot\partial_t\mathbf B+\nabla\cdot(\mathbf E\times\mathbf H)=-\mathbf J_f\cdot\mathbf E.}$$
A positive divergence represents net electromagnetic energy leaving a small volume.

Using the specified decompositions,
$$\mathbf E\cdot\partial_t\mathbf D=\partial_t\left(\frac{\epsilon_0E^2}{2}\right)+\mathbf E\cdot\partial_t\mathbf P,$$
$$\mathbf H\cdot\partial_t\mathbf B=\partial_t\left(\frac{\mu_0H^2}{2}\right)+\mu_0\mathbf H\cdot\partial_t\mathbf M.$$
Define, for this bookkeeping convention,
$$u_{\mathrm v}=\frac{\epsilon_0E^2}{2}+\frac{\mu_0H^2}{2},\qquad \mathbf S=\mathbf E\times\mathbf H.$$
The balance becomes
$$\boxed{\partial_tu_{\mathrm v}+\nabla\cdot\mathbf S=-p_{\mathrm{mat}},}$$
where
$$\boxed{p_{\mathrm{mat}}=\mathbf J_f\cdot\mathbf E+\mathbf E\cdot\partial_t\mathbf P+\mu_0\mathbf H\cdot\partial_t\mathbf M.}$$
Every term has units $\mathrm{W/m^3}$; for example, $(\mathrm{V/m})(\mathrm{C/(m^2s)})=\mathrm{W/m^3}$. Positive $p_{\mathrm{mat}}$ is electromagnetic power transferred to the non-vacuum sector under this allocation. It can temporarily become reversible internal, mechanical, or chemical energy rather than heat. Only with additional constitutive and thermodynamic assumptions may part or all of it be identified as heating.

For the prescribed polarization, let $\theta=\omega t$. Then
$$\partial_t\mathbf P=-\omega P_0\sin(\theta-\delta)\,\hat{\mathbf x},$$
so the polarization power density is
$$p_P(t)=\mathbf E\cdot\partial_t\mathbf P=-\omega E_0P_0\cos\theta\sin(\theta-\delta).$$
Equivalently,
$$\boxed{p_P(t)=\frac{\omega E_0P_0}{2}\left[\sin\delta-\sin(2\omega t-\delta)\right].}$$
It is not generally positive at every instant. The oscillatory term averages to zero, giving
$$\boxed{\langle p_P\rangle=\frac{\omega E_0P_0}{2}\sin\delta.}$$
Here $\omega=2\pi(1.00\times10^3)\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}$ and $E_0P_0=6.00\times10^{-2}\ \mathrm{J/m^3}$. Therefore
$$\boxed{\langle p_P\rangle=94.2\ \mathrm{W/m^3}.}$$
The period is $T=1.00\ \mathrm{ms}$, so the work transferred per unit volume per cycle is
$$W_P=\int_0^T p_P\,dt=\pi E_0P_0\sin\delta,$$
$$\boxed{W_P=9.42\times10^{-2}\ \mathrm{J/m^3\ per\ cycle}.}$$
In a periodic steady material state with no mechanical, chemical, or other exported energy, this positive net transfer must ultimately appear as heat. The prescribed-lag model by itself establishes only net material absorption.

Since $dP=\dot P\,dt$,
$$W_P=\oint E\,dP=\pi E_0P_0\sin\delta.$$
For $\delta\ne0$ this closed-path integral is nonzero. If $E\dot P$ were the total derivative of a single-valued material state energy, its integral around every closed state-space path would have to vanish. Hence no such universal energy exists for an arbitrary lagging polarization.

As a limiting check, when $\delta=0$, $P=(P_0/E_0)E$ and
$$E\dot P=\partial_t\left(\frac{P_0}{2E_0}E^2\right),$$
so the cycle work vanishes and reversible storage is possible. For $\delta<0$, $\langle p_P\rangle<0$; the prescribed medium is active over a cycle and returns energy to the electromagnetic field. Thus positivity cannot be asserted without a passivity assumption.

ED:179.title: Field momentum closes the Lorentz-force balance
ED:179.objective: Derive the local electromagnetic linear-momentum balance directly from Maxwell's equations, distinguish the momentum-flux tensor from the conventional Maxwell stress tensor, and interpret nonzero surface tractions in a uniform crossed-field control volume.
ED:179.statement:
Work in SI units with real time-domain fields; no phasors are used. Vacuum has $\mathbf D=\epsilon_0\mathbf E$, $\mathbf H=\mathbf B/\mu_0$, and $c^{-2}=\epsilon_0\mu_0$. Sources $\rho(\mathbf r,t)$ and $\mathbf J(\mathbf r,t)$ may be present, and all fields are differentiable in the region considered.

Define the field momentum density $\mathbf g=\epsilon_0\mathbf E\times\mathbf B$. Use the momentum-flux sign convention
$$T_{ij}=\left(\frac{\epsilon_0E^2}{2}+\frac{B^2}{2\mu_0}\right)\delta_{ij}-\epsilon_0E_iE_j-\frac{1}{\mu_0}B_iB_j,$$
so that $\mathbf T=-\boldsymbol\sigma$, where $\boldsymbol\sigma$ is the conventional Maxwell stress tensor. For a surface whose unit normal $\hat{\mathbf n}$ points outward from a field control volume, $\mathbf T\cdot\hat{\mathbf n}$ is outward field-momentum flux per area; the conventional stress traction is $\boldsymbol\sigma\cdot\hat{\mathbf n}=-\mathbf T\cdot\hat{\mathbf n}$.

(a) Starting only from Maxwell's equations, derive
$$\frac{\partial}{\partial t}(\epsilon_0\mathbf E\times\mathbf B)+\boldsymbol\nabla\cdot\mathbf T=-\left(\rho\mathbf E+\mathbf J\times\mathbf B\right).$$
State its integral form for a fixed volume $V$ with outward normal.

(b) Let a rectangular control volume of side lengths $L_x,L_y,L_z$ lie wholly inside a broad region with stationary uniform fields $\mathbf E=E_0\hat{\mathbf x}$ and $\mathbf B=B_0\hat{\mathbf y}$, where $(\hat{\mathbf x},\hat{\mathbf y},\hat{\mathbf z})$ is right-handed. Calculate $\mathbf g$, all three independent diagonal entries of $\mathbf T$, and $\mathbf T\cdot\hat{\mathbf n}$ on each pair of faces. Verify the balance by summing boundary fluxes, rather than by merely observing that $\boldsymbol\nabla\cdot\mathbf T=0$. Interpret the nonzero individual tractions and include a dimensional and limiting check.
