ED:179.canonicalSolution:
Define the conventional Maxwell stress tensor
$$\sigma_{ij}=\epsilon_0\left(E_iE_j-\frac12E^2\delta_{ij}\right)+\frac{1}{\mu_0}\left(B_iB_j-\frac12B^2\delta_{ij}\right),$$
so the tensor in the problem is $T_{ij}=-\sigma_{ij}$.

For the electric part, the dyadic product rule gives
$$\boldsymbol\nabla\cdot\boldsymbol\sigma_E=\epsilon_0\left[(\boldsymbol\nabla\cdot\mathbf E)\mathbf E+(\mathbf E\cdot\boldsymbol\nabla)\mathbf E-\frac12\boldsymbol\nabla E^2\right].$$
Using
$$(\mathbf E\cdot\boldsymbol\nabla)\mathbf E-\frac12\boldsymbol\nabla E^2=-\mathbf E\times(\boldsymbol\nabla\times\mathbf E),$$
and Maxwell's equations,
$$\boldsymbol\nabla\cdot\boldsymbol\sigma_E=\rho\mathbf E-\epsilon_0\mathbf E\times(\boldsymbol\nabla\times\mathbf E)=\rho\mathbf E+\epsilon_0\mathbf E\times\partial_t\mathbf B.$$
For the magnetic part, $\boldsymbol\nabla\cdot\mathbf B=0$ gives
$$\boldsymbol\nabla\cdot\boldsymbol\sigma_B=\frac{1}{\mu_0}\left[(\mathbf B\cdot\boldsymbol\nabla)\mathbf B-\frac12\boldsymbol\nabla B^2\right]=\frac{1}{\mu_0}(\boldsymbol\nabla\times\mathbf B)\times\mathbf B.$$
Ampere-Maxwell's law therefore yields
$$\boldsymbol\nabla\cdot\boldsymbol\sigma_B=\mathbf J\times\mathbf B+\epsilon_0(\partial_t\mathbf E)\times\mathbf B.$$
Adding the two parts and applying the time-product rule,
$$\boldsymbol\nabla\cdot\boldsymbol\sigma=\rho\mathbf E+\mathbf J\times\mathbf B+\epsilon_0\partial_t(\mathbf E\times\mathbf B).$$
Since $\mathbf T=-\boldsymbol\sigma$ and $\mathbf g=\epsilon_0\mathbf E\times\mathbf B$,
$$\boxed{\partial_t\mathbf g+\boldsymbol\nabla\cdot\mathbf T=-\mathbf f_L},\qquad \mathbf f_L=\rho\mathbf E+\mathbf J\times\mathbf B.$$
For a fixed volume,
$$\boxed{\frac{d}{dt}\int_V\mathbf g\,dV+\oint_{\partial V}\mathbf T\cdot\hat{\mathbf n}\,dA=-\int_V\mathbf f_L\,dV}.$$
Equivalently, the force on matter in $V$ is $\int_V\mathbf f_LdV=\oint_{\partial V}\boldsymbol\sigma\cdot\hat{\mathbf n}\,dA-d\int_V\mathbf g\,dV/dt$.

For the crossed fields,
$$\mathbf g=\epsilon_0E_0B_0\,\hat{\mathbf z}.$$
Let $u_E=\epsilon_0E_0^2/2$ and $u_B=B_0^2/(2\mu_0)$. In the ordered basis $(\hat{\mathbf x},\hat{\mathbf y},\hat{\mathbf z})$,
$$\mathbf T=\begin{pmatrix}u_B-u_E&0&0\\0&u_E-u_B&0\\0&0&u_E+u_B\end{pmatrix}.$$
Consequently,
$$\begin{aligned}
\hat{\mathbf n}=\pm\hat{\mathbf x}:&\quad \mathbf T\cdot\hat{\mathbf n}=\pm(u_B-u_E)\hat{\mathbf x},\\
\hat{\mathbf n}=\pm\hat{\mathbf y}:&\quad \mathbf T\cdot\hat{\mathbf n}=\pm(u_E-u_B)\hat{\mathbf y},\\
\hat{\mathbf n}=\pm\hat{\mathbf z}:&\quad \mathbf T\cdot\hat{\mathbf n}=\pm(u_E+u_B)\hat{\mathbf z}.
\end{aligned}$$
The two faces in each pair have equal area and opposite flux, so
$$\oint_{\partial V}\mathbf T\cdot\hat{\mathbf n}\,dA=\mathbf0.$$
The fields are stationary, so $d\int_V\mathbf g\,dV/dt=0$, and the integral balance gives zero net bulk Lorentz force. Nevertheless, each cut carries a generally nonzero traction; cancellation occurs only after all oriented faces are included. The conventional stress traction on the same oriented cut is the negative of the listed momentum flux.

Both $u_E$ and $u_B$ have units $\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}=\mathrm{N\,m^{-2}}$, while $[\mathbf g]=\mathrm{N\,s\,m^{-3}}$. Thus $\partial_t\mathbf g$ and $\boldsymbol\nabla\cdot\mathbf T$ both have units $\mathrm{N\,m^{-3}}$. As a limiting check, if $B_0=0$, then $T_{xx}=-u_E$ and $T_{yy}=T_{zz}=u_E$, corresponding to the opposite-sign conventional electric tension along $\mathbf E$ and transverse pressure, with paired face fluxes still canceling.

ED:180.title: Angular momentum balance requires a symmetric stress tensor
ED:180.objective: Convert local linear-momentum conservation into local angular-momentum conservation, identify precisely where stress-tensor symmetry is required, and track field and mechanical angular momentum during the quasistatic establishment of crossed coaxial fields.
ED:180.statement:
Use right-handed cylindrical coordinates $(r,\phi,z)$ with $\hat{\mathbf r}\times\hat{\boldsymbol\phi}=\hat{\mathbf z}$. Work in SI vacuum, $\mathbf D=\epsilon_0\mathbf E$ and $\mathbf H=\mathbf B/\mu_0$, with real time-domain fields and no phasors. Adopt the momentum balance and flux convention
$$\partial_t g_i+\partial_jT_{ij}=-f_i,$$
where $\mathbf g=\epsilon_0\mathbf E\times\mathbf B$, $\mathbf f=\rho\mathbf E+\mathbf J\times\mathbf B$, and
$$T_{ij}=\left(\frac{\epsilon_0E^2}{2}+\frac{B^2}{2\mu_0}\right)\delta_{ij}-\epsilon_0E_iE_j-\frac{1}{\mu_0}B_iB_j.$$

(a) Define $\boldsymbol\ell=\mathbf r\times\mathbf g$ and $\boldsymbol\tau=\mathbf r\times\mathbf f$. By an index calculation, derive the local angular-momentum balance and its flux tensor. Exhibit the extra term that would survive for a nonsymmetric momentum-flux tensor, and explain why it vanishes here.

(b) Two very long, thin, electrically insulating coaxial cylindrical shells have radii $a<b$ and fixed charge per unit length $+\lambda$ and $-\lambda$, respectively. End effects are neglected. In the annulus $a<r<b$, an externally produced final magnetic field is $\mathbf B=B_0\hat{\mathbf z}$. Derive the radial electric field, then calculate the electromagnetic angular momentum per unit axial length and determine its direction for $\lambda>0$ and $B_0>0$.

(c) To check the boundary torque signs, suppose the magnetic field is raised slowly from zero as $\mathbf B=B(t)\hat{\mathbf z}$, approximately uniform over every disk $r<b$. Neglect radiation and fringing, but retain the Faraday-induced azimuthal electric field. The outward normals of the annular field volume are $+\hat{\mathbf r}$ at $r=b$ and $-\hat{\mathbf r}$ at $r=a$. Derive $E_\phi(r,t)$, find the torque per unit length on each charged shell, and show that their sum is opposite to the rate of change of field angular momentum. Write
$$\ell_i=\epsilon_{ikl}x_kg_l,\qquad \tau_i=\epsilon_{ikl}x_kf_l.$$
Multiplying the linear-momentum equation for component $l$ by $\epsilon_{ikl}x_k$ gives
$$\partial_t\ell_i+\epsilon_{ikl}x_k\partial_jT_{lj}=-\tau_i.$$
Define the angular-momentum flux tensor
$$M_{ij}=\epsilon_{ikl}x_kT_{lj}.$$
Its divergence is
$$\partial_jM_{ij}=\epsilon_{ikl}\delta_{jk}T_{lj}+\epsilon_{ikl}x_k\partial_jT_{lj}=\epsilon_{ijl}T_{lj}+\epsilon_{ikl}x_k\partial_jT_{lj}.$$
Therefore the general balance is
$$\partial_t\ell_i+\partial_jM_{ij}=-\tau_i+\epsilon_{ijl}T_{lj}.$$
The contraction $\epsilon_{ijl}T_{lj}$ selects the antisymmetric part of $T_{lj}$. The stated electromagnetic tensor is symmetric because $\delta_{ij}$, $E_iE_j$, and $B_iB_j$ are all symmetric. Hence
$$\boxed{\partial_t\ell_i+\partial_jM_{ij}=-\tau_i},\qquad \boxed{M_{ij}=\epsilon_{ikl}x_kT_{lj}}.$$
Thus local orbital angular momentum follows from linear-momentum conservation only after the internal stress contribution is shown to be symmetric.

For the coaxial shells, a cylindrical Gaussian surface of radius $r$ and length $L$, with $a<r<b$, encloses charge $\lambda L$. Gauss's law gives
$$E_r(2\pi rL)=\frac{\lambda L}{\epsilon_0},\qquad \mathbf E=\frac{\lambda}{2\pi\epsilon_0r}\hat{\mathbf r}.$$
The field momentum density is
$$\mathbf g=\epsilon_0\mathbf E\times\mathbf B=-\epsilon_0E_rB_0\hat{\boldsymbol\phi}=-\frac{\lambda B_0}{2\pi r}\hat{\boldsymbol\phi}.$$
The axial component of angular-momentum density is
$$\ell_z=rg_\phi=-\frac{\lambda B_0}{2\pi}.$$
Integrating over the annular cross-section gives
$$\frac{L_{\mathrm{field},z}}{L}=\int_a^b\ell_z(2\pi r\,dr)=-\frac{\lambda B_0}{2}(b^2-a^2).$$
Thus
$$\boxed{\frac{\mathbf L_{\mathrm{field}}}{L}=-\frac{\lambda B_0}{2}(b^2-a^2)\hat{\mathbf z}}.$$
For $\lambda>0$ and $B_0>0$, the stored field angular momentum points along $-\hat{\mathbf z}$.

During the slow ramp, Maxwell-Faraday's law on a circle of radius $R<b$, oriented with normal $+\hat{\mathbf z}$, gives
$$2\pi R E_\phi(R,t)=-\frac{d}{dt}\left(\pi R^2B\right),$$
so
$$E_\phi(R,t)=-\frac{R}{2}\dot B(t).$$
A shell carrying charge per length $q'$ experiences tangential force per length $q'E_\phi$ and axial torque per length $Rq'E_\phi$. Hence
$$\frac{\tau_{a,z}}{L}=\lambda aE_\phi(a)=-\frac{\lambda a^2}{2}\dot B,$$
while the outer shell carries $q'=-\lambda$ and therefore
$$\frac{\tau_{b,z}}{L}=(-\lambda)bE_\phi(b)=+\frac{\lambda b^2}{2}\dot B.$$
For $\lambda>0$ and $\dot B>0$, the inner shell torque points along $-\hat{\mathbf z}$, the outer torque points along $+\hat{\mathbf z}$, and the larger outer moment arm makes the net torque positive:
$$\frac{\tau_{\mathrm{shells},z}}{L}=\frac{\lambda}{2}(b^2-a^2)\dot B.$$
Meanwhile,
$$\frac{d}{dt}\left(\frac{L_{\mathrm{field},z}}{L}\right)=-\frac{\lambda}{2}(b^2-a^2)\dot B,$$
so
$$\boxed{\frac{d}{dt}\left(\frac{L_{\mathrm{field},z}}{L}\right)+\frac{\tau_{\mathrm{shells},z}}{L}=0}.$$

The same result follows from angular-momentum flux. During the ramp, the relevant off-diagonal component is
$$T_{\phi r}=-\epsilon_0E_\phi E_r=-\frac{\lambda E_\phi}{2\pi r}.$$
The radial flux density of axial angular momentum is $M_{zr}=rT_{\phi r}$. Per unit axial length, the outer and inner surface contributions are respectively
$$2\pi b\,[bT_{\phi r}(b)]=-\lambda bE_\phi(b)=\frac{\tau_{b,z}}{L},$$
$$2\pi a\,[-aT_{\phi r}(a)]=\lambda aE_\phi(a)=\frac{\tau_{a,z}}{L},$$
where the minus sign in the second expression comes from the annulus's inner outward normal $-\hat{\mathbf r}$. Their sum is the positive outward angular-momentum flux, and the vacuum balance in the annulus reads $d(L_{\mathrm{field},z}/L)/dt+$ outward flux $=0$.

After the ramp, $\dot B=0$, so $E_\phi=0$, $T_{\phi r}=0$, and both boundary torques vanish even though the static crossed fields retain nonzero angular momentum. Dimensionally, $[\lambda B_0(b^2-a^2)]=\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}$, which is angular momentum per unit length. The result vanishes as $b\to a$ and reverses direction if either $\lambda$ or $B_0$ changes sign.

ED:184.title: Boundary conditions can forbid an otherwise legal gauge function
ED:184.objective: Construct a Lorenz-preserving bulk gauge transformation that leaves the fields unchanged but violates fixed potential boundary data, and characterize the residual gauge functions admitted by the complete boundary-value problem.
ED:184.statement: Let the vacuum interior of a rectangular perfectly conducting box be $$\Omega=(0,L_x)\times(0,L_y)\times(0,L_z),$$ with Cartesian basis $\hat{\mathbf x},\hat{\mathbf y},\hat{\mathbf z}$ and outward unit normal $\mathbf n$ on each face, such as $\mathbf n=-\hat{\mathbf y}$ at $y=0$. Work in the zero trapped-flux sector and use the Lorenz gauge $$\nabla\cdot\mathbf A+\frac{1}{c^2}\partial_t\phi=0.$$ A chosen potential boundary-value problem imposes, facewise for all times, $$\phi|_{\partial\Omega}=0,\qquad \mathbf P\mathbf A|_{\partial\Omega}=\mathbf 0,\qquad \mathbf P=\mathbf I-\mathbf n\mathbf n,$$ where $\mathbf P\mathbf A$ is the tangential component. Consider the gauge convention $$\mathbf A'=\mathbf A+\nabla\chi,\qquad \phi'=\phi-\partial_t\chi.$$ (a) Prove field invariance and derive the bulk PDE that $\chi$ must satisfy to preserve the Lorenz gauge. (b) Derive all boundary restrictions on $\chi$ required to preserve the stated potential data, and simplify them using the connectedness of $\partial\Omega$. (c) Starting from $\mathbf A=\mathbf 0$ and $\phi=0$, construct an explicit smooth $\chi$ that satisfies the bulk gauge PDE but violates the potential boundary data. Evaluate the violation on a named face. (d) Distinguish equality of electromagnetic fields from membership in this fixed boundary-value problem. Include an SI-dimensional check and a limiting check of the construction.

ED:185.title: Potentials reconstructed from fields still need integrability conditions
ED:185.objective: Prove the local reconstruction of electromagnetic potentials from the homogeneous Maxwell equations, distinguish local from global integrability, and execute the reconstruction for a time-dependent polynomial field pair.
ED:185.statement:
Let $U\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a connected, simply connected open domain with right-handed Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$, and let $I$ be a time interval. Assume $\mathbf E,\mathbf B\in C^2(U\times I)$ satisfy
$$\nabla\cdot\mathbf B=0,\qquad \nabla\times\mathbf E=-\partial_t\mathbf B.$$
(a) For any $\mathbf r_0\in U$, choose a ball $V\subset U$ centered at $\mathbf r_0$ and prove directly that
$$\mathbf A(\mathbf r,t)=\int_0^1 s\,\mathbf B\bigl(\mathbf r_0+s(\mathbf r-\mathbf r_0),t\bigr)\times(\mathbf r-\mathbf r_0)\,ds$$
satisfies $\nabla\times\mathbf A=\mathbf B$ on $V$.

(b) Prove that $\mathbf E+\partial_t\mathbf A$ is curl-free. Explain precisely when this defines a local scalar potential $\phi$ and when it defines one globally, using the convention
$$\mathbf B=\nabla\times\mathbf A,\qquad \mathbf E=-\nabla\phi-\partial_t\mathbf A.$$
State the gauge freedom.

(c) Explain why simple connectedness alone does not guarantee a global vector potential. Discuss the obstruction from flux through closed two-surfaces and the extra caveats introduced by excluded regions or boundary components.

(d) On $U=\mathbb R^3$, consider
$$\mathbf B=(-atx,0,atz),\qquad \mathbf E=(-2btx,-axz,0),$$
where $a$ has SI units $\mathrm{T\,m^{-1}\,s^{-1}}$ and $b$ has units $\mathrm{V\,m^{-2}\,s^{-1}}$. Verify both integrability conditions and reconstruct one pair $(\mathbf A,\phi)$. Check the gauge-invariant fields, SI dimensions, and the limits $a\to0$ and $b\to0$.
permittedResults: Stokes's theorem and the divergence theorem for sufficiently smooth oriented surfaces
Path independence of a curl-free field on a simply connected open domain
Differentiation under an integral and commutation of spatial and time derivatives for $C^2$ fields

acceptableStrategies.description: Work locally on a star-shaped ball and verify the proposed homotopy integral component by component rather than assuming a global vector potential. Apply Faraday's law only after establishing $\nabla\times\mathbf A=\mathbf B$. Then separate the topology required for a scalar potential from the stronger two-surface condition required for a global vector potential. For the polynomial pair, verify the Maxwell conditions before identifying simple polynomial potentials.

milestones.criterion: Derives the local homotopy formula for $\mathbf A$ through the component curl calculation and explicitly uses $\nabla\cdot\mathbf B=0$.
Obtains the correct sign for $\phi$, states the gauge transformation, and accurately distinguishes simple connectedness from the closed-two-surface condition for a global vector potential.
Verifies both polynomial Maxwell conditions and reconstructs potentials with correct fields, SI dimensions, and limiting checks.

commonErrors.description: Claims that simple connectedness by itself guarantees a smooth global vector potential.
commonErrors.consequence: Misses nontrivial closed two-surfaces, such as spheres around an excluded point, on which nonzero magnetic flux obstructs a global $\mathbf A$.

commonErrors.description: Defines $\phi$ with the positive line integral of $\mathbf E+\partial_t\mathbf A$ while retaining $\mathbf E=-\nabla\phi-\partial_t\mathbf A$.
commonErrors.consequence: Reconstructs the electric field with the wrong sign and fails even for the polynomial example.

hintTree.content: Write $\mathbf R=\mathbf r-\mathbf r_0$ and $A_i=\int_0^1s\epsilon_{ijk}B_j(\mathbf r_0+s\mathbf R,t)R_k\,ds$. In the curl, the divergence-free condition turns the integrand into an $s$-derivative.

Set $\mathbf F=\mathbf E+\partial_t\mathbf A$. Faraday's law determines $\nabla\times\mathbf F$; the sign in the line-integral definition of $\phi$ must agree with $\mathbf E=-\nabla\phi-\partial_t\mathbf A$.

For the polynomial fields, try a vector potential with only a $y$ component proportional to $txz$. A closed surface surrounding an excluded point provides a useful test of whether simple connectedness is enough for a global $\mathbf A$.

ED:185.canonicalSolution:
Let $\mathbf R=\mathbf r-\mathbf r_0$. On the chosen ball, define
$$A_i=\int_0^1s\epsilon_{ijk}B_j(\mathbf r_0+s\mathbf R,t)R_k\,ds.$$
Using $\epsilon_{\ell mi}\epsilon_{ijk}=\delta_{\ell j}\delta_{mk}-\delta_{\ell k}\delta_{mj}$ and differentiating with respect to $r_m$ gives
$$
(\nabla\times\mathbf A)_\ell
=\int_0^1s\left[sR_m\partial_mB_\ell+2B_\ell-sR_\ell\partial_jB_j\right]ds.
$$
The last term vanishes because $\nabla\cdot\mathbf B=0$. The remaining integrand is
$$s\left[s\mathbf R\cdot\nabla B_\ell+2B_\ell\right]
=\frac{d}{ds}\left[s^2B_\ell(\mathbf r_0+s\mathbf R,t)\right].$$
Therefore
$$
(\nabla\times\mathbf A)_\ell
=\left[s^2B_\ell(\mathbf r_0+s\mathbf R,t)\right]_{0}^{1}
=B_\ell(\mathbf r,t),
$$
so $\nabla\times\mathbf A=\mathbf B$ locally. Every interior point has such a ball, proving local existence.

Now define $\mathbf F=\mathbf E+\partial_t\mathbf A$. Smoothness permits the derivatives to commute, so
$$
\nabla\times\mathbf F
=\nabla\times\mathbf E+\partial_t(\nabla\times\mathbf A)
=-\partial_t\mathbf B+\partial_t\mathbf B=0.
$$
On any simply connected patch, choose a reference point $\mathbf r_*$ and define
$$
\phi(\mathbf r,t)=-\int_{\mathbf r_*}^{\mathbf r}\mathbf F(\boldsymbol\ell,t)\cdot d\boldsymbol\ell.
$$
The integral is path-independent, and $\nabla\phi=-\mathbf F$. Hence
$$\mathbf E=-\nabla\phi-\partial_t\mathbf A.$$
If a smooth global $\mathbf A$ already exists on simply connected $U$, this construction gives a global $\phi$. If only local vector potentials exist, it produces local scalar potentials on the same patches. The gauge transformation is
$$
\mathbf A' =\mathbf A+\nabla\chi,
\qquad
\phi'=\phi-\partial_t\chi,
$$
which leaves both fields unchanged.

Simple connectedness controls closed curves and therefore curl-free scalar-potential reconstruction, but it does not eliminate closed two-cycles. If a smooth global $\mathbf A$ existed, Stokes's theorem would require every closed oriented surface $\Sigma\subset U$ to satisfy
$$
\int_\Sigma\mathbf B\cdot\mathbf n\,dS
=\int_\Sigma(\nabla\times\mathbf A)\cdot\mathbf n\,dS=0.
$$
For example, $U=\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\}$ is simply connected, but the smooth field $\mathbf B=g\mathbf r/r^3$ has flux $4\pi g$ through every sphere centered at the excluded point, so it has no smooth global vector potential on $U$. A contractible domain, or more generally vanishing flux on all independent closed two-cycles, removes this obstruction. On a domain with boundary, $\nabla\cdot\mathbf B=0$ fixes the total flux through the full boundary but need not force zero flux through each separate boundary component. Extending potentials smoothly to the boundary or imposing additional normal or tangential boundary data can introduce further compatibility conditions.

For the polynomial pair,
$$
\nabla\cdot\mathbf B=\partial_x(-atx)+\partial_z(atz)=-at+at=0.
$$
Also,
$$
\nabla\times\mathbf E
=\left(-\partial_z(-axz),0,\partial_x(-axz)\right)
=(ax,0,-az),
$$
while
$$-\partial_t\mathbf B=(ax,0,-az).$$
Thus both integrability conditions hold. Choose
$$
\mathbf A=(0,atxz,0),\qquad \phi=btx^2.
$$
Then
$$
\nabla\times\mathbf A=(-atx,0,atz)=\mathbf B
$$
and
$$
-\nabla\phi-\partial_t\mathbf A
=(-2btx,0,0)+(0,-axz,0)=\mathbf E.
$$
The term $atxz$ has units $\mathrm{T\,m}$, as required for a vector potential, while $btx^2$ has units volts. Both terms in $\mathbf E$ have units $\mathrm{V/m}$. When $a\to0$, $\mathbf B$ and the inductive part of $\mathbf E$ vanish, leaving the gradient field generated by $\phi$. When $b\to0$, $\phi$ may be chosen zero and the electric field is entirely $-\partial_t\mathbf A$. These limits independently confirm the decomposition.

ED:186.title: Poynting's theorem is a signed local ledger
ED:186.objective: Derive the local and integral electromagnetic energy balances with all signs exposed, then use a steady cylindrical Ohmic region to verify that negative outward Poynting flux represents energy supplied through the boundary.
ED:186.statement:
In a right-handed Cartesian frame, let microscopic vacuum fields be $C^1$ on a fixed region and satisfy
$$
\nabla\times\mathbf E=-\partial_t\mathbf B,
\qquad
\nabla\times\mathbf B=\mu_0\mathbf J+\mu_0\epsilon_0\partial_t\mathbf E.
$$
The vacuum constants $\epsilon_0$ and $\mu_0$ are uniform. No polarization or magnetization fields are introduced.

(a) Starting from these curl equations, derive
$$
\partial_tu+\nabla\cdot\mathbf S=-\mathbf J\cdot\mathbf E,
\qquad
u=\frac{\epsilon_0E^2}{2}+\frac{B^2}{2\mu_0},
\qquad
\mathbf S=\frac{1}{\mu_0}\mathbf E\times\mathbf B.
$$
Derive the sign in the cross-product divergence identity explicitly in components.

(b) Integrate the result over a fixed volume $V$ with piecewise smooth boundary $\partial V$ and outward unit normal $\mathbf n$. Interpret each sign in the resulting energy ledger.

(c) Test the sign in a long cylindrical Ohmic region of radius $a$ and length $L$, with cylindrical orientation $\hat{\mathbf r}\times\hat{\boldsymbol\varphi}=\hat{\mathbf z}$. Neglect end effects and take
$$
\mathbf E=E_0\hat{\mathbf z},
\qquad
\mathbf J=J_0\hat{\mathbf z}=\sigma E_0\hat{\mathbf z},
\qquad \sigma>0.
$$
Use Ampère's law to obtain the interior magnetic field, calculate the Poynting flux through every part of the boundary, and compare it with the Ohmic power. Include a local divergence check, an SI dimensional audit, and the limits $\sigma\to0$ and $E_0\to0$.
permittedResults: The microscopic vacuum Maxwell curl equations stated in the problem
The divergence theorem for a fixed piecewise smooth volume with outward normal
Ampère's circulation law in the steady, axially symmetric cylindrical test

acceptableStrategies.description: Expand $\nabla\cdot(\mathbf E\times\mathbf B)$ in index notation so that its two curl terms and their relative minus sign cannot be guessed incorrectly. Substitute Maxwell's equations and convert dot products with time derivatives into derivatives of squared field magnitudes. For the sign test, derive the azimuthal magnetic field inside the cylindrical conductor and evaluate $\mathbf E\times\mathbf B$ relative to the outward radial normal.

milestones.criterion:
Derives $
abla\cdot(\mathbf E	imes\mathbf B)=\mathbf B\cdot
abla	imes\mathbf E-\mathbf E\cdot
abla	imes\mathbf B$ in components and carries its signs correctly through Maxwell substitution.
Produces the fixed-volume balance with an outward normal and correctly interprets negative outward flux as inward supplied power.
Derives the cylindrical magnetic and Poynting fields and verifies equality with Ohmic power using boundary, local-divergence, dimensional, and limiting checks.

commonErrors.description: Reverses the cross-product divergence identity and obtains a positive $\mathbf J\cdot\mathbf E$ on the right side of the local field-energy equation.
commonErrors.consequence: Predicts that passive Ohmic heating creates electromagnetic field energy rather than receiving energy from the field.

commonErrors.description: Treats positive $\oint_{\partial V}\mathbf S\cdot\mathbf n\,dA$ with an outward normal as power entering the volume.
commonErrors.consequence: Assigns the cylindrical side-wall Poynting flow the wrong direction and fails to balance the positive Joule power.

hintTree.content: In $\partial_i(\epsilon_{ijk}E_jB_k)$, rewrite the first product-rule term as $\mathbf B\cdot(\nabla\times\mathbf E)$ and inspect the index interchange needed in the second term.
After substituting the curl equations, use $\mathbf E\cdot\partial_t\mathbf E=\tfrac12\partial_tE^2$ and the analogous magnetic identity before moving any term across the equality.

For the cylinder, Ampère's loop encloses current $J_0\pi r^2$. Determine the direction of $\hat{\mathbf z}\times\hat{\boldsymbol\varphi}$ before deciding whether the side-wall flux is inward or outward.

ED:186.canonicalSolution:
Begin with the component form of the cross product:
$$
\nabla\cdot(\mathbf E\times\mathbf B)
=\partial_i(\epsilon_{ijk}E_jB_k)
=\epsilon_{ijk}(\partial_iE_j)B_k+\epsilon_{ijk}E_j\partial_iB_k.
$$
Because $\epsilon_{ijk}=\epsilon_{kij}$, the first term is $\mathbf B\cdot(\nabla\times\mathbf E)$. Because $\epsilon_{ijk}=-\epsilon_{jik}$, the second is $-\mathbf E\cdot(\nabla\times\mathbf B)$. Hence
$$
\nabla\cdot(\mathbf E\times\mathbf B)
=\mathbf B\cdot(\nabla\times\mathbf E)
-\mathbf E\cdot(\nabla\times\mathbf B).
$$
Substitution of Maxwell's curl equations gives
$$
\nabla\cdot(\mathbf E\times\mathbf B)
=-\mathbf B\cdot\partial_t\mathbf B
-\mu_0\mathbf J\cdot\mathbf E
-\mu_0\epsilon_0\mathbf E\cdot\partial_t\mathbf E.
$$
Since
$$
\mathbf B\cdot\partial_t\mathbf B=\frac12\partial_tB^2,
\qquad
\mathbf E\cdot\partial_t\mathbf E=\frac12\partial_tE^2,
$$
division by $\mu_0$ yields
$$
\nabla\cdot\left(\frac{\mathbf E\times\mathbf B}{\mu_0}\right)
=-\mathbf J\cdot\mathbf E
-\partial_t\left(\frac{B^2}{2\mu_0}+\frac{\epsilon_0E^2}{2}\right).
$$
Therefore, with
$$
u=\frac{\epsilon_0E^2}{2}+\frac{B^2}{2\mu_0},
\qquad
\mathbf S=\frac{\mathbf E\times\mathbf B}{\mu_0},$$
the local ledger is
$$\partial_tu+\nabla\cdot\mathbf S=-\mathbf J\cdot\mathbf E.$$
A positive $\mathbf J\cdot\mathbf E$ means that the field performs positive work per unit volume on matter, so electromagnetic field energy is depleted unless replenished by flux.

For a fixed volume, differentiation commutes with integration. The divergence theorem gives
$$
\frac{d}{dt}\int_Vu\,dV
+\oint_{\partial V}\mathbf S\cdot\mathbf n\,dA
=-\int_V\mathbf J\cdot\mathbf E\,dV.
$$
The first term is the rate of change of field energy inside $V$. The surface term is net outward electromagnetic power: it is positive when more energy leaves than enters. The right side is minus the power transferred from fields to matter. Equivalently,
$$
\frac{d}{dt}\int_Vu\,dV
=-\oint_{\partial V}\mathbf S\cdot\mathbf n\,dA
-\int_V\mathbf J\cdot\mathbf E\,dV,
$$
so negative outward flux is positive power supplied into the volume.

For the steady cylindrical test, take an Amperian circle of radius $r<a$. Axial symmetry makes $\mathbf B=B_\varphi(r)\hat{\boldsymbol\varphi}$, and Ampère's law gives
$$
2\pi rB_\varphi(r)=\mu_0J_0\pi r^2,
$$
so
$$
\mathbf B(r)=\frac{\mu_0J_0r}{2}\hat{\boldsymbol\varphi}.
$$
Because $\hat{\mathbf z}\times\hat{\boldsymbol\varphi}=-\hat{\mathbf r}$,
$$
\mathbf S(r)
=\frac{1}{\mu_0}E_0\hat{\mathbf z}\times
\frac{\mu_0J_0r}{2}\hat{\boldsymbol\varphi}
=-\frac{E_0J_0r}{2}\hat{\mathbf r}.
$$
Thus energy flows radially inward. On the curved wall, the outward normal is $\hat{\mathbf r}$, and therefore
$$
\int_{\text{side}}\mathbf S\cdot\mathbf n\,dA
=-\frac{E_0J_0a}{2}(2\pi aL)
=-E_0J_0\pi a^2L.
$$
The Poynting vector is radial, so its flux through the two endcaps, whose normals are $\pm\hat{\mathbf z}$, is zero. Hence
$$
\oint_{\partial V}\mathbf S\cdot\mathbf n\,dA
=-E_0J_0\pi a^2L
=-\sigma E_0^2V,
\qquad V=\pi a^2L.
$$
The field is steady, so $d\int_Vu\,dV/dt=0$, while the material receives
$$
\int_V\mathbf J\cdot\mathbf E\,dV
=J_0E_0V=\sigma E_0^2V.
$$
The negative outward flux therefore supplies exactly the positive Ohmic power.

A local check follows from the cylindrical divergence:
$$
\nabla\cdot\mathbf S
=\frac1r\frac{\partial}{\partial r}(rS_r)
=\frac1r\frac{\partial}{\partial r}\left(-\frac{E_0J_0r^2}{2}\right)
=-E_0J_0=-\mathbf J\cdot\mathbf E.
$$
Dimensionally, $u$ has units $\mathrm{J/m^3}$, $\mathbf S$ has units $\mathrm{W/m^2}$, and both $\nabla\cdot\mathbf S$ and $\mathbf J\cdot\mathbf E$ have units $\mathrm{W/m^3}$. If $\sigma\to0$ at fixed $E_0$, then $J_0$, the magnetic field, the Poynting flux, and the Ohmic power all vanish. They also all vanish when $E_0\to0$, confirming the sign and scaling independently.

graderFixtures.proofText:
Begin with the component form of the cross product:
$$
\nabla\cdot(\mathbf E\times\mathbf B)
=\partial_i(\epsilon_{ijk}E_jB_k)
=\epsilon_{ijk}(\partial_iE_j)B_k+\epsilon_{ijk}E_j\partial_iB_k.
$$
Because $\epsilon_{ijk}=\epsilon_{kij}$, the first term is $\mathbf B\cdot(\nabla\times\mathbf E)$. Because $\epsilon_{ijk}=-\epsilon_{jik}$, the second is $-\mathbf E\cdot(\nabla\times\mathbf B)$. Hence
$$
\nabla\cdot(\mathbf E\times\mathbf B)
=\mathbf B\cdot(\nabla\times\mathbf E)
-\mathbf E\cdot(\nabla\times\mathbf B).
$$
Substitution of Maxwell's curl equations gives
$$
\nabla\cdot(\mathbf E\times\mathbf B)
=-\mathbf B\cdot\partial_t\mathbf B
-\mu_0\mathbf J\cdot\mathbf E
-\mu_0\epsilon_0\mathbf E\cdot\partial_t\mathbf E.
$$
Since
$$
\mathbf B\cdot\partial_t\mathbf B=\frac12\partial_tB^2,
\qquad
\mathbf E\cdot\partial_t\mathbf E=\frac12\partial_tE^2,
$$
division by $\mu_0$ yields
$$
\nabla\cdot\left(\frac{\mathbf E\times\mathbf B}{\mu_0}\right)
=-\mathbf J\cdot\mathbf E
-\partial_t\left(\frac{B^2}{2\mu_0}+\frac{\epsilon_0E^2}{2}\right).
$$
Therefore, with
$$
u=\frac{\epsilon_0E^2}{2}+\frac{B^2}{2\mu_0},
\qquad
\mathbf S=\frac{\mathbf E\times\mathbf B}{\mu_0},$$
the local ledger is
$$\partial_tu+\nabla\cdot\mathbf S=-\mathbf J\cdot\mathbf E.$$
A positive $\mathbf J\cdot\mathbf E$ means that the field performs positive work per unit volume on matter, so electromagnetic field energy is depleted unless replenished by flux.

For a fixed volume, differentiation commutes with integration. The divergence theorem gives
$$
\frac{d}{dt}\int_Vu\,dV
+\oint_{\partial V}\mathbf S\cdot\mathbf n\,dA
=-\int_V\mathbf J\cdot\mathbf E\,dV.
$$
The first term is the rate of change of field energy inside $V$. The surface term is net outward electromagnetic power: it is positive when more energy leaves than enters. The right side is minus the power transferred from fields to matter. Equivalently,
$$
\frac{d}{dt}\int_Vu\,dV
=-\oint_{\partial V}\mathbf S\cdot\mathbf n\,dA
-\int_V\mathbf J\cdot\mathbf E\,dV,
$$
so negative outward flux is positive power supplied into the volume.

For the steady cylindrical test, take an Amperian circle of radius $r<a$. Axial symmetry makes $\mathbf B=B_\varphi(r)\hat{\boldsymbol\varphi}$, and Ampère's law gives
$$
2\pi rB_\varphi(r)=\mu_0J_0\pi r^2,
$$
so
$$
\mathbf B(r)=\frac{\mu_0J_0r}{2}\hat{\boldsymbol\varphi}.
$$
Because $\hat{\mathbf z}\times\hat{\boldsymbol\varphi}=-\hat{\mathbf r}$,
$$
\mathbf S(r)
=\frac{1}{\mu_0}E_0\hat{\mathbf z}\times
\frac{\mu_0J_0r}{2}\hat{\boldsymbol\varphi}
=-\frac{E_0J_0r}{2}\hat{\mathbf r}.
$$
Thus energy flows radially inward. On the curved wall, the outward normal is $\hat{\mathbf r}$, and therefore
$$
\int_{\text{side}}\mathbf S\cdot\mathbf n\,dA
=-\frac{E_0J_0a}{2}(2\pi aL)
=-E_0J_0\pi a^2L.
$$
The Poynting vector is radial, so its flux through the two endcaps, whose normals are $\pm\hat{\mathbf z}$, is zero. Hence
$$
\oint_{\partial V}\mathbf S\cdot\mathbf n\,dA
=-E_0J_0\pi a^2L
=-\sigma E_0^2V,
\qquad V=\pi a^2L.
$$
The field is steady, so $d\int_Vu\,dV/dt=0$, while the material receives
$$
\int_V\mathbf J\cdot\mathbf E\,dV
=J_0E_0V=\sigma E_0^2V.
$$
The negative outward flux therefore supplies exactly the positive Ohmic power.

A local check follows from the cylindrical divergence:
$$
\nabla\cdot\mathbf S
=\frac1r\frac{\partial}{\partial r}(rS_r)
=\frac1r\frac{\partial}{\partial r}\left(-\frac{E_0J_0r^2}{2}\right)
=-E_0J_0=-\mathbf J\cdot\mathbf E.
$$
Dimensionally, $u$ has units $\mathrm{J/m^3}$, $\mathbf S$ has units $\mathrm{W/m^2}$, and both $\nabla\cdot\mathbf S$ and $\mathbf J\cdot\mathbf E$ have units $\mathrm{W/m^3}$. If $\sigma\to0$ at fixed $E_0$, then $J_0$, the magnetic field, the Poynting flux, and the Ohmic power all vanish. They also all vanish when $E_0\to0$, confirming the sign and scaling independently.

Use
$$\boldsymbol\nabla\cdot(\mathbf E\times\mathbf B)=\mathbf E\cdot(\boldsymbol\nabla\times\mathbf B)-\mathbf B\cdot(\boldsymbol\nabla\times\mathbf E).$$
Maxwell's equations then give
$$\partial_tu+\boldsymbol\nabla\cdot\mathbf S=+\mathbf J\cdot\mathbf E.$$
After integration with the outward normal, $\int_V\mathbf J\cdot\mathbf E\,dV=dU_{\rm field}/dt+\oint_{\partial V}\mathbf S\cdot\mathbf n\,dA$.

ED:187.title: Energy enters a solenoid through its cylindrical boundary while current rises
ED:187.objective: Derive the magnetoquasistatic fields of a long solenoid and use their orientations to prove that magnetic energy enters through the cylindrical sidewall at exactly the rate at which interior magnetic energy grows.
ED:187.statement: Use right-handed cylindrical coordinates $(r,\phi,z)$ with $\hat{\mathbf r}\times\hat{\boldsymbol\phi}=\hat{\mathbf z}$. A long ideal solenoid of radius $a$ has turn density $n$ and carries current $I(t)$ in the $+\hat{\boldsymbol\phi}$ direction, represented by the surface current $\mathbf K=nI\hat{\boldsymbol\phi}$ at $r=a$. The interior and exterior are vacuum. Work far from the ends and suppose that $I$ varies on a timescale $T$ satisfying $a/(cT)\ll1$, so retardation, radiation, displacement-current corrections to $\mathbf B$, and electric-field energy are higher-order effects. Take the outward normal of the interior control volume to be $+\hat{\mathbf r}$ on its cylindrical side. During the interval of interest, $I>0$ and $\dot I>0$. (a) Derive the leading interior magnetic field from Ampere's law, including its sign, while explaining the ideal-solenoid exterior approximation. (b) Apply Faraday's law to circular contours to derive the induced azimuthal electric field for both $r<a$ and $r>a$. (c) Evaluate the Poynting vector immediately inside the sidewall, determine its direction, and integrate its inward flux per unit solenoid length. (d) Derive the magnetic energy per unit length directly from the field and prove that its time derivative equals the inward Poynting power. (e) Check the result locally or by calculating the work on the surface-current sheet, verify its SI dimensions, and state what changes when $I\dot I<0$.
permittedResults: The magnetoquasistatic integral law $\oint\mathbf B\cdot d\boldsymbol\ell=\mu_0 I_{\mathrm{enc}}$ may be used for the long-solenoid field.
Faraday's law $\oint\mathbf E\cdot d\boldsymbol\ell=-d\Phi_B/dt$ may be used with a fixed contour.
In vacuum, $u_B=B^2/(2\mu_0)$ and $\mathbf S=(1/\mu_0)\mathbf E\times\mathbf B$.

acceptableStrategies.description: First fix all orientations: the positive azimuthal winding current produces a positive axial magnetic field, while Faraday's minus sign makes the induced field negative azimuthal during a current rise. Evaluate $\mathbf S$ on the interior face of the discontinuous ideal current sheet, integrate over the cylindrical area per unit length, and compare with a direct volume integral of $u_B$. Use either the local divergence of $\mathbf S$ or the negative electromagnetic work on $\mathbf K$ as an independent sign and magnitude check.

milestones.criterion: Correctly derives $\mathbf B=\mu_0nI\hat{\mathbf z}$ and both radial branches of the Faraday-induced $E_\phi$, with the negative sign for an increasing positive current.
Computes the interior-side Poynting vector and integrates $-2\pi aS_r$ to obtain the inward power per unit length with the correct orientation and units.
Derives $U_B/L$ from the field integral, proves the power equality, and supplies a valid local or surface-current-work check together with the quasistatic and end-effect qualifications.

commonErrors.description: Dropping Faraday's minus sign and taking the induced electric field to point in $+\hat{\boldsymbol\phi}$ for $\dot I>0$.
commonErrors.consequence: The resulting Poynting vector points outward during magnetic-energy growth, reversing both Lenz's-law and energy-flow signs.

commonErrors.description: Multiplying the sidewall Poynting flux by the cross-sectional area $\pi a^2$ instead of the cylindrical area $2\pi aL$.
commonErrors.consequence: The calculated power neither matches $dU_B/dt$ nor has the correct per-unit-length geometry.

hintTree.content: For an Ampere rectangle in an $r$-$z$ plane, take the interior long side along $+\hat{\mathbf z}$ and the exterior side along $-\hat{\mathbf z}$; its spanning normal is $+\hat{\boldsymbol\phi}$.
For a circular Faraday contour with normal $+\hat{\mathbf z}$, the enclosed magnetic area is $\pi r^2$ when $r<a$ but saturates at $\pi a^2$ when $r>a$.
At $r=a^-$, combine $\hat{\boldsymbol\phi}\times\hat{\mathbf z}=\hat{\mathbf r}$ with the sign of $E_\phi$, then remember that the sidewall area per unit length is $2\pi a$.

ED:187.canonicalSolution:
For a long solenoid, symmetry makes the leading magnetic field axial and nearly uniform inside. Apply Ampere's law to a rectangle whose interior long side of length $\ell$ runs along $+\hat{\mathbf z}$ and whose exterior side runs along $-\hat{\mathbf z}$. The surface normal is $+\hat{\boldsymbol\phi}$, so $n\ell$ turns, each carrying $I$, pierce it positively. Thus
$$
(B_{\mathrm{in}}-B_{\mathrm{out}})\ell=\mu_0nI\ell.
$$
For an infinitely long, tightly wound ideal solenoid, the exterior field is neglected, giving
$$
\mathbf B(r<a,t)=\mu_0nI(t)\hat{\mathbf z},\qquad \mathbf B(r>a,t)\simeq\mathbf0.
$$
Finite-solenoid return flux and end fields are excluded by the stated long-solenoid approximation.

For a circular contour traversed in $+\hat{\boldsymbol\phi}$, Faraday's law gives $2\pi rE_\phi=-d\Phi_B/dt$. If $r<a$, then $\Phi_B=\pi r^2\mu_0nI$, and hence
$$
E_\phi(r,t)=-\frac{\mu_0n\dot I(t)}{2}r,\qquad 0\le r<a.
$$
If $r>a$, only the solenoid cross-section contributes to the leading magnetic flux, so
$$
E_\phi(r,t)=-\frac{\mu_0n\dot I(t)}{2}\frac{a^2}{r},\qquad r>a.
$$
The tangential electric field is continuous at $r=a$. For $\dot I>0$, it points in $-\hat{\boldsymbol\phi}$, as required by Lenz's law.

Immediately inside the current sheet,
$$
\mathbf S(a^-,t)=\frac{1}{\mu_0}\mathbf E\times\mathbf B
=-\frac{\mu_0n^2a}{2}I\dot I\,\hat{\mathbf r}.
$$
Thus energy flows radially inward when $I\dot I>0$. For a length $L$, the outward sidewall flux is $2\pi aL S_r(a^-)$; the inward electromagnetic power per unit length is therefore
$$
\frac{P_{\mathrm{in}}}{L}=-2\pi aS_r(a^-)=\pi\mu_0n^2a^2I\dot I.
$$
There is no leading endcap contribution because $\mathbf S$ is radial in the interior model.

The magnetic energy per unit length follows directly from the energy density:
$$
\frac{U_B}{L}=\int_0^a\frac{B^2}{2\mu_0}2\pi r\,dr
=\frac{1}{2}\mu_0n^2\pi a^2I^2.
$$
Consequently,
$$
\frac{1}{L}\frac{dU_B}{dt}=\pi\mu_0n^2a^2I\dot I=\frac{P_{\mathrm{in}}}{L}.
$$
A local check gives $S_r(r)=-(\mu_0n^2I\dot I/2)r$, so
$$
\boldsymbol\nabla\cdot\mathbf S=\frac{1}{r}\frac{\partial(rS_r)}{\partial r}=-\mu_0n^2I\dot I=-\frac{\partial}{\partial t}\left(\frac{B^2}{2\mu_0}\right).
$$
Equivalently, the electromagnetic work on the surface current per unit length is
$$
2\pi a\,\mathbf K\cdot\mathbf E(a)=-\pi\mu_0n^2a^2I\dot I,
$$
so an external agent must supply the opposite power, which enters the magnetic field. Dimensionally, $[\mu_0n^2aI\dot I]=\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}}$ and $[\pi\mu_0n^2a^2I\dot I]=\mathrm{W\,m^{-1}}$. If $I\dot I<0$, every flux sign reverses: magnetic energy decreases and the Poynting vector points outward. This equality is the leading-order magnetoquasistatic energy balance; omitted electric-field energy and retardation corrections are smaller by powers of $a/(cT)$, and a finite return geometry regularizes the ideal model's remote induced electric field.

ED:188.title: A discharging spherical capacitor sends energy through nested spheres
ED:188.objective: Synthesize Gauss's law, charge conservation, Ohmic conduction, displacement current, and Poynting's theorem to determine how a spherically symmetric leaky capacitor converts field energy into heat and whether electromagnetic energy crosses its nested spherical surfaces.
ED:188.statement: Two concentric perfectly conducting spherical electrodes have radii $a<b$. The gap $a<r<b$ is filled with a homogeneous, isotropic, linear, nondispersive medium of permittivity $\epsilon>0$, conductivity $\sigma>0$, and permeability $\mu$. There are no external leads, imposed magnetic fields, or trapped magnetic flux. At $t=0$, the inner electrode carries free charge $Q_0>0$ and the outer electrode carries $-Q_0$. The capacitor then discharges through the medium while preserving exact spherical symmetry. Use spherical coordinates with $\hat{\mathbf r}$ directed outward; for a material shell $a<r<R$, its outward normal is $-\hat{\mathbf r}$ at $r=a$ and $+\hat{\mathbf r}$ at $r=R$. Assume quasistatic constitutive laws $\mathbf D=\epsilon\mathbf E$, $\mathbf J=\sigma\mathbf E$, and $\mathbf B=\mu\mathbf H$. (a) Derive the potential, electric field, radial conduction current density, total current, and differential equation for the inner charge $Q(t)$. (b) Derive the equivalent capacitance and radial resistance from field integrals and verify their product against the relaxation time. (c) Calculate the electric-field energy and total Joule power, including their time dependence. (d) Use the displacement current in Maxwell-Ampere's law to determine the magnetic field and the direction, if any, of the Poynting vector. (e) Verify Poynting's theorem for both an arbitrary shell $a<r<R$ and the full gap, integrate the power over the complete discharge, and check SI dimensions and the limits $\sigma\to0$ and $b-a\ll a$.
permittedResults: Gauss's law $\oint\mathbf D\cdot d\mathbf a=Q_{\mathrm{free,enc}}$ and charge conservation may be used.
The macroscopic Maxwell-Ampere law is $\boldsymbol\nabla\times\mathbf H=\mathbf J+\partial\mathbf D/\partial t$.

Poynting's theorem may be used as $\partial(u_E+u_B)/\partial t+\boldsymbol\nabla\cdot\mathbf S=-\mathbf J\cdot\mathbf E$, with $u_E=\epsilon E^2/2$, $u_B=\mu H^2/2$, and $\mathbf S=\mathbf E\times\mathbf H$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Use spherical Gauss surfaces to express every electric quantity in terms of the instantaneous inner charge. Charge conservation at that electrode then gives Maxwell relaxation. Independently derive $C$ and $R$ to check the same time constant. Before assigning a magnetic field to the radial conduction current, include the displacement-current density; it cancels conduction pointwise. Apply Poynting's theorem to a partial shell to distinguish local Joule conversion from electromagnetic energy transported across a spherical boundary.

milestones.criterion: Derives the radial electric field and Ohmic current from Gauss's law, obtains $Q(t)=Q_0e^{-\sigma t/\epsilon}$ with correct signs, and independently verifies $RC=\epsilon/\sigma$.
Correctly integrates the field energy and Joule power, including the factor-of-two difference between charge and energy decay rates and the identity $-dU_E/dt=P_J$.

Shows pointwise cancellation of conduction and displacement currents, concludes $\mathbf H=\mathbf S=0$ under the stated symmetry, and verifies Poynting's theorem for the partial shell and full gap with valid dimensional and limiting checks.

commonErrors.description: Omitting displacement current and applying the straight-wire expression $H=I/(2\pi r)$ to the spherically distributed radial conduction current.
commonErrors.consequence: This invents a preferred axis, violates exact spherical symmetry, and produces a spurious magnetic field and Poynting flux.

commonErrors.description: Assigning the charge-relaxation factor $e^{-t/\tau}$ directly to the field energy even though $U_E$ is quadratic in $Q$.
commonErrors.consequence: The resulting $-dU_E/dt$ is smaller than the Joule power by a factor of two, so the energy balance fails.

hintTree.content: For $a<r<b$, spherical symmetry and Gauss's law imply that $4\pi r^2D_r$ is independent of $r$ and equals the instantaneous inner charge.
The outward current through every sphere is $4\pi r^2J_r$, and it must equal $-\dot Q$. This produces a first-order equation with a geometry-independent time constant.
Differentiate $\mathbf D=Q(t)\hat{\mathbf r}/(4\pi r^2)$ before using Maxwell-Ampere's law; compare $\partial\mathbf D/\partial t$ pointwise with $\mathbf J$.

ED:188.canonicalSolution:
Let $Q(t)$ denote the free charge on the inner electrode. A spherical Gaussian surface in the gap gives
$$
4\pi r^2D_r=Q(t).
$$
Therefore
$$
\mathbf E(r,t)=\frac{Q(t)}{4\pi\epsilon r^2}\hat{\mathbf r},\qquad
\phi(r,t)=\frac{Q(t)}{4\pi\epsilon}\left(\frac{1}{r}-\frac{1}{b}\right),
$$
where the outer electrode is assigned zero potential. The volume free-charge density in the homogeneous gap vanishes because $\boldsymbol\nabla\cdot\mathbf D=0$ there. Ohm's law gives
$$
\mathbf J(r,t)=\frac{\sigma Q(t)}{4\pi\epsilon r^2}\hat{\mathbf r}.
$$
The outward conduction current is independent of radius:
$$
I(t)=4\pi r^2J_r=\frac{\sigma}{\epsilon}Q(t).
$$
Because positive charge leaves the inner electrode, $\dot Q=-I$, and hence
$$
\dot Q=-\frac{\sigma}{\epsilon}Q,\qquad Q(t)=Q_0e^{-t/\tau},\qquad \tau=\frac{\epsilon}{\sigma}.
$$
Thus $\mathbf E$ and $\mathbf J$ have the same exponential factor.

The electrode voltage is
$$
V(t)=\phi(a,t)-\phi(b,t)=\frac{Q(t)}{4\pi\epsilon}\left(\frac{1}{a}-\frac{1}{b}\right).
$$
Writing $Q=CV$ yields
$$
C=\frac{4\pi\epsilon}{1/a-1/b}=\frac{4\pi\epsilon ab}{b-a}.
$$
For radial conduction, the potential drop generated by current $I$ is
$$
V=\int_a^b\frac{I}{4\pi\sigma r^2}\,dr
=I\frac{1}{4\pi\sigma}\left(\frac{1}{a}-\frac{1}{b}\right),
$$
so
$$
R=\frac{1}{4\pi\sigma}\left(\frac{1}{a}-\frac{1}{b}\right),\qquad RC=\frac{\epsilon}{\sigma}=\tau.
$$
This independently reproduces the field relaxation time.

Integrating the electric energy density over the gap gives
$$
U_E(t)=\int_a^b\frac{\epsilon E^2}{2}4\pi r^2\,dr
=\frac{Q(t)^2}{8\pi\epsilon}\left(\frac{1}{a}-\frac{1}{b}\right)
=U_E(0)e^{-2t/\tau}.
$$
The Joule power is
$$
P_J(t)=\int_a^b\sigma E^2 4\pi r^2\,dr
=\frac{\sigma Q(t)^2}{4\pi\epsilon^2}\left(\frac{1}{a}-\frac{1}{b}\right)
=\frac{2}{\tau}U_E(t).
$$
It also equals $I(t)V(t)=V(t)^2/R$. Consequently,
$$
\frac{dU_E}{dt}=-P_J.
$$

The magnetic-field issue requires displacement current. Since
$$
\frac{\partial\mathbf D}{\partial t}
=\frac{\dot Q}{4\pi r^2}\hat{\mathbf r}
=-\frac{\sigma Q}{4\pi\epsilon r^2}\hat{\mathbf r}
=-\mathbf J,
$$
Maxwell-Ampere's law becomes $\boldsymbol\nabla\times\mathbf H=0$ throughout the gap. Faraday's law also gives $\partial\mathbf B/\partial t=0$ because the radial electric field is curl-free. With no imposed or trapped magnetic field, the regular spherically symmetric solution is
$$
\mathbf H=\mathbf B=\mathbf0,\qquad \mathbf S=\mathbf E\times\mathbf H=\mathbf0.
$$
Thus there is no inward or outward Poynting flux through the nested spheres. Conduction charge crosses every sphere, but the field energy is converted into heat locally rather than transported radially by $\mathbf S$. A nonzero magnetic field from external leads would break the stipulated spherical symmetry.

For an arbitrary material shell $a<r<R<b$, its electric energy and Joule power are
$$
U_R=\frac{Q^2}{8\pi\epsilon}\left(\frac{1}{a}-\frac{1}{R}\right),
$$
$$
P_{J,R}=\frac{\sigma Q^2}{4\pi\epsilon^2}\left(\frac{1}{a}-\frac{1}{R}\right).
$$
Because $\mathbf S=0$ on both spherical boundaries,
$$
\oint_{\partial V_R}\mathbf S\cdot\hat{\mathbf n}\,da=0,\qquad
\frac{dU_R}{dt}+P_{J,R}=0.
$$
The same equation with $R=b$ verifies Poynting's theorem for the full gap. Over the complete discharge,
$$
\int_0^\infty P_J(t)\,dt=U_E(0),
$$
so all initial field energy becomes heat.

Dimensionally, $[\epsilon/\sigma]=\mathrm{s}$, $[C]=\mathrm F$, $[R]=\Omega$, $[U_E]=\mathrm J$, and $[P_J]=\mathrm W$. As $\sigma\to0$, $\tau\to\infty$, while $\mathbf J$ and $P_J$ vanish, recovering a nonleaking capacitor. If $d=b-a\ll a$, then $1/a-1/b\simeq d/a^2$, so
$$
C\simeq\frac{4\pi\epsilon a^2}{d},\qquad
R\simeq\frac{d}{4\pi\sigma a^2},\qquad RC=\frac{\epsilon}{\sigma},
$$
which agrees with a thin layer of area $4\pi a^2$ and thickness $d$.

where the outer electrode is assigned zero potential. The volume free-charge density in the homogeneous gap vanishes because $\boldsymbol\nabla\cdot\mathbf D=0$ there. Ohm's law gives

\mathbf J(r,t)=\frac{\sigma Q(t)}{4\pi\epsilon r^2}\hat{\mathbf r}.
$$
The outward conduction current is independent of radius:
$$
I(t)=4\pi r^2J_r=\frac{\sigma}{\epsilon}Q(t).
$$
Because positive charge leaves the inner electrode, $\dot Q=-I$, and hence
$$
\dot Q=-\frac{\sigma}{\epsilon}Q,\qquad Q(t)=Q_0e^{-t/\tau},\qquad \tau=\frac{\epsilon}{\sigma}.
$$
Thus $\mathbf E$ and $\mathbf J$ have the same exponential factor.

The electrode voltage is
$$
V(t)=\phi(a,t)-\phi(b,t)=\frac{Q(t)}{4\pi\epsilon}\left(\frac{1}{a}-\frac{1}{b}\right).
$$
Writing $Q=CV$ yields
$$
C=\frac{4\pi\epsilon}{1/a-1/b}=\frac{4\pi\epsilon ab}{b-a}.
$$
For radial conduction, the potential drop generated by current $I$ is
$$
V=\int_a^b\frac{I}{4\pi\sigma r^2}\,dr
=I\frac{1}{4\pi\sigma}\left(\frac{1}{a}-\frac{1}{b}\right),
$$
so
$$
R=\frac{1}{4\pi\sigma}\left(\frac{1}{a}-\frac{1}{b}\right),\qquad RC=\frac{\epsilon}{\sigma}=\tau.
$$
This independently reproduces the field relaxation time.

Integrating the electric energy density over the gap gives
$$
U_E(t)=\int_a^b\frac{\epsilon E^2}{2}4\pi r^2\,dr
=\frac{Q(t)^2}{8\pi\epsilon}\left(\frac{1}{a}-\frac{1}{b}\right)
=U_E(0)e^{-2t/\tau}.
$$
The Joule power is
$$
P_J(t)=\int_a^b\sigma E^2 4\pi r^2\,dr
=\frac{\sigma Q(t)^2}{4\pi\epsilon^2}\left(\frac{1}{a}-\frac{1}{b}\right)
=\frac{2}{\tau}U_E(t).
$$
It also equals $I(t)V(t)=V(t)^2/R$. Consequently,
$$
\frac{dU_E}{dt}=-P_J.
$$

The magnetic-field issue requires displacement current. Since
$$
\frac{\partial\mathbf D}{\partial t}
=\frac{\dot Q}{4\pi r^2}\hat{\mathbf r}
=-\frac{\sigma Q}{4\pi\epsilon r^2}\hat{\mathbf r}
=-\mathbf J,
$$
Maxwell-Ampere's law becomes $\boldsymbol\nabla\times\mathbf H=0$ throughout the gap. Faraday's law also gives $\partial\mathbf B/\partial t=0$ because the radial electric field is curl-free. With no imposed or trapped magnetic field, the regular spherically symmetric solution is
$$
\mathbf H=\mathbf B=\mathbf0,\qquad \mathbf S=\mathbf E\times\mathbf H=\mathbf0.
$$
Thus there is no inward or outward Poynting flux through the nested spheres. Conduction charge crosses every sphere, but the field energy is converted into heat locally rather than transported radially by $\mathbf S$. A nonzero magnetic field from external leads would break the stipulated spherical symmetry.

For an arbitrary material shell $a<r<R<b$, its electric energy and Joule power are
$$
U_R=\frac{Q^2}{8\pi\epsilon}\left(\frac{1}{a}-\frac{1}{R}\right),
$$
$$
P_{J,R}=\frac{\sigma Q^2}{4\pi\epsilon^2}\left(\frac{1}{a}-\frac{1}{R}\right).
$$
Because $\mathbf S=0$ on both spherical boundaries,
$$
\oint_{\partial V_R}\mathbf S\cdot\hat{\mathbf n}\,da=0,\qquad
\frac{dU_R}{dt}+P_{J,R}=0.
$$
The same equation with $R=b$ verifies Poynting's theorem for the full gap. Over the complete discharge,
$$
\int_0^\infty P_J(t)\,dt=U_E(0),
$$
so all initial field energy becomes heat.

Dimensionally, $[\epsilon/\sigma]=\mathrm{s}$, $[C]=\mathrm F$, $[R]=\Omega$, $[U_E]=\mathrm J$, and $[P_J]=\mathrm W$. As $\sigma\to0$, $\tau\to\infty$, while $\mathbf J$ and $P_J$ vanish, recovering a nonleaking capacitor. If $d=b-a\ll a$, then $1/a-1/b\simeq d/a^2$, so
$$
C\simeq\frac{4\pi\epsilon a^2}{d},\qquad
R\simeq\frac{d}{4\pi\sigma a^2},\qquad RC=\frac{\epsilon}{\sigma},
$$
which agrees with a thin layer of area $4\pi a^2$ and thickness $d$.

Gauss's law gives $E=Q/(4\pi\epsilon r^2)$ and the radial conduction current has magnitude $I=\sigma Q/\epsilon$. Omitting displacement current, treat this spherically distributed radial current as a straight wire and write $H_\phi=I/(2\pi r)$. The resulting nonzero magnetic field then produces a spurious Poynting flux through the nested spheres.

ED:191.title: Source-free Maxwell equations admit an electric-magnetic duality rotation
ED:191.objective: Prove the continuous electric-magnetic duality symmetry of source-free vacuum Maxwell theory, establish its energy and power-flow invariants, and identify precisely why ordinary electric charge and current destroy the continuous symmetry.
ED:191.statement:
Work in a right-handed Cartesian frame in vacuum, with $\mathbf D=\epsilon_0\mathbf E$, $\mathbf H=\mathbf B/\mu_0$, and $c=(\mu_0\epsilon_0)^{-1/2}$. Assume differentiable real fields on a source-free domain $\Omega$ satisfying
$$\nabla\cdot\mathbf E=0,\qquad \nabla\cdot\mathbf B=0,\qquad \nabla\times\mathbf E=-\frac{\partial\mathbf B}{\partial t},\qquad \nabla\times\mathbf B=\frac{1}{c^2}\frac{\partial\mathbf E}{\partial t}.$$
Define $\mathbf G=c\mathbf B$, so that $\mathbf E$ and $\mathbf G$ have identical SI units. For a constant real angle $\theta$, define
$$\mathbf E_\theta=\mathbf E\cos\theta+\mathbf G\sin\theta,\qquad \mathbf G_\theta=\mathbf G\cos\theta-\mathbf E\sin\theta.$$
(a) Prove that $(\mathbf E_\theta,\mathbf G_\theta)$ satisfies the same source-free Maxwell equations and that successive rotations add their angles. (b) Derive the vacuum energy density $u$ and Poynting vector $\mathbf S$ directly from Maxwell's equations, then prove that both are invariant under the rotation. (c) In a right-moving wave with $\mathbf E=E_0\cos(kz-\omega t)\,\hat{\mathbf x}$, $\mathbf G=E_0\cos(kz-\omega t)\,\hat{\mathbf y}$, and $\omega=ck$, perform the quarter-turn $\theta=\pi/2$ and check its propagation direction. (d) Restore ordinary electric sources $\rho$ and $\mathbf J$, but no magnetic charge or magnetic current. Transform all four Maxwell equations and show explicitly which source terms obstruct continuous duality. As a separate quarter-turn check, consider a static compact charge distribution with total charge $Q$ and use a Gaussian surface with outward unit normal $\hat{\mathbf n}$.
permittedResults: The vacuum Maxwell equations and constitutive relations displayed in the statement.

The vector identity $
abla\cdot(\mathbf A	imes\mathbf C)=\mathbf C\cdot(
abla	imes\mathbf A)-\mathbf A\cdot(
abla	imes\mathbf C)$.
The divergence theorem with the stated outward surface normal.

acceptableStrategies.description: Rewrite Maxwell's equations as a symmetric pair for two fields with the same dimensions. Treat the duality map as an ordinary rotation in the two-dimensional field space, derive energy conservation before identifying its density and flux, and then repeat the rotation algebra with electric source terms retained so that every symmetry-breaking term remains visible.

milestones.criterion: Correctly rewrites the source-free equations in terms of $\mathbf G=c\mathbf B$ and proves both curl equations, both divergence equations, and the angle-addition property after rotation.
Derives the vacuum energy conservation equation from Maxwell's equations and proves separately that $u$ and $\mathbf S$ are invariant, including the quarter-turn wave direction check.
Transforms every sourced equation with correct factors and signs and uses the outward-flux charge example to demonstrate the need for magnetic sources.

commonErrors.description: Rotating $\mathbf E$ directly into $\mathbf B$ without first multiplying $\mathbf B$ by $c$.
commonErrors.consequence: The proposed sums are dimensionally meaningless, and the curl equations cannot transform as an orthogonal pair.

commonErrors.description: Rotating only $\rho$ and $\mathbf J$ by a cosine factor while discarding the sine terms generated in $\nabla\cdot\mathbf G_\theta$ and $\nabla\times\mathbf E_\theta$.
commonErrors.consequence: The proof falsely claims that ordinary electric sources preserve continuous duality even though the rotated fields require magnetic charge and current.

hintTree.content: After setting $\mathbf G=c\mathbf B$, write the curl equations so that each time derivative carries the same factor $1/c$. Apply the rotation to these equations without expanding into components.

Express $u$ as a sum of the squared lengths of the two field-space components and express $\mathbf S$ as a constant times $\mathbf E\times\mathbf G$. Orthogonality of the rotation should then control both quantities.

With sources present, first derive $\nabla\times\mathbf G=\mathbf J/(\epsilon_0c)+(1/c)\,\partial_t\mathbf E$. The terms proportional to $\sin\theta$ reveal equations that would require magnetic sources.

ED:191.canonicalSolution:
Let $\mathbf G=c\mathbf B$. The source-free equations become
$$\nabla\cdot\mathbf E=0,\qquad \nabla\cdot\mathbf G=0,$$
$$\nabla\times\mathbf E=-\frac{1}{c}\frac{\partial\mathbf G}{\partial t},\qquad \nabla\times\mathbf G=\frac{1}{c}\frac{\partial\mathbf E}{\partial t}.$$
Because $\theta$ is constant,
$$\nabla\cdot\mathbf E_\theta=\cos\theta\,\nabla\cdot\mathbf E+\sin\theta\,\nabla\cdot\mathbf G=0,$$
and similarly $\nabla\cdot\mathbf G_\theta=0$. For the curls,
$$\begin{aligned}\nabla\times\mathbf E_\theta&=-\frac{\cos\theta}{c}\partial_t\mathbf G+\frac{\sin\theta}{c}\partial_t\mathbf E\\&=-\frac{1}{c}\partial_t(\mathbf G\cos\theta-\mathbf E\sin\theta)=-\frac{1}{c}\partial_t\mathbf G_\theta,\end{aligned}$$
while
$$\begin{aligned}\nabla\times\mathbf G_\theta&=\frac{\cos\theta}{c}\partial_t\mathbf E+\frac{\sin\theta}{c}\partial_t\mathbf G\\&=\frac{1}{c}\partial_t(\mathbf E\cos\theta+\mathbf G\sin\theta)=\frac{1}{c}\partial_t\mathbf E_\theta.
\end{aligned}$$
Thus every constant $\theta$ gives another source-free solution. Multiplication of the corresponding two-dimensional rotation matrices gives $R(\theta)R(\phi)=R(\theta+\phi)$, so the transformations form a continuous one-parameter rotation group. The checks $R(0)=1$ and $R(2\pi)=1$ recover the original fields.

To derive energy conservation, use the vector identity with $\mathbf A=\mathbf E$ and $\mathbf C=\mathbf B$:
$$\begin{aligned}\nabla\cdot\left(\frac{1}{\mu_0}\mathbf E\times\mathbf B\right)&=\frac{1}{\mu_0}\left[\mathbf B\cdot(\nabla\times\mathbf E)-\mathbf E\cdot(\nabla\times\mathbf B)\right]\\&=-\frac{1}{\mu_0}\mathbf B\cdot\partial_t\mathbf B-\epsilon_0\mathbf E\cdot\partial_t\mathbf E\\&=-\partial_t\left(\frac{B^2}{2\mu_0}+\frac{\epsilon_0E^2}{2}\right).
\end{aligned}$$
Hence $\partial_tu+\nabla\cdot\mathbf S=0$, with
$$u=\frac{\epsilon_0}{2}\left(E^2+G^2\right),\qquad \mathbf S=\frac{1}{\mu_0}\mathbf E\times\mathbf B=\epsilon_0c\,\mathbf E\times\mathbf G.$$
The rotation preserves the field-space norm:
$$E_\theta^2+G_\theta^2=E^2+G^2,$$
so $u_\theta=u$. Its cross product is
$$\begin{aligned}\mathbf E_\theta\times\mathbf G_\theta&=(\mathbf E\cos\theta+\mathbf G\sin\theta)\times(\mathbf G\cos\theta-\mathbf E\sin\theta)\\&=(\cos^2\theta+\sin^2\theta)\mathbf E\times\mathbf G,
\end{aligned}$$
because each self-cross-product vanishes and $\mathbf G\times\mathbf E=-\mathbf E\times\mathbf G$. Therefore $\mathbf S_\theta=\mathbf S$.

For the specified wave, the quarter-turn gives
$$\mathbf E_{\pi/2}=E_0\cos(kz-\omega t)\,\hat{\mathbf y},\qquad \mathbf G_{\pi/2}=-E_0\cos(kz-\omega t)\,\hat{\mathbf x}.$$
Its power-flow direction remains
$$\mathbf E_{\pi/2}\times\mathbf G_{\pi/2}\ \parallel\ \hat{\mathbf y}\times(-\hat{\mathbf x})=\hat{\mathbf z},$$
so the quarter-turn changes the field orientations but not the propagation direction or energy flux.

With ordinary electric sources, the scaled equations are
$$\nabla\cdot\mathbf E=\frac{\rho}{\epsilon_0},\qquad \nabla\cdot\mathbf G=0,$$
$$\nabla\times\mathbf E=-\frac{1}{c}\partial_t\mathbf G,
\qquad \nabla\times\mathbf G=\frac{1}{c}\partial_t\mathbf E+\frac{\mathbf J}{\epsilon_0c}.$$
Rotation now gives
$$\nabla\cdot\mathbf E_\theta=\frac{\rho\cos\theta}{\epsilon_0},\qquad \nabla\cdot\mathbf G_\theta=-\frac{\rho\sin\theta}{\epsilon_0},$$
$$\nabla\times\mathbf E_\theta=-\frac{1}{c}\partial_t\mathbf G_\theta+\frac{\mathbf J\sin\theta}{\epsilon_0c},$$
$$\nabla\times\mathbf G_\theta=\frac{1}{c}\partial_t\mathbf E_\theta+\frac{\mathbf J\cos\theta}{\epsilon_0c}.$$
The nonzero divergence of $\mathbf G_\theta$ and the added term in Faraday's law are incompatible with a theory containing only electric charge and current. They have exactly the locations where magnetic charge and magnetic current would have to appear. Thus the electric-source sector is preserved only when $\sin\theta=0$; if sources themselves may reverse sign, $\theta=\pi$ gives $(\rho,\mathbf J)\mapsto(-\rho,-\mathbf J)$, but there is no continuous symmetry within ordinary electric sources.

For a static charged distribution with $\mathbf G=0$, the quarter-turn gives $\mathbf E_{\pi/2}=0$ and $\mathbf G_{\pi/2}=-\mathbf E$. If a closed Gaussian surface encloses total charge $Q$, then
$$\oint \mathbf G_{\pi/2}\cdot\hat{\mathbf n}\,da=-\oint\mathbf E\cdot\hat{\mathbf n}\,da=-\frac{Q}{\epsilon_0},$$
whereas ordinary magnetism requires $\oint\mathbf G\cdot\hat{\mathbf n}\,da=0$. This independently exhibits the forbidden magnetic charge. Finally, $c\mathbf B$ has units $({\rm m\,s^{-1}})({\rm V\,s\,m^{-2}})={\rm V\,m^{-1}}$, matching $\mathbf E$, and $\mathbf J/(\epsilon_0c)$ has units ${\rm V\,m^{-2}}$, matching a curl.

ED:193.title: Energy conservation rejects a one-way lossless interface
ED:193.objective: Use power-normalized plane-wave amplitudes, the integral Poynting theorem, and Lorentz reciprocity to show that a passive lossless two-port interface cannot transmit perfectly in one direction while completely reflecting the reverse incident mode.
ED:193.statement:
Two homogeneous, isotropic, reciprocal, lossless half-spaces occupy $z<0$ and $z>0$, with real positive wave impedances $\eta_1$ and $\eta_2$. The interface is the plane $z=0$, whose normal points from side 1 to side 2 as $+\hat{\mathbf z}$. Use phasors with physical fields equal to the real parts of quantities proportional to $e^{-i\omega t}$. Consider one normally incident polarization, with $\mathbf E\parallel\hat{\mathbf x}$, and assume that this polarization is the only propagating channel on each side. Any localized interfacial structure is linear, time-invariant, reciprocal, source-free, and lossless; evanescent fields may occur near it but carry no normal power at infinity.

Define incoming power-normalized amplitudes $a_1,a_2$ and outgoing amplitudes $b_1,b_2$, and write $\mathbf b=S\mathbf a$. A proposed boundary rule claims unit forward transmission from side 1 to side 2 and complete reflection in the reverse experiment: $t_{21}=1$, $t_{12}=0$, and $|r_2|=1$.

(a) Derive the signed time-averaged Poynting flux of waves traveling along $\pm\hat{\mathbf z}$ and hence the required power normalization. Relate power-normalized transmission coefficients to electric-field transmission coefficients.

(b) Apply the source-free, lossless Poynting theorem to arbitrary simultaneous incidence and prove that $S$ must be unitary. Show directly that the proposed columns of $S$ cannot be orthogonal.

(c) Starting from the reciprocal frequency-domain Maxwell curl equations, derive the Lorentz reciprocity divergence identity and use it to prove $S=S^{\mathsf T}$. Identify the second contradiction with the proposal.

(d) State which assumptions can be relaxed to obtain nonreciprocal transmission, and explain why breaking reciprocity alone still cannot realize the stated ideal behavior as a passive lossless two-port. Include one impedance or limiting check.
permittedResults: The time-averaged Poynting vector for $e^{-i\omega t}$ phasors is $\langle\mathbf S\rangle=\tfrac12\operatorname{Re}(\mathbf E\times\mathbf H^*)$.

The vector identity $
abla\cdot(\mathbf A	imes\mathbf B)=\mathbf B\cdot(
abla	imes\mathbf A)-\mathbf A\cdot(
abla	imes\mathbf B)$ may be used.
For reciprocal media, the constitutive tensors are symmetric; here they reduce to real positive scalars $\epsilon_j$ and $\mu_j$.
The divergence theorem may be applied to a slab enclosing the interface.

acceptableStrategies.description: First normalize each traveling mode by the square root of its impedance so that squared amplitude measures normal power. Treat the interface as a two-port and apply Poynting conservation to arbitrary coherent inputs, not merely to each incidence experiment separately; this supplies the column-orthogonality condition that rules out the proposal. Independently derive the reciprocity identity from Maxwell's curl equations and evaluate it for the two single-port scattering states. Finally separate the conditions needed for nonreciprocity from those needed to evade two-port unitarity.

milestones.criterion: Correctly derives $\langle S_z\rangle=\pm|E|^2/(2\eta_j)$, defines power-normalized amplitudes, and obtains the impedance-weighted relation between $t_{ij}$ and $T_{ij}$.
Uses power conservation for arbitrary coherent incidence to establish $S^\dagger S=I$ and explicitly demonstrates the nonorthogonality of the proposed scattering columns.

Derives the reciprocal divergence identity, obtains $t_{21}=t_{12}$, and accurately distinguishes reciprocity breaking from the additional loss, active exchange, or extra channels needed to evade two-port unitarity.

commonErrors.description: Treating equal electric-field amplitudes in media of different impedances as equal transmitted powers.
commonErrors.consequence: The inferred energy balance omits the factor $1/\eta_j$ and can falsely label a power-violating interface as lossless.

commonErrors.description: Claiming that breaking reciprocity by itself permits perfect forward transmission and complete reverse reflection in a passive lossless two-port.
commonErrors.consequence: This ignores the column-orthogonality condition imposed by unitarity, which remains valid even for a nonreciprocal lossless device.

hintTree.content: For a $+z$ wave, use $\nabla\times\mathbf E=i\omega\mathbf B$ to find $\mathbf H=(E/\eta)\hat{\mathbf y}$; reverse the propagation direction and track the sign of $\mathbf H$.

Write $S=\begin{pmatrix}r_1&t_{12}\\ t_{21}&r_2\end{pmatrix}$. Conservation for every incident vector $\mathbf a$ implies equality of two quadratic forms in $\mathbf a$, which is stronger than checking the two column norms separately.

Apply the reciprocity divergence identity to solution A incident only from side 1 and solution B incident only from side 2. Evaluate the bounding-plane terms far from the interface using power-normalized modes.

ED:193.canonicalSolution:
For a $+z$ wave, let $\mathbf E=E\hat{\mathbf x}e^{ikz}$. With the $e^{-i\omega t}$ convention, Faraday's law is $\nabla\times\mathbf E=i\omega\mathbf B$. Thus $\mathbf B=(k/\omega)E\hat{\mathbf y}$ and $\mathbf H=(E/\eta_j)\hat{\mathbf y}$, where $\eta_j=\sqrt{\mu_j/\epsilon_j}$. For a $-z$ wave, $\mathbf H=-(E/\eta_j)\hat{\mathbf y}$. Therefore
$$
\langle S_z\rangle=\frac12\operatorname{Re}(\mathbf E\times\mathbf H^*)\cdot\hat{\mathbf z}=\begin{cases}|E|^2/(2\eta_j),&+z,\\-|E|^2/(2\eta_j),&-z.\end{cases}
$$
Define a modal amplitude $u=E/\sqrt{\eta_j}$. Its power per unit area is $|u|^2/2$. Let $a_1$ denote incidence from side 1, $a_2$ incidence from side 2, and let $b_1,b_2$ be outgoing waves on sides 1 and 2. Then
$$
\begin{pmatrix}b_1\\b_2\end{pmatrix}=
S\begin{pmatrix}a_1\\a_2\end{pmatrix},\qquad
S=\begin{pmatrix}r_1&t_{12}\\t_{21}&r_2\end{pmatrix}.
$$
If $T_{21}=E_{t,2}/E_{i,1}$ is an electric-field coefficient, then
$$
t_{21}=T_{21}\sqrt{\frac{\eta_1}{\eta_2}},\qquad
t_{12}=T_{12}\sqrt{\frac{\eta_2}{\eta_1}}.
$$
Thus raw electric-field amplitudes cannot be compared as powers unless the impedances agree.

Enclose the interface by planes in the two uniform media. In monochromatic steady state, the average stored energy does not change. There is no impressed work, interfacial dissipation, or net power carried away by evanescent fields. The integral Poynting theorem therefore gives, for every incident vector $\mathbf a$,
$$
\frac12\mathbf a^\dagger\mathbf a=\frac12\mathbf b^\dagger\mathbf b
=\frac12\mathbf a^\dagger S^\dagger S\mathbf a.
$$
Because this holds for every complex $\mathbf a$,
$$
S^\dagger S=I.
$$
The columns of $S$ must consequently be orthonormal. The proposal gives
$$
\mathbf c_1=\begin{pmatrix}r_1\\1\end{pmatrix},\qquad
\mathbf c_2=\begin{pmatrix}0\\r_2\end{pmatrix},\qquad |r_2|=1.
$$
The norm of $\mathbf c_1$ forces $r_1=0$, but then
$$
\mathbf c_1^\dagger\mathbf c_2=r_2\ne0.
$$
Hence the two experiments cannot be parts of one linear, passive, lossless two-port. Checking their powers separately would miss this coherent-input orthogonality condition.

For reciprocity, consider two source-free solutions A and B at the same frequency. Maxwell's curl equations are
$$
\nabla\times\mathbf E^{A}=i\omega\boldsymbol\mu\mathbf H^{A},\qquad
\nabla\times\mathbf H^{A}=-i\omega\boldsymbol\epsilon\mathbf E^{A},
$$
with corresponding equations for B. Using the cross-product divergence identity gives
$$
\begin{aligned}
&\nabla\cdot(\mathbf E^{A}\times\mathbf H^{B}-\mathbf E^{B}\times\mathbf H^{A})\\
&=i\omega\bigl[\mathbf H^{B}\cdot\boldsymbol\mu\mathbf H^{A}-\mathbf H^{A}\cdot\boldsymbol\mu\mathbf H^{B}
+\mathbf E^{A}\cdot\boldsymbol\epsilon\mathbf E^{B}-\mathbf E^{B}\cdot\boldsymbol\epsilon\mathbf E^{A}\bigr]=0,
\end{aligned}
$$
where the last equality follows from symmetric reciprocal constitutive tensors. A reciprocal localized boundary contributes no additional antisymmetric surface term. Integrating over the enclosing slab and choosing A and B as unit incidence from ports 1 and 2 makes the incoming-incoming and outgoing-outgoing terms cancel, leaving
$$
t_{21}=t_{12}.
$$
The claimed values $t_{21}=1$ and $t_{12}=0$ therefore also violate reciprocity. In electric-field normalization, this symmetry reads
$$
\eta_1T_{21}=\eta_2T_{12},
$$
so a nonzero forward coefficient requires a nonzero reverse coefficient. For $\eta_1=\eta_2$, it reduces to $T_{21}=T_{12}$, providing the impedance check.

A magnetic bias with gyrotropic constitutive tensors, temporal modulation, or a deliberately nonreciprocal active boundary can invalidate $S=S^{\mathsf T}$. Nevertheless, a passive lossless two-port still has unitary $S$, so reciprocity breaking alone cannot produce the stated columns. Practical one-way transport additionally requires reverse absorption, gain or external power exchange, nonlinear or state-dependent operation, or extra ports, frequencies, or polarizations into which reverse power is redirected. If reverse power is redirected, it is not completely reflected into the stated single reverse mode.

graderFixtures.proofText:
For a $+z$ wave, let $\mathbf E=E\hat{\mathbf x}e^{ikz}$. With the $e^{-i\omega t}$ convention, Faraday's law is $\nabla\times\mathbf E=i\omega\mathbf B$. $$
\langle S_z\rangle=\frac12\operatorname{Re}(\mathbf E\times\mathbf H^*)\cdot\hat{\mathbf z}=\begin{cases}|E|^2/(2\eta_j),&+z,\\-|E|^2/(2\eta_j),&-z.\end{cases}
$$
Define a modal amplitude $u=E/\sqrt{\eta_j}$. Its power per unit area is $|u|^2/2$. Let $a_1$ denote incidence from side 1, $a_2$ incidence from side 2, and let $b_1,b_2$ be outgoing waves on sides 1 and 2. Then
$$
\begin{pmatrix}b_1\\b_2\end{pmatrix}=
S\begin{pmatrix}a_1\\a_2\end{pmatrix},\qquad
S=\begin{pmatrix}r_1&t_{12}\\t_{21}&r_2\end{pmatrix}.
$$
If $T_{21}=E_{t,2}/E_{i,1}$ is an electric-field coefficient, then
$$
t_{21}=T_{21}\sqrt{\frac{\eta_1}{\eta_2}},\qquad
t_{12}=T_{12}\sqrt{\frac{\eta_2}{\eta_1}}.
$$
Thus raw electric-field amplitudes cannot be compared as powers unless the impedances agree.

Enclose the interface by planes in the two uniform media. In monochromatic steady state, the average stored energy does not change. There is no impressed work, interfacial dissipation, or net power carried away by evanescent fields. The integral Poynting theorem therefore gives, for every incident vector $\mathbf a$,
$$
\frac12\mathbf a^\dagger\mathbf a=\frac12\mathbf b^\dagger\mathbf b
=\frac12\mathbf a^\dagger S^\dagger S\mathbf a.
$$
Because this holds for every complex $\mathbf a$,
$$
S^\dagger S=I.
$$
The columns of $S$ must consequently be orthonormal. The proposal gives
$$
\mathbf c_1=\begin{pmatrix}r_1\\1\end{pmatrix},\qquad
\mathbf c_2=\begin{pmatrix}0\\r_2\end{pmatrix},\qquad |r_2|=1.
$$
The norm of $\mathbf c_1$ forces $r_1=0$, but then
$$
\mathbf c_1^\dagger\mathbf c_2=r_2\ne0.
$$
Hence the two experiments cannot be parts of one linear, passive, lossless two-port. Checking their powers separately would miss this coherent-input orthogonality condition.

For reciprocity, consider two source-free solutions A and B at the same frequency. Maxwell's curl equations are
$$
\nabla\times\mathbf E^{A}=i\omega\boldsymbol\mu\mathbf H^{A},\qquad
\nabla\times\mathbf H^{A}=-i\omega\boldsymbol\epsilon\mathbf E^{A},
$$
with corresponding equations for B. Using the cross-product divergence identity gives
$$
\begin{aligned}
&\nabla\cdot(\mathbf E^{A}\times\mathbf H^{B}-\mathbf E^{B}\times\mathbf H^{A})\\
&=i\omega\bigl[\mathbf H^{B}\cdot\boldsymbol\mu\mathbf H^{A}-\mathbf H^{A}\cdot\boldsymbol\mu\mathbf H^{B}
+\mathbf E^{A}\cdot\boldsymbol\epsilon\mathbf E^{B}-\mathbf E^{B}\cdot\boldsymbol\epsilon\mathbf E^{A}\bigr]=0,
\end{aligned}
$$
where the last equality follows from symmetric reciprocal constitutive tensors. A reciprocal localized boundary contributes no additional antisymmetric surface term. Integrating over the enclosing slab and choosing A and B as unit incidence from ports 1 and 2 makes the incoming-incoming and outgoing-outgoing terms cancel, leaving
$$
t_{21}=t_{12}.
$$
The claimed values $t_{21}=1$ and $t_{12}=0$ therefore also violate reciprocity. In electric-field normalization, this symmetry reads
$$
\eta_1T_{21}=\eta_2T_{12},
$$
so a nonzero forward coefficient requires a nonzero reverse coefficient. For $\eta_1=\eta_2$, it reduces to $T_{21}=T_{12}$, providing the impedance check.

A magnetic bias with gyrotropic constitutive tensors, temporal modulation, or a deliberately nonreciprocal active boundary can invalidate $S=S^{\mathsf T}$. Nevertheless, a passive lossless two-port still has unitary $S$, so reciprocity breaking alone cannot produce the stated columns. Practical one-way transport additionally requires reverse absorption, gain or external power exchange, nonlinear or state-dependent operation, or extra ports, frequencies, or polarizations into which reverse power is redirected. If reverse power is redirected, it is not completely reflected into the stated single reverse mode.

For forward incidence, the transmitted electric field has the same amplitude as the incident electric field. Therefore $|E_t|^2=|E_i|^2$, so I conclude that the transmitted power equals the incident power for every pair of positive impedances $\eta_1$ and $\eta_2$. Hence the forward experiment is lossless.
