ED:207.canonicalSolution:
Using the angle-addition formula and eliminating $\sin\theta$ gives
$$E_x^2+E_y^2-2E_xE_y\cos\delta=E_0^2\sin^2\delta.$$
For $\delta=0$, $E_y=E_x$ and the field is linear along $y=x$. For $\delta=\pi$, $E_y=-E_x$ and it is linear along $y=-x$. For either $\delta=\pm\pi/2$, the cross term vanishes and the locus is
$$E_x^2+E_y^2=E_0^2,$$
so the polarization is circular. At $z=0$ and $\delta=+\pi/2$,
$$\mathbf E=E_0[\cos(\omega t)\hat{\mathbf x}+\sin(\omega t)\hat{\mathbf y}],$$
which moves from +x toward +y and is counterclockwise in the stated view. For $\delta=-\pi/2$, the y term reverses and the rotation is clockwise. All expressions depend on sine and cosine of $\delta$, so $\delta\mapsto\delta+2\pi$ changes nothing.

ED:208.objective: Normalize a Jones vector, reconstruct its real field, read the ellipse axes and rotation sense, and check invariance under overall phase.
ED:208.statement:

$$\mathbf E(z,t)=E_*\operatorname{Re}\{\mathbf j e^{i(kz-\omega t)}\},\qquad
\mathbf J=\begin{pmatrix}2\\ i\end{pmatrix}.$$
The wave travels along +z, and an observer on the positive-z side looks along -z with +x rightward and +y upward. (a) Normalize J to obtain j. (b) Reconstruct the real field and derive its polarization ellipse. (c) State the semiaxes, orientation, and clockwise or counterclockwise rotation in the stated view. (d) Show that multiplying j by $e^{i\alpha}$ changes none of those polarization properties.

The physical field is the real part of the phasor expression.
An overall phase shifts the common wave phase.

commonErrors.consequence: Produces incorrect semiaxes.

commonErrors.description: Treats overall phase as a relative phase between components.
commonErrors.consequence: Incorrectly changes the ellipse or handedness.

ED:208.canonicalSolution:
The normalized vector is
$$\mathbf j=\frac1{\sqrt5}\begin{pmatrix}2\\ i\end{pmatrix},$$
up to an overall phase. With $\theta=kz-\omega t$,
$$E_x=\frac{2E_*}{\sqrt5}\cos\theta,\qquad
E_y=-\frac{E_*}{\sqrt5}\sin\theta.$$
Therefore
$$\frac{E_x^2}{(2E_*/\sqrt5)^2}+\frac{E_y^2}{(E_*/\sqrt5)^2}=1.$$
The axes align with x and y, with semimajor axis $2E_*/\sqrt5$ along x and semiminor axis $E_*/\sqrt5$ along y. At z=0, $\theta=-\omega t$, so $E_y=(E_*/\sqrt5)\sin\omega t$: the field moves from +x toward +y and is counterclockwise in the stated view. Multiplication by $e^{i\alpha}$ replaces $\theta$ by $\theta+\alpha$, only changing where the field starts on the same ellipse.

ED:209.title: Stokes parameters obey a sphere identity for a Jones state
ED:209.objective: Compute Stokes parameters from a deterministic Jones vector and verify the normalized sphere identity and polarization classification.
ED:209.statement:
For a deterministic Jones vector $(E_x,E_y)^T$, define
$$S_0=|E_x|^2+|E_y|^2,\quad S_1=|E_x|^2-|E_y|^2,$$
$$S_2=2\operatorname{Re}(E_x^*E_y),\quad S_3=2\operatorname{Im}(E_x^*E_y).$$
(a) Algebraically verify $S_1^2+S_2^2+S_3^2=S_0^2$. (b) Evaluate the four parameters for $E_x=2E_*$, $E_y=iE_*$, where $E_*=1.00\ \mathrm{V\,m^{-1}}$. (c) Give the normalized Stokes vector $(S_1,S_2,S_3)/S_0$, verify its length, and classify the state as linear, circular, or elliptical.

The Stokes definitions in the statement fix the sign convention.

acceptableStrategies.description: Expand the S1 square and combine S2 and S3 through the modulus of the cross term. Then substitute the simple Jones components.

milestones.criterion: Proves the Stokes sphere identity from the definitions.

commonErrors.description: Uses $E_xE_y$ instead of $E_x^*E_y$.
commonErrors.consequence: Gets the cross Stokes parameters and sphere identity wrong.

commonErrors.description: Calls any state with nonzero S3 circular.
commonErrors.consequence: Ignores the requirement that the circular coordinate have magnitude S0.

hintTree.content: For the data, $E_x^*E_y=2iE_*^2$.

ED:209.canonicalSolution:
Let $a=|E_x|^2$ and $b=|E_y|^2$. Then
$$S_1^2=(a-b)^2,\qquad S_2^2+S_3^2=4|E_x^*E_y|^2=4ab.$$
Their sum is $(a+b)^2=S_0^2$. For the specified vector,
$$S_0=5E_*^2,\qquad S_1=3E_*^2,\qquad S_2=0,\qquad S_3=4E_*^2.$$
Thus
$$\frac{(S_1,S_2,S_3)}{S_0}=\left(\frac35,0,\frac45\right),$$
whose length is one. Because $S_3\ne0$ but $|S_3|<S_0$, the state is elliptical rather than linear or circular. Each S parameter has units $(\mathrm{V\,m^{-1}})^2$.

$$S_1=S_0\cos2\psi,\qquad S_2=S_0\sin2\psi,\qquad S_3=0.$$
(b) The coordinate axes rotate counterclockwise by $\theta$, so the same physical polarization angle has coordinate $\psi'=\psi-\theta$. Explain why the Stokes equatorial angle changes by $2\theta$. (c) For $\psi=40.0^\circ$ and $\theta=15.0^\circ$, calculate $S_1'/S_0$ and $S_2'/S_0$ and verify their quadratic invariant.

$$S_0=E_0^2,\quad S_1=E_0^2(\cos^2\psi-\sin^2\psi)=S_0\cos2\psi,$$
$$S_2=2E_0^2\sin\psi\cos\psi=S_0\sin2\psi,\qquad S_3=0.$$
After the axes rotate, $\psi'=\psi-\theta$, so the equatorial Stokes angle becomes $2\psi'=2\psi-2\theta$: it changes twice as fast as the physical coordinate angle. Numerically, $\psi'=25.0^\circ$, hence
$$\frac{S_1'}{S_0}=\cos50.0^\circ=0.642788,\qquad
\frac{S_2'}{S_0}=\sin50.0^\circ=0.766044.$$

ED:213.title: Absorption and reflection transfer different momentum for the same incident energy
ED:213.objective: Derive normal radiation pressure from vacuum field momentum and the Maxwell stress tensor, then reconcile the different absorber and mirror forces with separate energy and momentum balances.
ED:213.statement:
Vacuum fills $z<0$. A planar opaque panel has its illuminated face at $z=0$, with front-face normal $-\hat{\mathbf z}$, and an incident plane wave propagates in $+\hat{\mathbf z}$. Positive force on the panel is defined along $+\hat{\mathbf z}$. Use real fields $\mathbf E_i=E_0\cos(kz-\omega t)\hat{\mathbf x}$ and $\mathbf B_i=(E_0/c)\cos(kz-\omega t)\hat{\mathbf y}$; equivalently, the phasor convention is $\operatorname{Re}\{\widetilde{\mathbf E}e^{i(kz-\omega t)}\}$. The vacuum relations are $c=1/\sqrt{\mu_0\epsilon_0}$, $\mathbf S=\mathbf E\times\mathbf B/\mu_0$, $\mathbf g=\mathbf S/c^2$, and
$$T_{ij}=\epsilon_0\left(E_iE_j-\frac12\delta_{ij}E^2\right)+\frac1{\mu_0}\left(B_iB_j-\frac12\delta_{ij}B^2\right).$$
For a control volume around the panel, take the entrance-plane outward normal as $-\hat{\mathbf z}$ and the exit-plane outward normal as $+\hat{\mathbf z}$. Assume steady periodic fields, normal incidence, negligible edge diffraction, and a panel held fixed so that mirror recoil-energy corrections are negligible. (a) Derive $I=c\langle u\rangle$, $\langle\mathbf g\rangle=(I/c^2)\hat{\mathbf z}$, and the incident-wave value of $\langle T_{zz}\rangle$. (b) If the reflected and transmitted intensities are $I_r$ and $I_t$, use Maxwell stress and momentum balance to derive the pressure. Specialize to perfect absorption and perfect specular reflection. (c) For an incident pulse of energy $U$, write separate energy and momentum balances for the absorber and mirror. Explain why pressure must not be identified with energy density merely because the two have the same SI dimensions. (d) A uniform beam of intensity $1.50\times10^4\ \mathrm{W\,m^{-2}}$ illuminates a finite panel of area $6.00\times10^{-2}\ \mathrm{m^2}$ for $20.0\ \mathrm{s}$. Calculate the pressures, forces, intercepted energy, and impulses for perfect absorption and reflection. Use $c=2.99792458\times10^8\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.
permittedResults: The vacuum momentum balance $\mathbf F_{\mathrm{matter}}=\oint \mathbf T\cdot\hat{\mathbf n}\,dA-d(\int\mathbf g\,dV)/dt$.
The harmonic average $\langle\cos^2\theta\rangle=1/2$.
Energy conservation for a fixed passive panel, with no transmitted field for an opaque panel.

Apply the stress integral on the two faces of a control volume, and independently check the result by comparing the initial and final momenta of a finite pulse.

commonErrors.description: Treating the reflected pulse momentum as $+U/c$ because its energy is positive, rather than as $-U/c$ because it propagates in $-\hat{\mathbf z}$.
commonErrors.consequence: The mirror is assigned zero or incorrect impulse instead of $2U/c$.

commonErrors.description: Declaring $p=\langle u\rangle$ solely from the shared units $\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}=\mathrm{Pa}$ and applying that equality to both surface types.
commonErrors.consequence: The Maxwell-stress origin of pressure is lost and absorption is incorrectly predicted to exert the same pressure as reflection.

hintTree.content: For a transverse vacuum wave, the electric and magnetic terms in $u$ are equal, while both contribute negatively to $T_{zz}$.
On the incident side write $\mathbf E=(E_i+E_r)\hat{\mathbf x}$ and $\mathbf B=(E_i-E_r)\hat{\mathbf y}/c$; inspect what happens to the cross terms in $T_{zz}$.
In the pulse momentum balance, reflected energy travels in $-\hat{\mathbf z}$, so its momentum has the opposite sign even though its energy remains positive.

ED:213.canonicalSolution:
The instantaneous vacuum energy density is
$$u=\frac12\epsilon_0E_i^2+\frac1{2\mu_0}B_i^2=\epsilon_0E_i^2,$$
because $B_i=E_i/c$ and $1/(\mu_0c^2)=\epsilon_0$. Also,
$$\mathbf S=\frac{E_iB_i}{\mu_0}\hat{\mathbf z}=\epsilon_0cE_i^2\hat{\mathbf z}=cu\hat{\mathbf z}.$$
Thus
$$I=\langle S_z\rangle=c\langle u\rangle,\qquad \langle\mathbf g\rangle=\frac{\langle\mathbf S\rangle}{c^2}=\frac{I}{c^2}\hat{\mathbf z}.$$
The longitudinal stress is
$$T_{zz}=-\frac12\epsilon_0E_i^2-\frac1{2\mu_0}B_i^2=-u,$$
so $\langle T_{zz}\rangle=-I/c$.

On the incident side, represent the signed transverse fields as
$$\mathbf E=(E_i+E_r)\hat{\mathbf x},\qquad \mathbf B=\frac{E_i-E_r}{c}\hat{\mathbf y}.$$
The minus sign in the reflected magnetic field follows from its propagation in $-\hat{\mathbf z}$. Therefore
$$T_{zz}=-\frac12\epsilon_0(E_i+E_r)^2-\frac1{2\mu_0c^2}(E_i-E_r)^2=-\epsilon_0(E_i^2+E_r^2).$$
The interference terms cancel exactly, giving
$$\langle T_{zz}\rangle_{\mathrm{left}}=-\frac{I_i+I_r}{c}.$$
On the transmitted side, $\langle T_{zz}\rangle_{\mathrm{right}}=-I_t/c$. The time-averaged field-momentum derivative vanishes in steady state. The entrance normal is $-\hat{\mathbf z}$ and the exit normal is $+\hat{\mathbf z}$, so the force per area is
$$p=\frac{F_z}{A}=\frac{I_i+I_r-I_t}{c}.$$
With $R=I_r/I_i$, $T=I_t/I_i$, and absorbed fraction $\mathcal A=1-R-T$,
$$p=\frac{(\mathcal A+2R)I_i}{c}.$$
Hence a perfectly absorbing opaque panel has
$$p_{\mathrm{abs}}=\frac{I_i}{c},$$
while a perfect mirror has
$$p_{\mathrm{refl}}=\frac{2I_i}{c}.$$
The transparent limit $R=0$, $T=1$ gives $p=0$, as required.

For an incident pulse, $\mathbf g=\mathbf S/c^2$ implies incident momentum $+U\hat{\mathbf z}/c$. A perfect absorber leaves no outgoing field: the panel-support system receives momentum $+U\hat{\mathbf z}/c$, while the energy $U$ becomes internal energy, principally heat. A fixed perfect mirror returns field energy $U$ but the outgoing field momentum is $-U\hat{\mathbf z}/c$. The mirror-support impulse is therefore
$$\Delta\mathbf p_{\mathrm{matter}}=\frac{U}{c}\hat{\mathbf z}-\left(-\frac{U}{c}\hat{\mathbf z}\right)=\frac{2U}{c}\hat{\mathbf z}.$$
The ideal fixed mirror does no mechanical work because its displacement is zero; the field retains its energy. For a freely recoiling finite-mass mirror, a small Doppler energy transfer would have to be included.

Although $I/c$, energy density, and pressure all have units $\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}=\mathrm{N\,m^{-2}}$, dimensional agreement does not establish equality. The equality for absorption follows from the stress or momentum flux. Indeed, reflection gives twice the pressure for the same incident energy density.

Numerically, the intercepted power and energy are
$$P=IA=(1.50\times10^4)(6.00\times10^{-2})=9.00\times10^2\ \mathrm W,$$
$$U=P\Delta t=(9.00\times10^2)(20.0)=1.80\times10^4\ \mathrm J.$$
For absorption,
$$p_{\mathrm{abs}}=\frac{1.50\times10^4}{2.99792458\times10^8}=5.00\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{Pa},$$
$$F_{\mathrm{abs}}=pA=3.00\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm N,\qquad J_{\mathrm{abs}}=F\Delta t=6.00\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{N\,s}=\frac{U}{c}.$$
For reflection,
$$p_{\mathrm{refl}}=1.00\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{Pa},$$
$$F_{\mathrm{refl}}=6.00\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm N,\qquad J_{\mathrm{refl}}=1.20\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{N\,s}=\frac{2U}{c}.$$
The pressure unit check is $(\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}})/(\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}})=\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}=\mathrm{Pa}$, while the pulse-momentum calculation independently verifies both factors.

ED:214.title: Energy velocity equals phase speed only under declared material assumptions
ED:214.objective: Prove that averaged electromagnetic energy is transported at the phase speed in an ideal homogeneous medium and identify precisely why the conclusion need not survive dispersion or loss.
ED:214.statement:
Consider an unbounded, homogeneous, time-independent medium with no free charge or current. Its constitutive laws are local, linear, isotropic, and uncoupled:
$$\mathbf D=\epsilon\mathbf E,\qquad \mathbf B=\mu\mathbf H,$$
where $\epsilon>0$ and $\mu>0$ are real scalar constants independent of frequency. Thus the medium is lossless and nondispersive, with no conductivity or magnetoelectric coupling. A monochromatic plane wave propagates along $+\hat{\mathbf z}$ with $\mathbf E$ along $\hat{\mathbf x}$ and $\mathbf H$ along $\hat{\mathbf y}$. Use the phasor convention $\operatorname{Re}\{\widetilde{\mathbf F}(z)e^{-i\omega t}\}$, with $\widetilde{\mathbf F}\propto e^{ikz}$ and $k>0$. (a) Starting from the source-free Maxwell curl equations, derive the dispersion relation and field-amplitude ratio. (b) Derive the instantaneous Poynting theorem for the declared constitutive model and hence its electromagnetic energy density. (c) Prove that the energy velocity defined by $\mathbf v_E=\langle\mathbf S\rangle/\langle u\rangle$ is
$$\mathbf v_E=\frac1{\sqrt{\mu\epsilon}}\hat{\mathbf z},$$
and equals the phase-velocity vector. (d) Verify the theorem for $\epsilon=3.00\epsilon_0$, $\mu=1.20\mu_0$, and peak electric amplitude $E_0=100\ \mathrm{V\,m^{-1}}$ by calculating the impedance, magnetic amplitude, average flux, average energy density, and both velocities. Use $c=2.99792458\times10^8\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ and $Z_0=376.730\ \Omega$. (e) List the assumptions used and give a specific warning showing which proof step fails in a dispersive or lossy medium, without developing a causality theory.
permittedResults: The source-free curl equations $\nabla\times\mathbf E=-\partial\mathbf B/\partial t$ and $\nabla\times\mathbf H=\partial\mathbf D/\partial t$.

The vector identity $
abla\cdot(\mathbf E	imes\mathbf H)=\mathbf H\cdot(
abla	imes\mathbf E)-\mathbf E\cdot(
abla	imes\mathbf H)$.
The harmonic average $\langle\cos^2\theta\rangle=1/2$ and the vacuum identity $c=1/\sqrt{\mu_0\epsilon_0}$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Use the phasor curl equations first to determine $k$ and the wave impedance. Derive rather than assume the appropriate energy density by combining the time-domain curl equations. Then use equality of the cycle-averaged electric and magnetic energies to simplify the flux-to-energy ratio, and audit the theorem by locating the exact constitutive steps that fail with loss or dispersion.

milestones.criterion: Derives $k^2=\omega^2\mu\epsilon$ and $E_0/H_0=\sqrt{\mu/\epsilon}$ with signs consistent with the declared propagation and phasor convention.
Derives the nondispersive energy density from Maxwell's equations and uses both electric and magnetic contributions to prove $\langle\mathbf S\rangle/\langle u\rangle=1/\sqrt{\mu\epsilon}$.
Completes the numerical verification and identifies the precise constitutive or conservation-law step invalidated by dispersion or loss.

commonErrors.description: Using only $\epsilon E^2/2$ as the instantaneous energy density, or only $\epsilon E_0^2/4$ after averaging, while omitting the equal magnetic contribution.
commonErrors.consequence: The calculated energy velocity is twice the phase speed.

commonErrors.description: Applying the real, frequency-independent formulas unchanged when $\epsilon$, $\mu$, or the propagation constant are frequency-dependent or complex.
commonErrors.consequence: The proof ignores material stored energy or dissipation and asserts an energy-velocity equality outside its assumptions.

hintTree.content: With the stated phasor convention, Faraday's law gives $k\hat{\mathbf z}\times\widetilde{\mathbf E}=\omega\mu\widetilde{\mathbf H}$.
Dot the time-domain Faraday equation with $\mathbf H$, dot the Ampere-Maxwell equation with $\mathbf E$, and use the divergence identity.
After finding $H_0/E_0$, compare $\mu H_0^2$ with $\epsilon E_0^2$ before forming $\langle S\rangle/\langle u\rangle$.

ED:214.canonicalSolution:
For phasors proportional to $e^{ikz}$, Faraday's law gives
$$ik\hat{\mathbf z}\times\widetilde{\mathbf E}=i\omega\mu\widetilde{\mathbf H},$$
so
$$\widetilde{\mathbf H}=\frac{k}{\omega\mu}\hat{\mathbf z}\times\widetilde{\mathbf E}.$$
The Ampere-Maxwell equation gives
$$ik\hat{\mathbf z}\times\widetilde{\mathbf H}=-i\omega\epsilon\widetilde{\mathbf E}.$$
Substitution, using $\hat{\mathbf z}\times(\hat{\mathbf z}\times\widetilde{\mathbf E})=-\widetilde{\mathbf E}$ for a transverse wave, yields
$$k^2=\omega^2\mu\epsilon.$$
For $k>0$,
$$k=\omega\sqrt{\mu\epsilon},\qquad v_p=\frac{\omega}{k}=\frac1{\sqrt{\mu\epsilon}}.$$
The field ratio is
$$\frac{E_0}{H_0}=\frac{\omega\mu}{k}=\sqrt{\frac{\mu}{\epsilon}}\equiv Z,$$
where $Z$ is real because the medium is lossless under the stated model.

To derive the energy density, use the time-domain equations
$$\nabla\times\mathbf E=-\mu\frac{\partial\mathbf H}{\partial t},\qquad \nabla\times\mathbf H=\epsilon\frac{\partial\mathbf E}{\partial t}.$$
The divergence identity gives
$$\nabla\cdot(\mathbf E\times\mathbf H)=-\mu\mathbf H\cdot\frac{\partial\mathbf H}{\partial t}-\epsilon\mathbf E\cdot\frac{\partial\mathbf E}{\partial t}.$$
Because $\epsilon$ and $\mu$ are real, time-independent constants, this becomes
$$\frac{\partial}{\partial t}\left(\frac12\epsilon E^2+\frac12\mu H^2\right)+\nabla\cdot(\mathbf E\times\mathbf H)=0.$$
Thus
$$u=\frac12\epsilon E^2+\frac12\mu H^2,\qquad \mathbf S=\mathbf E\times\mathbf H.$$
The real fields may be written
$$\mathbf E=E_0\cos(kz-\omega t)\hat{\mathbf x},\qquad \mathbf H=H_0\cos(kz-\omega t)\hat{\mathbf y}.$$
Therefore
$$\langle\mathbf S\rangle=\frac12E_0H_0\hat{\mathbf z},$$
$$\langle u\rangle=\frac14\epsilon E_0^2+\frac14\mu H_0^2.$$
Since $H_0=E_0\sqrt{\epsilon/\mu}$, the electric and magnetic contributions are equal:
$$\mu H_0^2=\epsilon E_0^2.$$
Consequently,
$$\langle u\rangle=\frac12\epsilon E_0^2,$$
while
$$\langle S\rangle=\frac12E_0^2\sqrt{\frac{\epsilon}{\mu}}.$$
Their ratio is
$$\mathbf v_E=\frac{\langle\mathbf S\rangle}{\langle u\rangle}=\frac1{\sqrt{\mu\epsilon}}\hat{\mathbf z}=v_p\hat{\mathbf z}.$$
Its dimensions are $(\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}})/(\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}})=\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. The vacuum limit $\epsilon=\epsilon_0$, $\mu=\mu_0$ gives $v_E=v_p=c$, providing an independent check.

For the numerical medium,
$$\epsilon=2.65626\times10^{-11}\ \mathrm{F\,m^{-1}},\qquad \mu=1.50796\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{H\,m^{-1}}.$$
The impedance is
$$Z=Z_0\sqrt{\frac{1.20}{3.00}}=(376.730)\sqrt{0.400}=2.3827\times10^2\ \Omega.$$
Thus
$$H_0=\frac{E_0}{Z}=0.4197\ \mathrm{A\,m^{-1}}.$$
The average flux and energy density are
$$\langle S\rangle=\frac12E_0H_0=20.99\ \mathrm{W\,m^{-2}},$$
$$\langle u\rangle=\frac12\epsilon E_0^2=1.328\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}.$$
Hence
$$v_E=\frac{20.99}{1.328\times10^{-7}}=1.580\times10^8\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}.$$
Independently,
$$v_p=\frac{c}{\sqrt{(3.00)(1.20)}}=1.580\times10^8\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}},$$
which verifies the theorem.

The proof used linearity; homogeneity; isotropic scalar $\epsilon$ and $\mu$; local and instantaneous constitutive response; frequency independence; real positive parameters; absence of conductivity, free sources, and magnetoelectric coupling; and propagation away from interfaces. In a dispersive medium, $\mathbf D(t)$ is not generally an instantaneous constant multiple of $\mathbf E(t)$, so $\mathbf E\cdot\partial\mathbf D/\partial t$ cannot be replaced by $\partial(\epsilon E^2/2)/\partial t$. Material degrees of freedom then contribute to stored energy, and energy velocity need not equal phase velocity. In a lossy medium with conductivity $\sigma>0$, Ampere's law contains $\sigma\mathbf E$, and the energy equation acquires $-\sigma E^2$ on its right-hand side. The propagation constant and impedance are then generally complex, so the lossless proof and its velocity equality do not apply.

ED:215.title: Impedance and speed determine both permittivity and permeability
ED:215.objective: Recover both constitutive parameters of a lossless medium from independent speed and impedance measurements, then use the reconstructed parameters to determine wave amplitudes, energy density, and power flow with dimensional and physical checks.
ED:215.statement: A homogeneous, linear, isotropic, nondispersive, lossless medium fills all space and has real positive permittivity $\epsilon$ and permeability $\mu$. There are no free charges or currents. Use the phasor convention $\mathbf E(\mathbf r,t)=\operatorname{Re}\{\widetilde{\mathbf E}(\mathbf r)e^{-i\omega t}\}$. A linearly polarized plane wave travels in the $+z$ direction with $\mathbf E\parallel\hat{\mathbf x}$, so choose $\mathbf H\parallel\hat{\mathbf y}$ and define the positive intrinsic impedance by $\eta=E_0/H_0$. Measurements give $v=2.00\times10^8\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, $\eta=250\ \Omega$, and peak electric-field amplitude $E_0=120\ \mathrm{V\,m^{-1}}$. (a) Starting from the source-free Maxwell equations and the constitutive laws, derive $\epsilon=1/(\eta v)$ and $\mu=\eta/v$. (b) Calculate $\epsilon$ and $\mu$. (c) Predict the peak magnetic flux density $B_0$, the cycle-averaged total electromagnetic energy density $\langle u\rangle$, and the cycle-averaged intensity $\langle\mathbf S\rangle$. (d) Verify the SI units and positivity of the inferred parameters, and independently check the intensity using both energy transport and field amplitudes.
permittedResults: The source-free macroscopic Maxwell equations $\nabla\times\mathbf E=-\partial\mathbf B/\partial t$ and $\nabla\times\mathbf H=\partial\mathbf D/\partial t$.
The constitutive laws $\mathbf D=\epsilon\mathbf E$ and $\mathbf B=\mu\mathbf H$ for the stated medium.
The definitions $u=(\mathbf E\cdot\mathbf D+\mathbf B\cdot\mathbf H)/2$ and $\mathbf S=\mathbf E\times\mathbf H$, together with $\langle\cos^2\theta\rangle=1/2$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Represent the wave by mutually orthogonal electric and magnetic phasors proportional to $e^{ikz}$. Apply both curl equations separately: one expresses $E_0/H_0$ as $\mu v$, while the other expresses it as $1/(\epsilon v)$. After reconstructing the material parameters, exploit the equality of electric and magnetic energy contributions in a traveling lossless plane wave and cross-check $\langle S\rangle$ against $v\langle u\rangle$.

milestones.criterion: Correctly applies both phasor curl equations with the stated orientation to derive $\eta=\mu v=1/(\epsilon v)$ and hence both constitutive parameters.
Correctly obtains $\epsilon$, $\mu$, $H_0$, $B_0$, $\langle u\rangle$, and the directed intensity with peak rather than RMS amplitudes.
Explicitly verifies SI dimensions, positive material parameters, equal averaged electric and magnetic energies, and agreement between $v\langle u\rangle$ and $E_0H_0/2$.

commonErrors.description: Treats intrinsic impedance as $E_0/B_0$ rather than $E_0/H_0$.
commonErrors.consequence: Produces a dimensionally invalid magnetic-flux amplitude and destroys the distinction between ohms and wave speed.

commonErrors.description: Interchanges the solutions for the constitutive parameters, writing $\epsilon=\eta/v$ and $\mu=1/(\eta v)$.
commonErrors.consequence: Assigns permeability units to the claimed permittivity and permittivity units to the claimed permeability.

hintTree.content: With the stated convention, the phasor curl equations are $\nabla\times\widetilde{\mathbf E}=i\omega\widetilde{\mathbf B}$ and $\nabla\times\widetilde{\mathbf H}=-i\omega\widetilde{\mathbf D}$.
For phasors proportional to $e^{ikz}$, use $\hat{\mathbf z}\times\hat{\mathbf x}=\hat{\mathbf y}$ and $\hat{\mathbf z}\times\hat{\mathbf y}=-\hat{\mathbf x}$, then set $v=\omega/k$.
Compute $H_0=E_0/\eta$ and $B_0=\mu H_0$; for the checks, compare $E_0H_0/2$, $v\langle u\rangle$, and $E_0^2/(2\eta)$.

ED:215.canonicalSolution:
Take
$$\widetilde{\mathbf E}=E_0e^{ikz}\hat{\mathbf x},\qquad \widetilde{\mathbf H}=H_0e^{ikz}\hat{\mathbf y},\qquad k>0.$$
Faraday's law gives
$$ikE_0\hat{\mathbf y}=i\omega\mu H_0\hat{\mathbf y},$$
so
$$\eta=\frac{E_0}{H_0}=\frac{\omega\mu}{k}=\mu v.$$
The Ampere-Maxwell equation gives
$$-ikH_0\hat{\mathbf x}=-i\omega\epsilon E_0\hat{\mathbf x},$$
so
$$\eta=\frac{E_0}{H_0}=\frac{k}{\omega\epsilon}=\frac{1}{\epsilon v}.$$
Solving these two independently derived relations yields
$$\boxed{\epsilon=\frac{1}{\eta v}},\qquad \boxed{\mu=\frac{\eta}{v}}.$$
Numerically,

$$\mu=\frac{250\ \Omega}{2.00\times10^8\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}}=1.25\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{H\,m^{-1}}.$$
The magnetic-field amplitudes are

ED:217.title: Standing-wave Poynting flow oscillates at twice the field frequency
ED:217.objective: Prove pointwise energy conservation in an equal-amplitude electromagnetic standing wave and distinguish vanishing time-averaged transport from nonzero instantaneous oscillatory energy flow.
ED:217.statement:
Use a right-handed Cartesian system with propagation along $z$ and polarization along $x$. A homogeneous, linear, isotropic, lossless medium fills all space and obeys $\mathbf D=\epsilon\mathbf E$ and $\mathbf B=\mu\mathbf H$, where $\epsilon$ and $\mu$ are positive constants. There are no free charges, currents, interfaces, or boundaries in the domain. Define $v=1/\sqrt{\mu\epsilon}$, $\eta=\sqrt{\mu/\epsilon}$, $k=\omega/v$, and $T=2\pi/\omega$. Positive flux is measured through a plane $z=\mathrm{constant}$ with unit normal $+\hat{\mathbf z}$. Phasors, when used, follow $\mathbf E=\operatorname{Re}(\widetilde{\mathbf E}e^{-i\omega t})$.

Two coherent waves of equal peak electric amplitude $E_0$ have real electric fields
$$\mathbf E_+=E_0\cos(kz-\omega t)\hat{\mathbf x},\qquad \mathbf E_-=E_0\cos(kz+\omega t)\hat{\mathbf x}.$$
(a) Derive the corresponding magnetic fields from Faraday's law, including the sign of the backward-wave field, and superpose the waves.
(b) Compute the instantaneous Poynting vector $\mathbf S=\mathbf E\times\mathbf H$, the electromagnetic energy density $u=(\epsilon E^2+B^2/\mu)/2$, and $\partial_tu$.
(c) Verify the source-free local Poynting theorem $\partial_tu+\nabla\cdot\mathbf S=0$ pointwise.
(d) Find all spatial and temporal locations where $|\mathbf S|$ is maximal, specify its direction there, and determine its time average. Explain precisely how often the instantaneous flow changes direction, without inferring that zero average flux means zero instantaneous flux.
permittedResults: The source-free Maxwell curl equations $\nabla\times\mathbf E=-\partial_t\mathbf B$ and $\nabla\times\mathbf H=\partial_t\mathbf D$.
The definitions $\mathbf S=\mathbf E\times\mathbf H$ and $u=(\mathbf E\cdot\mathbf D+\mathbf B\cdot\mathbf H)/2$.
Standard trigonometric product-to-sum identities and the time average of a sinusoid over an integer number of periods.

acceptableStrategies.description: First use the wave-vector direction in Faraday's law to fix the opposite magnetic-field signs. Reduce the superposed fields to standing-wave products, then calculate $u$, $\partial_tu$, and $\partial_zS_z$ independently. Finally maximize the separated spatial and temporal sine factors and compare instantaneous and averaged transport.

milestones.criterion: Correctly derives the backward-wave magnetic-field sign and obtains the product-form standing fields.
Computes $\mathbf S$, $u$, and $\partial_tu$ and demonstrates pointwise cancellation using $k/\eta=\epsilon\omega$.
Identifies all flux maxima and directions and accurately distinguishes twice-frequency instantaneous energy-flow oscillation from zero time-averaged transport.

commonErrors.description: Concluding that cancellation of the two waves' average powers makes the total instantaneous Poynting vector zero.
commonErrors.consequence: This removes the local oscillatory energy exchange and prevents the pointwise Poynting balance from being demonstrated.

commonErrors.description: Assigning the backward wave a $+\hat{\mathbf y}$ magnetic field instead of the sign required by $(-\hat{\mathbf z})\times\hat{\mathbf x}=-\hat{\mathbf y}$.
commonErrors.consequence: The resulting fields do not represent oppositely directed plane waves and produce an incorrect energy flux and conservation check.

hintTree.content: With the stated phasor convention, Faraday's law gives $\widetilde{\mathbf B}=(1/\omega)\mathbf k\times\widetilde{\mathbf E}$; the wave vectors are $+k\hat{\mathbf z}$ and $-k\hat{\mathbf z}$.
After superposition, use the sum and difference of cosines. The electric and magnetic standing-wave factors are shifted by one-quarter wavelength and one-quarter period.
Write $S_z$ as a product of $\sin(2kz)$ and $\sin(2\omega t)$. When checking conservation, reduce the material constants with $k/\eta=\epsilon\omega$ before comparing terms.

ED:217.canonicalSolution:
For a monochromatic phasor, Faraday's law becomes $\nabla\times\widetilde{\mathbf E}=i\omega\widetilde{\mathbf B}$. For the forward wave, $\mathbf k_+=k\hat{\mathbf z}$, so
$$\widetilde{\mathbf B}_+=\frac{1}{\omega}\mathbf k_+\times\widetilde{\mathbf E}_+=\frac{E_0}{v}e^{ikz}\hat{\mathbf y}.$$
For the backward wave, $\mathbf k_-=-k\hat{\mathbf z}$, giving the essential sign reversal
$$\widetilde{\mathbf B}_-=\frac{1}{\omega}\mathbf k_-\times\widetilde{\mathbf E}_-=-\frac{E_0}{v}e^{-ikz}\hat{\mathbf y}.$$
Thus the real magnetic fields are
$$\mathbf B_+=\frac{E_0}{v}\cos(kz-\omega t)\hat{\mathbf y},\qquad \mathbf B_-=-\frac{E_0}{v}\cos(kz+\omega t)\hat{\mathbf y}.$$
Superposition and the sum-difference identities give
$$\mathbf E=2E_0\cos(kz)\cos(\omega t)\hat{\mathbf x},$$
$$\mathbf B=\frac{2E_0}{v}\sin(kz)\sin(\omega t)\hat{\mathbf y}.$$
Because $\mathbf H=\mathbf B/\mu$ and $\mu v=\eta$, the instantaneous Poynting vector is
$$\mathbf S=\mathbf E\times\mathbf H
=\frac{4E_0^2}{\eta}\cos(kz)\sin(kz)\cos(\omega t)\sin(\omega t)\hat{\mathbf z},$$
so
$$\boxed{\mathbf S(z,t)=\frac{E_0^2}{\eta}\sin(2kz)\sin(2\omega t)\hat{\mathbf z}}.$$
Its SI dimensions are $(\mathrm{V/m})^2/\Omega=\mathrm{W/m^2}$.

The electric contribution to the energy density is
$$\frac{\epsilon E^2}{2}=2\epsilon E_0^2\cos^2(kz)\cos^2(\omega t).$$
Since $1/(\mu v^2)=\epsilon$, the magnetic contribution is
$$\frac{B^2}{2\mu}=2\epsilon E_0^2\sin^2(kz)\sin^2(\omega t).$$
Therefore
$$u=2\epsilon E_0^2\left[\cos^2(kz)\cos^2(\omega t)+\sin^2(kz)\sin^2(\omega t)\right],$$
and differentiation gives
$$\boxed{\partial_tu=-2\epsilon\omega E_0^2\cos(2kz)\sin(2\omega t)}.$$
The divergence is purely longitudinal:
$$\nabla\cdot\mathbf S=\partial_zS_z=\frac{2kE_0^2}{\eta}\cos(2kz)\sin(2\omega t).$$
Using $1/\eta=\epsilon v$ and $k=\omega/v$ gives $k/\eta=\epsilon\omega$, hence
$$\nabla\cdot\mathbf S=2\epsilon\omega E_0^2\cos(2kz)\sin(2\omega t)=-\partial_tu.$$
Thus $\partial_tu+\nabla\cdot\mathbf S=0$ at every $z$ and $t$.

The magnitude reaches its largest possible value $E_0^2/\eta$ when both sine factors have unit magnitude. For integers $m,n$,
$$z=\frac{(2m+1)\pi}{4k}=\frac{\lambda}{8}+m\frac{\lambda}{4},\qquad t=\frac{(2n+1)\pi}{4\omega}=\frac{T}{8}+n\frac{T}{4}.$$
At these events,
$$\mathbf S=\frac{E_0^2}{\eta}(-1)^{m+n}\hat{\mathbf z},$$
so even $m+n$ gives $+\hat{\mathbf z}$ flow and odd $m+n$ gives $-\hat{\mathbf z}$ flow. At any position with $\sin(2kz)\ne0$, the flow has temporal period $T/2$ and switches sign at $t=nT/4$. It therefore executes two complete energy-flow oscillations during one field period $T$, with four sign changes over that field period; within each energy-flow period it reverses direction twice. Its time average is
$$\boxed{\langle\mathbf S\rangle_t=\mathbf0},$$
because $\langle\sin(2\omega t)\rangle_t=0$. This cancellation does not make the instantaneous flux vanish. As an independent check, $\langle u\rangle_t=\epsilon E_0^2$ is independent of $z$, consistent with no net long-term energy accumulation or transport.

ED:218.title: Unequal counterpropagating waves leave a standing-wave ratio and net power
ED:218.objective: Construct the partially standing field produced by unequal coherent counterpropagating waves, derive its envelope and net power, and recover both wave amplitudes from SWR and power measurements.
ED:218.statement:
A homogeneous, linear, isotropic, lossless medium fills all space, with $\mathbf D=\epsilon\mathbf E$, $\mathbf B=\mu\mathbf H$, $v=1/\sqrt{\mu\epsilon}$, $\eta=\sqrt{\mu/\epsilon}$, and $k=\omega/v$. There are no free sources, interfaces, or imposed boundary conditions in the domain. Use right-handed coordinates, with $x$ polarization and positive flux through a plane $z=\mathrm{constant}$ defined by normal $+\hat{\mathbf z}$. Phasors follow $\mathbf E=\operatorname{Re}(\widetilde{\mathbf E}e^{-i\omega t})$.

Two coherent waves have positive peak electric amplitudes $E_+>E_->0$ and real fields
$$\mathbf E_+=E_+\cos(kz-\omega t)\hat{\mathbf x},\qquad \mathbf E_-=E_-\cos(kz+\omega t)\hat{\mathbf x}.$$
(a) Derive their magnetic fields and construct the complex electric envelope $A(z)=|\widetilde E_x(z)|$.
(b) Find every location of the envelope maxima and minima. Derive $A_{\max}$, $A_{\min}$, and the standing-wave ratio $\mathrm{SWR}=A_{\max}/A_{\min}$.
(c) Derive the instantaneous longitudinal Poynting flux and its time average, showing explicitly why interference terms do not alter the net average power.
(d) A measurement in a medium with $\eta=200\ \Omega$ gives $\mathrm{SWR}=3.00$ and net average flux $\langle S_z\rangle=8.00\ \mathrm{W/m^2}$ in the $+z$ direction. Recover $E_+$ and $E_-$, including SI units, and check the measurements by substitution.
permittedResults: Linear superposition and the source-free Maxwell curl equations.
For the stated phasor convention, the relation derived from Faraday's law between a plane wave's electric field, wave vector, and magnetic field.
The identities $|a+be^{i\phi}|^2=a^2+b^2+2ab\cos\phi$ and $\langle\cos^2(\omega t+\phi)\rangle=1/2$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Represent the electric field by a two-term phasor and square its magnitude to expose the spatial envelope. Use the propagation direction to obtain opposite magnetic signs, multiply the total electric and magnetic fields before averaging, and then invert the measured SWR and power through the sum and difference of the two amplitudes.

milestones.criterion: Derives the phasor envelope, its extrema and locations, and the stated SWR using $E_+>E_-$.
Uses the correct backward-wave magnetic sign to obtain $\langle S_z\rangle=(E_+^2-E_-^2)/(2\eta)$ and explains cross-term cancellation.
Correctly inverts the numerical SWR and power data to obtain both amplitudes with units and checks both measured quantities.

commonErrors.description: Giving the backward wave the same magnetic-field sign as the forward wave and therefore adding rather than subtracting their directed powers.
commonErrors.consequence: The derived net flux is proportional to $E_+^2+E_-^2$ and fails the equal-amplitude standing-wave limit.

commonErrors.description: Treating the measured SWR as the traveling-wave amplitude ratio $E_+/E_-$ instead of the envelope ratio $(E_++E_-)/(E_+-E_-)$.
commonErrors.consequence: The reconstructed amplitudes do not reproduce the measured envelope maxima and minima.

hintTree.content: The electric phasor is proportional to $E_+e^{ikz}+E_-e^{-ikz}$; calculate its modulus squared before searching for extrema.
For the power calculation, the backward wave's magnetic field has the opposite sign. Multiplying the total $E_x$ and $H_y$ causes the two cross terms to cancel exactly.
Let $\Delta=E_+-E_-$. The SWR gives $E_++E_-=R\Delta$, while the measured power relates to the product $(E_++E_-)(E_+-E_-)$.

ED:218.canonicalSolution:
Faraday's law in phasor form is $\nabla\times\widetilde{\mathbf E}=i\omega\widetilde{\mathbf B}$. The forward wave has wave vector $+k\hat{\mathbf z}$, whereas the backward wave has wave vector $-k\hat{\mathbf z}$. Consequently,
$$\mathbf B_+=\frac{E_+}{v}\cos(kz-\omega t)\hat{\mathbf y},\qquad \mathbf B_-=-\frac{E_-}{v}\cos(kz+\omega t)\hat{\mathbf y}.$$
The total electric phasor is
$$\widetilde{\mathbf E}(z)=\left(E_+e^{ikz}+E_-e^{-ikz}\right)\hat{\mathbf x}.$$
Its local peak envelope satisfies
$$A^2(z)=\left|E_+e^{ikz}+E_-e^{-ikz}\right|^2
=E_+^2+E_-^2+2E_+E_-\cos(2kz).$$
Because $E_+E_->0$, maxima occur when $\cos(2kz)=1$ and minima when $\cos(2kz)=-1$. Thus, for $m\in\mathbb Z$,
$$z_{\max}=\frac{m\pi}{k}=m\frac{\lambda}{2},\qquad A_{\max}=E_++E_-,$$
$$z_{\min}=\frac{(2m+1)\pi}{2k}=(2m+1)\frac{\lambda}{4},\qquad A_{\min}=E_+-E_-.$$
The difference is positive by hypothesis, so no absolute-value ambiguity remains. Therefore
$$\boxed{\mathrm{SWR}=\frac{E_++E_-}{E_+-E_-}}.$$

Set $C_+=\cos(kz-\omega t)$ and $C_-=\cos(kz+\omega t)$. Since $\mu v=\eta$, the total fields needed for the flux are
$$E_x=E_+C_++E_-C_-,$$
$$H_y=\frac{1}{\eta}\left(E_+C_+-E_-C_-\right).$$
Their product is
$$S_z=E_xH_y=\frac{1}{\eta}\left(E_+^2C_+^2-E_-^2C_-^2\right).$$
The interference cross terms cancel algebraically before any averaging because they enter with opposite signs. Averaging the remaining squared cosines gives
$$\boxed{\langle S_z\rangle=\frac{E_+^2-E_-^2}{2\eta}}.$$
This is positive because $E_+>E_-$ and has dimensions $(\mathrm{V/m})^2/\Omega=\mathrm{W/m^2}$.

For the inversion, write $R=\mathrm{SWR}$ and $\Delta=E_+-E_-$. The envelope result gives
$$E_++E_-=R\Delta.$$
The power measurement then becomes
$$\langle S_z\rangle=\frac{(E_++E_-)(E_+-E_-)}{2\eta}=\frac{R\Delta^2}{2\eta},$$
so
$$\Delta=\sqrt{\frac{2\eta\langle S_z\rangle}{R}}.$$
The individual amplitudes are half the sum and difference:
$$E_+=\frac{R+1}{2}\Delta,\qquad E_-=\frac{R-1}{2}\Delta.$$
With $R=3.00$, $\eta=200\ \Omega$, and $\langle S_z\rangle=8.00\ \mathrm{W/m^2}$,
$$\Delta=\sqrt{\frac{2(200\ \Omega)(8.00\ \mathrm{W/m^2})}{3.00}}=32.66\ \mathrm{V/m}.$$
Hence
$$\boxed{E_+=65.3\ \mathrm{V/m},\qquad E_-=32.7\ \mathrm{V/m}}.$$
The reconstructed envelope values are $A_{\max}=98.0\ \mathrm{V/m}$ and $A_{\min}=32.7\ \mathrm{V/m}$, whose ratio is $3.00$. Also,
$$\frac{E_+^2-E_-^2}{2\eta}=\frac{(65.3\ \mathrm{V/m})^2-(32.7\ \mathrm{V/m})^2}{400\ \Omega}\approx8.00\ \mathrm{W/m^2}.$$
As limiting checks, $E_-\to0$ gives $\mathrm{SWR}\to1$ and the usual single-wave flux $E_+^2/(2\eta)$, while $E_-\to E_+$ gives zero net power and a divergent SWR because the envelope minima approach zero.

With $R=3.00$, $\eta=200\ \Omega$, and $\langle S_z\rangle=8.00\ \mathrm{W/m^2}$,
$$\Delta=\sqrt{\frac{2(200\ \Omega)(8.00\ \mathrm{W/m^2})}{3.00}}=32.66\ \mathrm{V/m}.$$
Hence
$$\boxed{E_+=65.3\ \mathrm{V/m},\qquad E_-=32.7\ \mathrm{V/m}}.$$
The reconstructed envelope values are $A_{\max}=98.0\ \mathrm{V/m}$ and $A_{\min}=32.7\ \mathrm{V/m}$, whose ratio is $3.00$. Also,
$$\frac{E_+^2-E_-^2}{2\eta}=\frac{(65.3\ \mathrm{V/m})^2-(32.7\ \mathrm{V/m})^2}{400\ \Omega}\approx8.00\ \mathrm{W/m^2}.$$
As limiting checks, $E_-\to0$ gives $\mathrm{SWR}\to1$ and the usual single-wave flux $E_+^2/(2\eta)$, while $E_-\to E_+$ gives zero net power and a divergent SWR because the envelope minima approach zero.

The measured standing-wave ratio gives
$$3=\frac{E_++E_-}{E_+-E_-},\qquad E_+=2E_-.$$
Assign the backward wave the same magnetic-field sign as the forward wave, so both directed powers add:
$$8.00=\frac{E_+^2+E_-^2}{2\eta}.$$
For $\eta=200\ \Omega$, this gives $E_-=25.3\ \mathrm{V/m}$ and $E_+=50.6\ \mathrm{V/m}$.

ED:222.title: Oblique PEC reflection determines surface charge and current together
ED:222.objective: Synthesize plane-wave transversality, PEC reflection, electromagnetic boundary conditions, and local charge conservation to determine coupled surface charge and current at oblique incidence.
ED:222.statement:
Vacuum occupies $z<0$ and an ideal PEC occupies $z>0$, with interface $z=0$ and conductor-outward normal $\mathbf n=-\hat{\mathbf z}$. The plane of incidence is the $xz$ plane, and the incidence angle $\theta$ is measured from $+\hat{\mathbf z}$. Use SI units and the phasor convention $\operatorname{Re}\{\widetilde{\mathbf F}e^{-i\omega t}\}$. A p-polarized wave of peak electric amplitude $E_0$ has
$$
\hat{\mathbf k}_i=\sin\theta\,\hat{\mathbf x}+\cos\theta\,\hat{\mathbf z},
\qquad
\hat{\mathbf e}_i=\cos\theta\,\hat{\mathbf x}-\sin\theta\,\hat{\mathbf z}.
$$
Assume the oscillatory fields inside the PEC vanish.

(a) Derive the reflected propagation direction and both components of its electric polarization by imposing transversality and $\mathbf E_t=0$. Derive the incident and reflected magnetic fields from Faraday's law.

(b) Construct the total real fields in $z<0$ and evaluate their limiting values at $z=0^-$. From the normal electric field and tangential magnetic field, determine the time-dependent surface charge density $\sigma(x,t)$ and surface current density $\mathbf K(x,t)$.

(c) Verify the local surface-continuity equation $\partial\sigma/\partial t+\nabla_s\cdot\mathbf K=0$ point by point.

(d) For $E_0=120\ \mathrm{V/m}$ and $\theta=35.0^\circ$, calculate the peak magnitudes of the normal surface electric field, $\sigma$, and $\mathbf K$. Check the normal-incidence limit.
permittedResults: Vacuum Maxwell equations and plane-wave transversality
Electric and magnetic PEC boundary conditions derived from infinitesimal pillboxes and loops
The local surface charge-conservation equation

acceptableStrategies.description: Resolve the p-polarized electric field into tangential and normal components. The tangential PEC condition fixes the reflected tangential component, while orthogonality to the reflected wave vector fixes its normal component. Add the waves before applying the pillbox and loop boundary conditions. Finally, retain the shared surface phase when differentiating the charge and current so that local, rather than merely global, conservation is tested.

milestones.criterion: Derives $\hat{\mathbf k}_r$ and the reflected polarization using both tangential-field cancellation and transversality, including the fact that the two reflected electric components have negative amplitudes in the chosen basis.
Obtains the correct phase-dependent boundary fields and uses $\mathbf n=-\hat{\mathbf z}$ to find $\sigma=2\epsilon_0E_0\sin\theta\cos\psi$ and $\mathbf K=(2E_0/Z_0)\cos\psi\,\hat{\mathbf x}$.
Verifies local surface continuity with the spatial derivative of $K_x$, reports the three numerical peak values with units, and recovers zero surface charge at normal incidence.

commonErrors.description: Reversing the entire incident electric vector on reflection instead of fixing the tangential component first and using transversality for the reflected normal component.
commonErrors.consequence: The normal electric fields are made to cancel, incorrectly eliminating the induced surface charge and producing a reflected field that is not transverse.

commonErrors.description: Claiming charge conservation from the absence of net accumulated charge while omitting the surface divergence $\partial K_x/\partial x$.
commonErrors.consequence: The pointwise continuity equation is not tested, and an inconsistent phase or amplitude between surface charge and current can go unnoticed.

hintTree.content: Specular reflection preserves the $x$ component of the wave vector and reverses its $z$ component. If $\widetilde{\mathbf E}_r=A\hat{\mathbf x}+C\hat{\mathbf z}$, use both $A=-E_0\cos\theta$ and $\mathbf k_r\cdot\widetilde{\mathbf E}_r=0$.
Define $\psi=kx\sin\theta-\omega t$. At the surface, the incident and reflected phases both reduce to $\psi$, so their normal electric components add even though their tangential components cancel.
Write $\sigma=\sigma_0\cos\psi$ and $\mathbf K=K_0\cos\psi\,\hat{\mathbf x}$. In the continuity check, use $k=\omega/c$ and $1/(cZ_0)=\epsilon_0$.

ED:222.canonicalSolution:
Specular reflection preserves the phase variation parallel to the surface and reverses the normal wave-vector component. Thus
$$
\hat{\mathbf k}_r=\sin\theta\,\hat{\mathbf x}-\cos\theta\,\hat{\mathbf z}.
$$
Let the reflected electric amplitude be $A\hat{\mathbf x}+C\hat{\mathbf z}$. Cancellation of the tangential electric field at $z=0$ requires $A=-E_0\cos\theta$. Plane-wave transversality then gives
$$
0=\hat{\mathbf k}_r\cdot\widetilde{\mathbf E}_r=A\sin\theta-C\cos\theta,
$$
so $C=A\tan\theta=-E_0\sin\theta$. Therefore
$$
\widetilde{\mathbf E}_r=-E_0(\cos\theta\,\hat{\mathbf x}+\sin\theta\,\hat{\mathbf z}).
$$
For the stated phasor convention, Faraday's law gives $\widetilde{\mathbf B}=\hat{\mathbf k}\times\widetilde{\mathbf E}/c$. Direct cross products yield
$$
\widetilde{\mathbf B}_i=\frac{E_0}{c}\hat{\mathbf y},
\qquad
\widetilde{\mathbf B}_r=\frac{E_0}{c}\hat{\mathbf y}.
$$
The magnetic amplitudes therefore add at the conductor.

Define
$$
\psi=kx\sin\theta-\omega t,
\qquad
a=kz\cos\theta.
$$
The real incident and reflected electric fields are
$$
\mathbf E_i=E_0(\cos\theta\,\hat{\mathbf x}-\sin\theta\,\hat{\mathbf z})\cos(\psi+a),
$$
$$
\mathbf E_r=-E_0(\cos\theta\,\hat{\mathbf x}+\sin\theta\,\hat{\mathbf z})\cos(\psi-a).
$$
Adding them gives, for $z<0$,
$$
\mathbf E=-2E_0\cos\theta\sin\psi\sin a\,\hat{\mathbf x}
-2E_0\sin\theta\cos\psi\cos a\,\hat{\mathbf z},
$$
while the magnetic field is
$$
\mathbf B=\frac{2E_0}{c}\cos\psi\cos a\,\hat{\mathbf y}.
$$
At $z=0^-$, where $a=0$,
$$
\mathbf E_{out}=-2E_0\sin\theta\cos\psi\,\hat{\mathbf z},
\qquad
\mathbf H_{out}=\frac{2E_0}{Z_0}\cos\psi\,\hat{\mathbf y}.
$$
The tangential electric field vanishes as required, but the normal electric field generally does not.

A Gaussian pillbox with normal $\mathbf n=-\hat{\mathbf z}$ gives, because the interior field vanishes,
$$
\sigma=\mathbf n\cdot\epsilon_0\mathbf E_{out}
=2\epsilon_0E_0\sin\theta\cos(kx\sin\theta-\omega t).
$$
The magnetic jump condition gives
$$
\mathbf K=\mathbf n\times\mathbf H_{out}
=\frac{2E_0}{Z_0}\cos(kx\sin\theta-\omega t)\,\hat{\mathbf x}.
$$
Thus the traveling surface-charge modulation and the current have the same phase.

Let $q=k\sin\theta$. Their derivatives are
$$
\frac{\partial\sigma}{\partial t}
=2\epsilon_0E_0\omega\sin\theta\sin(qx-\omega t),
$$
$$
\nabla_s\cdot\mathbf K
=\frac{\partial K_x}{\partial x}
=-\frac{2E_0q}{Z_0}\sin(qx-\omega t).
$$
Since $q=k\sin\theta=(\omega/c)\sin\theta$ and $1/(cZ_0)=\epsilon_0$,
$$
\nabla_s\cdot\mathbf K
=-2\epsilon_0E_0\omega\sin\theta\sin(qx-\omega t)
=-\frac{\partial\sigma}{\partial t}.
$$
Local surface charge conservation is therefore satisfied point by point.

For $E_0=120\ \mathrm{V/m}$ and $\theta=35.0^\circ$, using $\sin35.0^\circ=0.573576$, $\epsilon_0=8.85419\times10^{-12}\ \mathrm{F/m}$, and $Z_0=376.730\ \Omega$, the peak normal electric field is
$$
E_{n,\mathrm{pk}}=2E_0\sin\theta=137.7\ \mathrm{V/m}.
$$
The peak surface charge density is
$$
\sigma_{\mathrm{pk}}=2\epsilon_0E_0\sin\theta
=1.22\times10^{-9}\ \mathrm{C/m^2},
$$
and the peak surface current density is
$$
K_{\mathrm{pk}}=\frac{2E_0}{Z_0}=0.637\ \mathrm{A/m}.
$$
The dimensions follow from $\epsilon_0E$ giving $\mathrm{C/m^2}$ and $E/Z_0$ giving $\mathrm{A/m}$. In the limit $\theta\to0$, the normal electric field and $\sigma$ vanish, while $K_{\mathrm{pk}}\to2E_0/Z_0$, reproducing normal-incidence PEC reflection.

ED:227.title: Brewster cancellation belongs to p polarization and an impedance condition
ED:227.objective: Derive the oblique-incidence Fresnel coefficient for p polarization, prove the Brewster-angle and complementary-angle relations, and verify field and normal-power continuity numerically.
ED:227.statement: Two homogeneous, isotropic, lossless, nondispersive, nonmagnetic dielectrics occupy $z<0$ and $z>0$, with refractive indices $n_1$ and $n_2$, permittivities $\epsilon_j=\epsilon_0n_j^2$, permeabilities $\mu_j=\mu_0$, and intrinsic impedances $\eta_j=\eta_0/n_j$. The interface $z=0$ has unit normal $+\hat{\mathbf z}$ directed from medium 1 to medium 2 and carries no free surface charge or current. Use peak-amplitude phasors with physical fields $\operatorname{Re}[\mathbf E(\mathbf r)e^{-i\omega t}]$. The plane of incidence is the $xz$ plane, and all angles lie in $(0,\pi/2)$ and are measured from $+\hat{\mathbf z}$. For p polarization choose $\hat{\mathbf e}_{pi}=\cos\theta_i\hat{\mathbf x}-\sin\theta_i\hat{\mathbf z}$, $\hat{\mathbf e}_{pr}=\cos\theta_i\hat{\mathbf x}+\sin\theta_i\hat{\mathbf z}$, and $\hat{\mathbf e}_{pt}=\cos\theta_t\hat{\mathbf x}-\sin\theta_t\hat{\mathbf z}$; define $r_p=E_{0r}/E_{0i}$ and $t_p=E_{0t}/E_{0i}$ in these bases. (a) Starting from phase matching and tangential-field continuity, derive Snell's law and $r_p,t_p$ in terms of $n_1,n_2,\theta_i,\theta_t$. Identify the impedance condition for $r_p=0$. (b) For positive unequal indices, prove that cancellation implies $\theta_i+\theta_t=\pi/2$ and hence $\tan\theta_B=n_2/n_1$. (c) Set $n_1=1.50$, $n_2=2.00$, and $E_{0i}=120\ \mathrm{V\,m^{-1}}$. Calculate $\theta_B$, $\theta_t$, the incident, reflected, and transmitted electric and magnetic phasor amplitudes at $x=z=0$, and their time-averaged normal powers per unit interface area. (d) Derive the s-polarized reflection coefficient under the same sign convention and prove that it cannot vanish for positive unequal indices. Include an energy check and one limiting check.
permittedResults: The source-free phasor Maxwell equations in a homogeneous linear medium may be used.
At an interface with no free surface current, tangential components of $\mathbf E$ and $\mathbf H$ are continuous.
The time-averaged Poynting vector for peak-amplitude phasors is $\langle\mathbf S\rangle=\tfrac12\operatorname{Re}(\mathbf E\times\mathbf H^*)$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Use tangential phase matching to obtain the conserved wavevector component. Construct each magnetic field directly from $\mathbf H=(1/\eta)\hat{\mathbf k}\times\mathbf E$, taking special care with the reflected p basis. Solve the two boundary equations algebraically, interpret the zero of the numerator as an impedance condition, and combine it with Snell's law. For the numerical check, compare normal rather than total Poynting magnitudes.

milestones.criterion: Correctly derives the p-polarized coefficients with the stated reflected-field basis and identifies $\eta_2\cos\theta_t=\eta_1\cos\theta_i$ as the zero-reflection condition.
Proves complementarity and $\tan\theta_B=n_2/n_1$, then obtains the numerical field vectors, impedances, and equal normal powers with correct SI units.
Derives the s coefficient and gives a valid unequal-index impossibility argument, together with an energy or equal-index limiting check.

commonErrors.description: Uses the s-polarized boundary equations or coefficient while labeling the result as p polarized.
commonErrors.consequence: The numerator gives the wrong angular cancellation condition and falsely removes or misplaces the Brewster zero.

commonErrors.description: Equates transmitted power fraction with $|t_p|^2$ and omits the impedance and direction-cosine factors.
commonErrors.consequence: It predicts missing energy even when the reflected amplitude is zero.

hintTree.content: Tangential phase matching at $z=0$ requires $k_1\sin\theta_i=k_1\sin\theta_r=k_2\sin\theta_t$; the reflected magnetic field points along $-\hat{\mathbf y}$ for the stated p basis.
At a p-polarized zero, combine $n_1\cos\theta_t=n_2\cos\theta_i$ with Snell's law. The nontrivial solution of the resulting double-angle relation has complementary angles.
For s polarization, a hypothetical zero combined with Snell's law forces $\tan\theta_i=\tan\theta_t$; examine what that means for unequal positive indices.

ED:227.canonicalSolution:
Let $k_j=n_j\omega/c$. Equality of the phase along every point of $z=0$ gives $k_1\sin\theta_i=k_1\sin\theta_r=k_2\sin\theta_t$. Thus $\theta_r=\theta_i$ and
$$n_1\sin\theta_i=n_2\sin\theta_t.$$
From $\mathbf k\times\mathbf E=\omega\mu_0\mathbf H$, the chosen p bases give
$$\mathbf H_i=\frac{E_{0i}}{\eta_1}\hat{\mathbf y},\qquad \mathbf H_r=-\frac{E_{0r}}{\eta_1}\hat{\mathbf y},\qquad \mathbf H_t=\frac{E_{0t}}{\eta_2}\hat{\mathbf y}.$$
Continuity of $E_x$ and $H_y$ therefore gives
$$E_{0i}\cos\theta_i+E_{0r}\cos\theta_i=E_{0t}\cos\theta_t,$$
$$\frac{E_{0i}-E_{0r}}{\eta_1}=\frac{E_{0t}}{\eta_2}.$$
After division by $E_{0i}$ and elimination of $t_p$,
$$r_p=\frac{\eta_2\cos\theta_t-\eta_1\cos\theta_i}{\eta_2\cos\theta_t+\eta_1\cos\theta_i}=\frac{n_1\cos\theta_t-n_2\cos\theta_i}{n_1\cos\theta_t+n_2\cos\theta_i},$$
$$t_p=\frac{2\eta_2\cos\theta_i}{\eta_2\cos\theta_t+\eta_1\cos\theta_i}=\frac{2n_1\cos\theta_i}{n_1\cos\theta_t+n_2\cos\theta_i}.$$
The sign of $r_p$ depends on the declared reflected p basis; its zero and all powers do not. The cancellation condition is the impedance relation
$$\eta_2\cos\theta_t=\eta_1\cos\theta_i,$$
or, for nonmagnetic dielectrics, $n_1\cos\theta_t=n_2\cos\theta_i$. Together with Snell's law it gives
$$\frac{\cos\theta_i}{\cos\theta_t}=\frac{\sin\theta_t}{\sin\theta_i},\qquad \sin(2\theta_i)=\sin(2\theta_t).$$
For unequal indices, $\theta_i\ne\theta_t$. Since both angles are acute, the remaining solution is $2\theta_i=\pi-2\theta_t$, so $\theta_i+\theta_t=\pi/2$. Substitution into Snell's law gives
$$n_1\sin\theta_B=n_2\cos\theta_B,
\qquad \tan\theta_B=\frac{n_2}{n_1}.$$
For $n_1=1.50$ and $n_2=2.00$,
$$\theta_B=\tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac43\right)=53.130^\circ,
\qquad \theta_t=36.870^\circ.$$
Hence $\sin\theta_B=0.8$, $\cos\theta_B=0.6$, $\sin\theta_t=0.6$, and $\cos\theta_t=0.8$. Also $r_p=0$ and
$$t_p=\frac{2(1.50)(0.6)}{(1.50)(0.8)+(2.00)(0.6)}=0.750.$$
Using $\eta_0=376.73\ \Omega$, the impedances are $\eta_1=251.15\ \Omega$ and $\eta_2=188.37\ \Omega$. At $x=z=0$, the peak phasor amplitudes are
$$\mathbf E_i=(72\hat{\mathbf x}-96\hat{\mathbf z})\ \mathrm{V\,m^{-1}},\qquad \mathbf H_i=0.4778\hat{\mathbf y}\ \mathrm{A\,m^{-1}},$$
$$\mathbf E_r=\mathbf H_r=\mathbf 0,$$
$$\mathbf E_t=(72\hat{\mathbf x}-54\hat{\mathbf z})\ \mathrm{V\,m^{-1}},\qquad \mathbf H_t=0.4778\hat{\mathbf y}\ \mathrm{A\,m^{-1}}.$$
The equal tangential components $E_x=72\ \mathrm{V\,m^{-1}}$ and $H_y=0.4778\ \mathrm{A\,m^{-1}}$ independently verify both boundary conditions. For a lossless plane wave, $\langle S_n\rangle=E_0^2\cos\theta/(2\eta)$ with a negative sign for outward reflected power. Thus
$$\langle S_{i,z}\rangle=\frac{(120\ \mathrm{V\,m^{-1}})^2}{2(251.15\ \Omega)}(0.6)=17.20\ \mathrm{W\,m^{-2}},$$
$$\langle S_{r,z}\rangle=0,
\qquad \langle S_{t,z}\rangle=\frac{(90\ \mathrm{V\,m^{-1}})^2}{2(188.37\ \Omega)}(0.8)=17.20\ \mathrm{W\,m^{-2}}.$$
Equivalently, $R_p=|r_p|^2=0$ and
$$T_p=\frac{\eta_1}{\eta_2}\frac{\cos\theta_t}{\cos\theta_i}|t_p|^2=1,$$
which checks energy conservation. For s polarization, taking $\mathbf E\parallel\hat{\mathbf y}$ and applying the same boundary conditions gives
$$r_s=\frac{n_1\cos\theta_i-n_2\cos\theta_t}{n_1\cos\theta_i+n_2\cos\theta_t}.$$
If $r_s=0$, then $n_1\cos\theta_i=n_2\cos\theta_t$. Division of Snell's law by this equation yields $\tan\theta_i=\tan\theta_t$, so the acute angles are equal; Snell's law then requires $n_1=n_2$. Thus no s zero exists for positive unequal indices. As a limiting check, when $n_1=n_2$, both Fresnel coefficients vanish at every angle, consistent with the absence of an optical interface.

Using $\eta_0=376.73\ \Omega$, the impedances are $\eta_1=251.15\ \Omega$ and $\eta_2=188.37\ \Omega$. At $x=z=0$, the peak phasor amplitudes are
$$\mathbf E_i=(72\hat{\mathbf x}-96\hat{\mathbf z})\ \mathrm{V\,m^{-1}},\qquad \mathbf H_i=0.4778\hat{\mathbf y}\ \mathrm{A\,m^{-1}},$$
$$\mathbf E_r=\mathbf H_r=\mathbf 0,$$
$$\mathbf E_t=(72\hat{\mathbf x}-54\hat{\mathbf z})\ \mathrm{V\,m^{-1}},\qquad \mathbf H_t=0.4778\hat{\mathbf y}\ \mathrm{A\,m^{-1}}.$$
The equal tangential components $E_x=72\ \mathrm{V\,m^{-1}}$ and $H_y=0.4778\ \mathrm{A\,m^{-1}}$ independently verify both boundary conditions. For a lossless plane wave, $\langle S_n\rangle=E_0^2\cos\theta/(2\eta)$ with a negative sign for outward reflected power. Thus
$$\langle S_{i,z}\rangle=\frac{(120\ \mathrm{V\,m^{-1}})^2}{2(251.15\ \Omega)}(0.6)=17.20\ \mathrm{W\,m^{-2}},$$
$$\langle S_{r,z}\rangle=0,
\qquad \langle S_{t,z}\rangle=\frac{(90\ \mathrm{V\,m^{-1}})^2}{2(188.37\ \Omega)}(0.8)=17.20\ \mathrm{W\,m^{-2}}.$$
Equivalently, $R_p=|r_p|^2=0$ and
$$T_p=\frac{\eta_1}{\eta_2}\frac{\cos\theta_t}{\cos\theta_i}|t_p|^2=1,$$
which checks energy conservation. For s polarization, taking $\mathbf E\parallel\hat{\mathbf y}$ and applying the same boundary conditions gives
$$r_s=\frac{n_1\cos\theta_i-n_2\cos\theta_t}{n_1\cos\theta_i+n_2\cos\theta_t}.$$
If $r_s=0$, then $n_1\cos\theta_i=n_2\cos\theta_t$. Division of Snell's law by this equation yields $\tan\theta_i=\tan\theta_t$, so the acute angles are equal; Snell's law then requires $n_1=n_2$. Thus no s zero exists for positive unequal indices. As a limiting check, when $n_1=n_2$, both Fresnel coefficients vanish at every angle, consistent with the absence of an optical interface.

For the requested p polarization, use the s-polarized amplitude coefficient
$$r_p=\frac{\eta_2\cos\theta_i-\eta_1\cos\theta_t}
{\eta_2\cos\theta_i+\eta_1\cos\theta_t},\qquad t_p=1+r_p.$$
Convert the transmitted amplitude to power with
$$T=\frac{\eta_1\cos\theta_t}{\eta_2\cos\theta_i}|t_p|^2,$$
and take $R=|r_p|^2$.

ED:228.title: Total internal reflection carries a phase but no average normal power
ED:228.objective: Derive the evanescent transmitted wave and complex s-polarized reflection coefficient under total internal reflection, then connect its phase, penetration depth, and Poynting flux.
ED:228.statement: A homogeneous, isotropic, lossless, nondispersive, nonmagnetic dielectric of index $n_1$ occupies $z<0$, and a second such dielectric of index $n_2<n_1$ occupies $z>0$. The interface $z=0$ has normal $+\hat{\mathbf z}$ and no free surface charge or current. Use peak-amplitude phasors with physical fields $\operatorname{Re}[\mathbf E(\mathbf r)e^{-i\omega t}]$. An s-polarized plane wave is incident in the $xz$ plane from medium 1, with $\mathbf E_i\parallel\hat{\mathbf y}$, incidence angle $\theta_i$ measured from $+\hat{\mathbf z}$, and $\theta_i>\theta_c=\sin^{-1}(n_2/n_1)$. (a) Use tangential phase matching and the dispersion relation in medium 2 to derive the transmitted wavevector $\mathbf k_t=k_x\hat{\mathbf x}+i\kappa\hat{\mathbf z}$ and select the physically admissible sign of $\kappa$. (b) Derive the s-polarized reflection and transmission amplitudes from tangential $E_y$ and $H_x$ continuity. Prove that $|r_s|=1$ and obtain its principal phase. (c) Derive the full transmitted magnetic phasor and use it to prove that the evanescent field has zero time-averaged normal Poynting flux, while allowing tangential power flow. Relate this result to the incident and reflected normal powers. (d) For $n_1=1.50$, $n_2=1.00$, $\theta_i=60.0^\circ$, vacuum wavelength $\lambda_0=600\ \mathrm{nm}$, and incident peak amplitude $E_0=100\ \mathrm{V\,m^{-1}}$, calculate $k_x$, $\kappa$, the amplitude penetration depth $\delta=1/\kappa$, $r_s$, its principal phase, and the transmitted tangential Poynting flux at $z=0$. Include dimensional and limiting checks.
permittedResults: The homogeneous-medium dispersion relation $k^2=n^2(\omega/c)^2$ may be derived from or used with the source-free Maxwell equations.
Tangential components of $\mathbf E$ and $\mathbf H$ are continuous because the interface has no free surface current.
For peak phasors, $\langle\mathbf S\rangle=\tfrac12\operatorname{Re}(\mathbf E\times\mathbf H^*)$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Conserve the real tangential wavevector at the interface. Above critical incidence, solve the transmitted dispersion relation for an imaginary normal component and choose the branch that decays into $z>0$. Obtain $\mathbf H_t$ from $\mathbf k_t\times\mathbf E_t=\omega\mu_0\mathbf H_t$, use its tangential component in the boundary equations, and retain complex conjugation when evaluating the Poynting vector.

milestones.criterion: Correctly derives the decaying branch $k_{tz}=i\kappa$ and the stated decay constant from tangential phase matching and the transmitted dispersion relation.
Obtains the complex s-polarized amplitudes, proves $|r_s|=1$, and computes $k_x$, $\kappa$, $\delta$, $r_s$, and its phase accurately with units.
Constructs $\mathbf H_t$ and uses the phasor conjugate to show zero average normal flux, nonzero tangential flux, and cancellation of incident and reflected normal powers.

commonErrors.description: Chooses $k_{tz}=-i\kappa$ with the convention $e^{i\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf r-i\omega t}$, or treats the imaginary normal wavevector as a real propagating component.
commonErrors.consequence: The transmitted field grows into the passive half-space or acquires the conjugate reflection phase.

commonErrors.description: Drops the complex conjugate in $\mathbf E\times\mathbf H^*$ or replaces the quadrature normal magnetic component by its magnitude.
commonErrors.consequence: It assigns a nonzero average normal Poynting flux to the evanescent field and violates total-reflection power balance.

hintTree.content: Because $k_x=n_1k_0\sin\theta_i>n_2k_0$, the equation $k_x^2+k_{tz}^2=n_2^2k_0^2$ makes $k_{tz}$ imaginary. With spatial dependence $e^{ik_{tz}z}$, choose the branch that decays for $z>0$.
Write $k_{z1}=n_1k_0\cos\theta_i$. Tangential continuity gives $1+r_s=t_s$ and $k_{z1}(1-r_s)=i\kappa t_s$.
In $\mathbf E_t\times\mathbf H_t^*$, the term associated with $\kappa$ is purely imaginary, whereas the term associated with the real $k_x$ survives the real-part operation.

ED:228.canonicalSolution:
Let $k_0=\omega/c$. Tangential phase matching gives
$$k_x=n_1k_0\sin\theta_i.$$
The transmitted dispersion relation is $k_x^2+k_{tz}^2=n_2^2k_0^2$. Above the critical angle, $k_x>n_2k_0$, so
$$k_{tz}^2=-k_0^2\left(n_1^2\sin^2\theta_i-n_2^2\right).$$
Define
$$\kappa=k_0\sqrt{n_1^2\sin^2\theta_i-n_2^2}>0.$$
Since the adopted spatial factor is $e^{ik_{tz}z}$ and medium 2 extends to $z\to+\infty$, finite energy requires $k_{tz}=i\kappa$, giving
$$\mathbf k_t=k_x\hat{\mathbf x}+i\kappa\hat{\mathbf z},
\qquad \mathbf E_t=\hat{\mathbf y}\,t_sE_0e^{ik_xx-\kappa z}.$$
The other sign would grow exponentially into a passive half-space. Let $k_{z1}=n_1k_0\cos\theta_i$. From $\mathbf H=(\mathbf k\times\mathbf E)/(\mu_0\omega)$, the incident, reflected, and transmitted tangential magnetic components at $z=0$ are
$$H_{i,x}=-\frac{k_{z1}E_0}{\mu_0\omega},\qquad H_{r,x}=\frac{k_{z1}r_sE_0}{\mu_0\omega},\qquad H_{t,x}=-\frac{i\kappa t_sE_0}{\mu_0\omega}.$$
Thus continuity of $E_y$ and $H_x$ gives
$$1+r_s=t_s,
\qquad k_{z1}(1-r_s)=i\kappa t_s.$$
Solving,
$$r_s=\frac{k_{z1}-i\kappa}{k_{z1}+i\kappa},
\qquad t_s=\frac{2k_{z1}}{k_{z1}+i\kappa}.$$
Writing $a=n_1\cos\theta_i$ and $\gamma=\sqrt{n_1^2\sin^2\theta_i-n_2^2}$ gives
$$r_s=\frac{a-i\gamma}{a+i\gamma},
\qquad |r_s|=1,
\qquad \phi_s=\arg r_s=-2\tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac{\gamma}{a}\right),$$
where the last expression is the principal phase for $0<\theta_i<\pi/2$. The transmitted magnetic phasor is
$$\mathbf H_t=\frac{t_sE_0}{\mu_0\omega}\left(-i\kappa\hat{\mathbf x}+k_x\hat{\mathbf z}\right)e^{ik_xx-\kappa z}.$$
Consequently,
$$\langle\mathbf S_t\rangle=\frac12\operatorname{Re}(\mathbf E_t\times\mathbf H_t^*)
=\frac{|t_sE_0|^2e^{-2\kappa z}}{2\mu_0\omega}\operatorname{Re}\left(k_x\hat{\mathbf x}-i\kappa\hat{\mathbf z}\right),$$
so
$$\langle\mathbf S_t\rangle=\frac{|t_sE_0|^2k_x}{2\mu_0\omega}e^{-2\kappa z}\hat{\mathbf x},
\qquad \langle S_{t,z}\rangle=0.$$
Thus the normal electric-magnetic relation is in quadrature and carries reactive, not average, normal energy flow. Because $|r_s|=1$, the incident and reflected normal powers have equal magnitudes and opposite signs:
$$\langle S_{i,z}\rangle=\frac{E_0^2}{2\eta_1}\cos\theta_i,
\qquad \langle S_{r,z}\rangle=-\langle S_{i,z}\rangle.$$
For the numerical data, $k_0=2\pi/\lambda_0=1.04720\times10^7\ \mathrm{m^{-1}}$. Therefore
$$k_x=(1.50)k_0\sin60^\circ=1.36035\times10^7\ \mathrm{m^{-1}},$$
$$\gamma=\sqrt{(1.50)^2\sin^260^\circ-1}=0.829156,$$
$$\kappa=k_0\gamma=8.6829\times10^6\ \mathrm{m^{-1}},
\qquad \delta=\frac1\kappa=1.1517\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm m=115.2\ \mathrm{nm}.$$
Here $a=(1.50)\cos60^\circ=0.750$. Hence
$$r_s=\frac{0.750-i(0.829156)}{0.750+i(0.829156)}=-0.1000-0.99499i,$$
$$|r_s|=1,
\qquad \phi_s=-1.67096\ \mathrm{rad}=-95.739^\circ.$$
Also
$$t_s=1+r_s=0.9000-0.99499i,
\qquad |t_s|^2=1.800.$$
Using $\mu_0c=\eta_0=376.73\ \Omega$, the tangential flux at the interface is
$$\langle S_{t,x}(0)\rangle=\frac{|t_s|^2E_0^2}{2\eta_0}n_1\sin\theta_i=31.0\ \mathrm{W\,m^{-2}},$$
while $\langle S_{t,z}\rangle=0$. The incident and reflected normal flux magnitudes are each
$$\frac{E_0^2}{2(\eta_0/n_1)}\cos60^\circ=9.95\ \mathrm{W\,m^{-2}}.$$
The dimensions check because $k_x$ and $\kappa$ have units $\mathrm{m^{-1}}$, $\delta$ has units of length, and $E^2/\eta_0$ has units $\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}}$. As $\theta_i\to\theta_c^+$, $\kappa\to0$, so $\delta\to\infty$ and $r_s\to1$. As $\theta_i\to90^\circ$, $a\to0$ and $r_s\to-1$, consistent with the phase approaching $-\pi$.

ED:229.title: Normal-interface amplitude matching is not power matching
ED:229.objective: Derive electric-field reflection and transmission amplitudes at a lossless normal interface, then distinguish those amplitudes from reflected and transmitted power fractions by an impedance-weighted energy-flux audit.
ED:229.statement:
An infinite, sharp interface occupies $z=0$, with unit normal $+\hat{\mathbf z}$ directed from medium 1 in $z<0$ to medium 2 in $z>0$. Each medium is homogeneous, isotropic, linear, lossless, and source-free, with real constants $\epsilon_i>0$ and $\mu_i>0$. There are no imposed surface currents or surface charges. Use phasors with physical fields $\operatorname{Re}\{\widetilde{\mathbf F}e^{-i\omega t}\}$, and define $k_i=\omega\sqrt{\mu_i\epsilon_i}$ and $\eta_i=\sqrt{\mu_i/\epsilon_i}$. A normally incident wave travels in $+\hat{\mathbf z}$ and has electric amplitude $E_0\hat{\mathbf x}$.

(a) Write the incident, reflected, and transmitted electric and magnetic phasors, explicitly obtaining the magnetic-field sign for the reflected wave from Maxwell's equations.

(b) Apply the tangential interface conditions to derive the electric-field amplitude coefficients
$$r=\frac{E_r}{E_0}=\frac{\eta_2-\eta_1}{\eta_2+\eta_1},\qquad t=\frac{E_t}{E_0}=\frac{2\eta_2}{\eta_1+\eta_2}.$$

(c) Starting from the time-averaged Poynting vector, derive the power coefficients $R$ and $T$. Prove that
$$T=\frac{\eta_1}{\eta_2}|t|^2$$
and verify $R+T=1$. Explain why $|t|^2$ alone is generally not the transmitted power fraction.

(d) Evaluate $r,t,R,T$ for incidence from vacuum onto a nonmagnetic dielectric of refractive index $n=1.50$. Use $\eta_0=376.73\ \Omega$ if impedances are quoted numerically.

(e) Check the matched-impedance limit $\eta_2=\eta_1$, including the possibility that $k_1\ne k_2$.
permittedResults: The source-free frequency-domain Maxwell equations for the declared $e^{-i\omega t}$ convention may be used.
At an interface with no imposed electric or magnetic surface current, tangential $\mathbf E$ and tangential $\mathbf H$ are continuous.
For phasors, the time-averaged Poynting vector is $\langle\mathbf S\rangle=\tfrac12\operatorname{Re}(\widetilde{\mathbf E}\times\widetilde{\mathbf H}^{*})$.

acceptableStrategies.description: Use the propagation direction in Maxwell-Faraday, rather than a memorized field sketch, to fix each magnetic-field sign. Match tangential fields at $z=0$, solve the resulting two linear equations for electric amplitudes, and only then convert amplitudes to powers using the impedance-dependent Poynting flux. Audit the result algebraically, numerically, and in the impedance-matched limit.

milestones.criterion: Correctly derives all six field phasors, including the minus sign in $\widetilde{\mathbf H}_r$, and obtains the two interface equations.
Derives $r$ and $t$ and performs the impedance-weighted Poynting calculation proving $R+T=1$, rather than identifying power fractions with electric-amplitude squares.
Obtains $r=-0.200$, $t=0.800$, $R=0.0400$, and $T=0.960$ for $n=1.50$, and correctly interprets the matched-impedance limit even when $k_1\ne k_2$.

commonErrors.description: Assigning the reflected magnetic phasor the same propagation sign as the incident magnetic phasor, despite the reflected wave vector being $-k_1\hat{\mathbf z}$.
commonErrors.consequence: The tangential magnetic boundary equation is wrong, so the interface coefficients fail for unequal impedances or become internally inconsistent.

commonErrors.description: Taking the transmitted power fraction to be $|t|^2$ without accounting for the different wave impedances.
commonErrors.consequence: The vacuum-to-$n=1.50$ case gives a false transmitted fraction $0.640$ and violates the lossless power balance.

hintTree.content: For a plane-wave phasor proportional to $e^{i\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf r}$, Maxwell-Faraday relates $\widetilde{\mathbf H}$ to $\mathbf k\times\widetilde{\mathbf E}$. Reversing $\mathbf k$ therefore reverses the magnetic direction relative to a fixed electric polarization.
At $z=0$, tangential electric continuity gives one equation involving $1,r,t$. Tangential magnetic continuity gives a second equation in which the reflected term has the opposite propagation sign.

Compute each directed flux from $\tfrac12\operatorname{Re}(\widetilde{\mathbf E}\times\widetilde{\mathbf H}^{*})$. The incident and transmitted media have different ratios of electric amplitude to magnetic amplitude.

ED:229.canonicalSolution:
For a plane-wave phasor $\widetilde{\mathbf E}=\mathbf E_a e^{i\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf r}$, Maxwell-Faraday gives
$$i\mathbf k\times\widetilde{\mathbf E}=i\omega\mu\widetilde{\mathbf H},$$
so
$$\widetilde{\mathbf H}=\frac{\mathbf k\times\widetilde{\mathbf E}}{\omega\mu}.$$
Combining this with Maxwell-Ampere gives $k^2=\omega^2\mu\epsilon$. Hence $k/(\omega\mu)=\sqrt{\epsilon/\mu}=1/\eta$.

The three electric phasors are
$$\widetilde{\mathbf E}_i=\hat{\mathbf x}E_0e^{ik_1z},\qquad \widetilde{\mathbf E}_r=\hat{\mathbf x}rE_0e^{-ik_1z},\qquad \widetilde{\mathbf E}_t=\hat{\mathbf x}tE_0e^{ik_2z}.$$
For the incident wave, $\hat{\mathbf z}\times\hat{\mathbf x}=\hat{\mathbf y}$; for the reflected wave, $(-\hat{\mathbf z})\times\hat{\mathbf x}=-\hat{\mathbf y}$. Therefore
$$\widetilde{\mathbf H}_i=\hat{\mathbf y}\frac{E_0}{\eta_1}e^{ik_1z},\qquad \widetilde{\mathbf H}_r=-\hat{\mathbf y}\frac{rE_0}{\eta_1}e^{-ik_1z},\qquad \widetilde{\mathbf H}_t=\hat{\mathbf y}\frac{tE_0}{\eta_2}e^{ik_2z}.$$
The reflected magnetic sign is thus fixed by its $-\hat{\mathbf z}$ propagation direction.

At $z=0$, continuity of tangential $\mathbf E$ and $\mathbf H$ gives
$$1+r=t,\qquad \frac{1-r}{\eta_1}=\frac{t}{\eta_2}.$$
Substituting $t=1+r$ into the second equation yields
$$\eta_2(1-r)=\eta_1(1+r),$$
so
$$r=\frac{\eta_2-\eta_1}{\eta_2+\eta_1},\qquad t=1+r=\frac{2\eta_2}{\eta_1+\eta_2}.$$
Both coefficients are dimensionless.

For a forward wave of electric amplitude $E_a$ in a lossless medium,
$$\langle\mathbf S\rangle=\frac{|E_a|^2}{2\eta}\hat{\mathbf k}.$$
Thus
$$\langle\mathbf S_i\rangle=\frac{|E_0|^2}{2\eta_1}\hat{\mathbf z},\qquad \langle\mathbf S_r\rangle=-\frac{|rE_0|^2}{2\eta_1}\hat{\mathbf z},\qquad \langle\mathbf S_t\rangle=\frac{|tE_0|^2}{2\eta_2}\hat{\mathbf z}.$$
Taking outgoing power magnitudes relative to incident power gives
$$R=|r|^2,\qquad T=\frac{\eta_1}{\eta_2}|t|^2.$$
The impedance factor appears because equal electric amplitudes do not imply equal magnetic amplitudes or equal fluxes in different media. Since the impedances are real,
$$R+T=\frac{(\eta_2-\eta_1)^2}{(\eta_1+\eta_2)^2}+\frac{\eta_1}{\eta_2}\frac{4\eta_2^2}{(\eta_1+\eta_2)^2}$$
$$=\frac{(\eta_2-\eta_1)^2+4\eta_1\eta_2}{(\eta_1+\eta_2)^2}=1.$$
This independently confirms lossless energy conservation.

For vacuum incident on a nonmagnetic dielectric with $n=1.50$, $\mu_2=\mu_0$, $\epsilon_2=n^2\epsilon_0$, and
$$\eta_1=\eta_0=376.73\ \Omega,\qquad \eta_2=\frac{\eta_0}{n}=251.15\ \Omega.$$
Therefore
$$r=\frac{1-n}{1+n}=-0.200,\qquad t=\frac{2}{1+n}=0.800,$$
$$R=0.0400,
\qquad T=n|t|^2=1.50(0.800)^2=0.960.$$
Thus $R+T=1.000$. Although the transmitted electric amplitude is only $80\%$ of the incident amplitude, it carries $96\%$ of the incident power. As a magnetic-field boundary check, $1-r=1.20$ and $t\eta_1/\eta_2=0.800(1.50)=1.20$.

Finally, if $\eta_2=\eta_1$, then
$$r=0,\qquad t=1,\qquad R=0,\qquad T=1.$$
This remains true even if $k_1\ne k_2$: impedance controls normal-incidence reflection, while the unequal wave numbers merely produce different phase accumulation away from the interface. All Poynting expressions have units $|E|^2/\eta=\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}}$.

$$\widetilde{\mathbf E}_i=\hat{\mathbf x}E_0e^{ik_1z},\qquad \widetilde{\mathbf E}_r=\hat{\mathbf x}rE_0e^{-ik_1z},\qquad \widetilde{\mathbf E}_t=\hat{\mathbf x}tE_0e^{ik_2z}.$$

$$\widetilde{\mathbf H}_i=\hat{\mathbf y}\frac{E_0}{\eta_1}e^{ik_1z},\qquad \widetilde{\mathbf H}_r=-\hat{\mathbf y}\frac{rE_0}{\eta_1}e^{-ik_1z},\qquad \widetilde{\mathbf H}_t=\hat{\mathbf y}\frac{tE_0}{\eta_2}e^{ik_2z}.$$
The reflected magnetic sign is thus fixed by its $-\hat{\mathbf z}$ propagation direction.

At $z=0$, continuity of tangential $\mathbf E$ and $\mathbf H$ gives
$$1+r=t,\qquad \frac{1-r}{\eta_1}=\frac{t}{\eta_2}.$$
Substituting $t=1+r$ into the second equation yields
$$\eta_2(1-r)=\eta_1(1+r),$$
so
$$r=\frac{\eta_2-\eta_1}{\eta_2+\eta_1},\qquad t=1+r=\frac{2\eta_2}{\eta_1+\eta_2}.$$
Both coefficients are dimensionless.

For a forward wave of electric amplitude $E_a$ in a lossless medium,
$$\langle\mathbf S\rangle=\frac{|E_a|^2}{2\eta}\hat{\mathbf k}.$$
Thus
$$\langle\mathbf S_i\rangle=\frac{|E_0|^2}{2\eta_1}\hat{\mathbf z},\qquad \langle\mathbf S_r\rangle=-\frac{|rE_0|^2}{2\eta_1}\hat{\mathbf z},\qquad \langle\mathbf S_t\rangle=\frac{|tE_0|^2}{2\eta_2}\hat{\mathbf z}.$$
Taking outgoing power magnitudes relative to incident power gives
$$R=|r|^2,\qquad T=\frac{\eta_1}{\eta_2}|t|^2.$$
The impedance factor appears because equal electric amplitudes do not imply equal magnetic amplitudes or equal fluxes in different media. Since the impedances are real,
$$R+T=\frac{(\eta_2-\eta_1)^2}{(\eta_1+\eta_2)^2}+\frac{\eta_1}{\eta_2}\frac{4\eta_2^2}{(\eta_1+\eta_2)^2}$$
$$=\frac{(\eta_2-\eta_1)^2+4\eta_1\eta_2}{(\eta_1+\eta_2)^2}=1.$$
This independently confirms lossless energy conservation.

For vacuum incident on a nonmagnetic dielectric with $n=1.50$, $\mu_2=\mu_0$, $\epsilon_2=n^2\epsilon_0$, and
$$\eta_1=\eta_0=376.73\ \Omega,\qquad \eta_2=\frac{\eta_0}{n}=251.15\ \Omega.$$
Therefore
$$r=\frac{1-n}{1+n}=-0.200,\qquad t=\frac{2}{1+n}=0.800,$$
$$R=0.0400,
\qquad T=n|t|^2=1.50(0.800)^2=0.960.$$
Thus $R+T=1.000$. Although the transmitted electric amplitude is only $80\%$ of the incident amplitude, it carries $96\%$ of the incident power. As a magnetic-field boundary check, $1-r=1.20$ and $t\eta_1/\eta_2=0.800(1.50)=1.20$.

Finally, if $\eta_2=\eta_1$, then
$$r=0,\qquad t=1,\qquad R=0,\qquad T=1.$$
This remains true even if $k_1\ne k_2$: impedance controls normal-incidence reflection, while the unequal wave numbers merely produce different phase accumulation away from the interface. All Poynting expressions have units $|E|^2/\eta=\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}}$.

Give the reflected magnetic phasor the same propagation sign as the incident one:
$$H_i=\frac{E_i}{\eta_1},\qquad H_r=\frac{E_r}{\eta_1},\qquad H_t=\frac{E_t}{\eta_2}.$$
Tangential continuity therefore gives
$$1+r=t,\qquad \frac{1+r}{\eta_1}=\frac{t}{\eta_2},$$
which are the interface equations for the electric-field amplitudes.
